Prisoner sightings at that moment were checked against the lists of men Hanoi agreed to free. Anyone sighted but not listed became an open question for years. Analysts therefore handled January 1973 reports with special care. This file preserves one such sighting in full, a district-level claim from the war's final settlement.
cia-0000013854: North Vietnamese officials in Vinh put shot down American planes on show, and a CIA note dated June 2, 1967, reports the display. Photos and wreckage were set out for the public to see. Such shows aimed to prove that the north could beat American air power. They also told watching pilots what a crash could mean.
cia-0000015254: Argentina is the source of a short CIA file on unidentified flying objects, dated April 2, 1965. The file holds only page three of its source, per the title. Saucer reports from South America reached Washington through the clipping net. A lone page shows how thin some of those far off reports could be.
cia-0000015454: Unidentified flying objects came before the Intelligence Advisory Committee in a CIA record dated January 3, 1953. That committee brought senior intelligence leaders together to weigh matters jointly. Saucer reports had grown too loud by early 1953 to stay at a low level. The entry marks the moment the subject reached the top tables of American intelligence, if only as one item among many.
cia-0000022354: Thanks from the Abel family for the return of Rudolf Abel fill a letter kept in a CIA record dated in 1962. Abel came home to the Soviet Union in the February 1962 swap that freed Gary Powers. A family's gratitude, filed by an intelligence agency, is an odd and human relic. The letter closes the swap story on a note of relief.
cia-0000023754: President Frei and the highest levels of the armed forces are the concern of a CIA document dated in 1970. The title breaks off at the words remain, leaving their state unstated. Eduardo Frei was Chile's president until late 1970, when Allende was set to succeed him. A document joining the president and the top brass belongs to that tense change of power.
cia-0000025054: An American Air Force pilot was captured near Ban Toumlan, in Saravane Province, Laos, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. The title adds subsequent events, then breaks off in the catalog. Saravane was a southern province crossed by the Ho Chi Minh Trail. A capture there in 1973 came at the very end of the air war over the trail.
cia-0000036854:
An editorial looking back over enemy losses fills a CIA record dated January 3, 1968. It recalls the numbers from November 1966 through November 1967, a full year of war. Counts of enemy dead were among the most argued-over figures of the Vietnam War.

The editorial returns to those yearly numbers and the claims built on them. American strategy leaned on loss counts, so each figure carried political weight. The file preserves a piece of that argument as it appeared in print at the time. A year-end editorial was a natural place to defend the count, since critics attacked it often.
cia-0000037954:
A CIA Latin America review dated August 1, 1982 takes up Peru and its Sendero Luminoso movement. Sendero Luminoso, the Shining Path, had launched its armed campaign in Peru in 1980. The review weighs the group early in its long and violent war.

Inside, the focus is the movement itself: its aims, its methods, and its growth. Reviews of this kind warned officials about threats still small enough to overlook. The file captures a turning point for the movement. The Shining Path was passing from a local problem in the Andes into a national danger. Peru would fight that danger for more than a decade.
cia-0000038454:
Lieutenant Commander James E. Teague is the subject of a CIA record dated January 2, 1974. The file notes that Mr. and Mrs. Erlan M. Teague requested information on his MIA and POW status. Family requests drove much of the accounting work in those years.

Inside, the parents' request stands at the center of the record. For every missing man there was a family asking the government what it knew. The file shows the human engine behind the vast paperwork. Two parents and one missing son stand behind it. An official system was built to give them an answer, however long it took.
cia-0000039954:
A CIA country survey titled simply Cuba is dated July 4, 1965. By then Fidel Castro's revolution had ruled the island for six years. Cuba sat at the center of Cold War tension in the Americas.

Inside, the survey presents the island as American analysts saw it in mid-decade. Country surveys of this kind covered government, economy, and armed strength in one brief. The file gives readers a dated portrait of Cuba in 1965. It came three years after the missile crisis. The island was still watched more closely than almost any other small country on earth.
cia-0000049154: Lt. Col. Guillermo Alfredo Benavides Moreno is the named subject of a CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. Benavides commanded the military academy whose troops carried out the Jesuit murders the year before. His file, kept while his case moved, is one of the series' most consequential dossiers.
cia-0000049254:
El Salvador's judicial process is assessed in a CIA paper from 1989, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. Courts were the war's weakest institution: judges were threatened, witnesses vanished, and cases against soldiers almost never reached a verdict. The paper grades that system while the war still ran through it.

Inside, the process is followed as a case would meet it, from arrest through investigation to the rare courtroom ending. The grade mattered beyond El Salvador, since American aid arguments leaned on claims that justice there worked. The paper survives as one of the clearest measures of how far those claims stood from the truth on the ground.
cia-0000049354: A Salvadoran insurgent offensive is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049354, dated February 1, 1982, filed under Central America. The item carries a Truth Commission note and centers on insurgent action. It is a short declassified record whose heading states the event type plainly, one of the agency's early-war notices on fighting in El Salvador.
cia-0000072254: Iraq's chemical warfare program, described as more self-reliant and more deadly, is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000072254, dated August 1, 1990. The record notes the paper as sanitized. Readers find a short declassified assessment whose heading states the program's direction in stark terms, preserved as the agency summarized Iraq's chemical effort at that date.
cia-0000096654: Nicaragua factors and figures in the process leading to a transition government, in shortened heading form, fill declassified CIA document 0000096654, dated August 4, 1978. The title promises both analysis and numbers. Readers find a short declassified paper on Nicaragua's path toward a new government, preserved as a dated item from the year before that transition.
cia-0000102954:
Incarceration of Prisoners is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000102954, dated March 2, 1986. The sample text covers Soviet practice across 1955 to 1979. It explains what happened to a prisoner after an investigation ended and a court had passed sentence.

After sentencing, the prisoner was moved to a labor camp, except that grave crimes could bring up to five years in prison first. For theft and hooliganism, the investigation usually lasted about two months, though it could run longer with permission. Prisons were usually overcrowded, yet no new ones were planned, a choice one Estonian official tied to ideology.
cia-0000108154: The Significance of the New Indonesian Government is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000108154, dated August 5, 1953. The heading asks what a new government in Indonesia meant, in one word: significance. No leader or party is named in the title itself. The brief record is a government change item from the summer of 1953 in the files.
cia-0000115454: Insurgency and Instability in Central America -- National Intelligence Estimate is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000115454, dated August 5, 1981. The title marks a formal estimate on unrest across one region, Central America. Two linked words, insurgency and instability, fill the front of the heading. The brief record is a regional estimate item from the summer of 1981 as released.
cia-0000119754: An October 1956 status report on Hungary, given by the CIA Director at the White House to a bipartisan group of leaders. The heading breaks off before finishing that word, but the setting is clear: the agency chief briefing both parties as the crisis deepened. Briefing leaders of both parties together was crisis practice in Washington, meant to keep the response united while events abroad moved at revolutionary speed.
cia-0000132654:
The views of Latin American governments toward Cuba are surveyed in a CIA paper dated January 1, 1961. The American break with Havana was days away, and the region was picking sides fast. Mexico stood apart from the rest, as it often did on Cuba.

Most other governments leaned toward Washington, though with varied warmth. The paper sets out each stance as analysts read it at the new year. For readers, it is a map of the hemisphere at a turning point. The lines drawn that winter would hold, with few changes, through the invasion spring that followed.
cia-0000132754:
Most Cuba papers in this record look at the island alone, but this CIA briefing of January 4, 1961 pairs Cuba with Central America. It was written the day after the United States cut diplomatic ties with Havana. Analysts were already asking where Cuban influence might spread next.

That wider lens is the paper's point: Castro's revolution treated as a regional force, not a local event. Washington feared friendly governments or movements taking root in nearby countries. Preserved through the CIA Reading Room, the briefing shows the post-break alarm extending across the map of Central America.
cia-0000135754: A Spanish document dated 2 February 1961, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force. February 1961 was a month of final training before the brigade embarked for Cuba. The catalog record names no subject for this item. Preserved in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, it is a dated piece of the brigade's own archive from the operation's last weeks of preparation.
cia-0000136254: Dated 6 May 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records the location of CADICK, delegation of authority, and Calligeris, the chain of command mapped. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136354: An objective look at the aircraft problem opens this June 1954 LINCOLN cable. SYNCARP planes in Guatemala City would stand out either way. The planes could pass close inspection. But they would raise hard questions. How many planes are there? Who flew them? Who bombed which target? Answers would need an elaborate story. All would have to stick to it under investigation. Blaming military prerogative raises its own risks. The cable weighs exposure against use.
cia-0000136554: Dated 3 October 1960, this Spanish-language document comes from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506. The exile brigade was in training that fall, growing under CIA direction toward the force that would land in Cuba. The catalog record gives no subject for the item. It is held in the original Spanish, a primary source from the brigade's buildup period, released decades later with the rest of its archive.
cia-0000136754: An estimated date of 1 January 1961 heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, with the estimate marked in the catalog title. The brigade was the CIA's exile force, then in winter training. The record gives the document no subject. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, one of the turn-of-the-year records in the brigade's archive, its timing approximate by the catalog's own account.
cia-0000136854: Rifle configurations cause a problem in this January 1954 cable to the senior representative at LINCOLN. Overall length with folding stock and barrel extension removed is thirty-six inches. An immediate reply is needed on whether any named category is satisfactory so work can continue; the writer's opinion is that none is completely satisfactory, though they may have to suffice. Shortening the barrel would widen the dispersion pattern at fifty yards and above, and disassembly takes two to five minutes under stress.
cia-0000136954: Hold a conference with Jimenez, REELFOOT is urged in this May 1954 cable, and return for debriefing when negotiations complete. CALLIGERIS requested representation with Jimenez, and Estrada was sent to confer with him and survey the situation on the spot. At a cordial meeting, CALLIGERIS said he needed three planes and pilots, preferably P-51s, to counterbalance Guatemala's new arms shipment; failing that, 200,000 dollars. Estrada promised to pass the request to Jimenez and send an answer soonest.
cia-03155154: October 29, 1957: the daily bulletin went to the leadership. The intelligence summary covered global affairs. The Cold War's late-October reading. The paper lived through the years. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Time has kept the file intact.
cia-06232654: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1958/12/02, a CIA publication. The December briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-06692054: REASONS BEHIND THE ARREST OF CONGOLESE ARMED FORCES OFFICERS KAPEND AND YAV, a CIA document. The Congolese arrests. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06739054: SADDAM HUSAYN, a CIA document. The dictator's file. This file preserves that declassified paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
copyright-renewals-1954: This official Library of Congress volume lists every copyright renewal registered in the United States during 1954. Authors, publishers, and lawyers used such catalogs to track who still held rights in books, music, films, and plays. Today the volume serves researchers and rights-holders as a historical record of American creative ownership in the mid-twentieth century.
dods-spirit-manifestations-1854:
Dods answered the spirit rapping craze in Spirit Manifestations Examined and Explained, from 1854. Judge Edmonds, a noted believer, had defended the rappings as true spirit speech. Dods, the electrical psychologist, refuses that reading outright. The wonders, he argues, flow from minds and bodies under electrical laws.

He examines famous cases and mediums with his rival system in hand. The book records the passage from mesmerism to spiritualism in America. It speaks from the mesmerist side of that divide. Dods had built his name before the Fox sisters' knocks were heard. His defense of an older wonder against a newer one fascinates. Historians prize the primary view it gives.
edwards-freedom-of-will-1754:
Edwards's Inquiry into the Freedom of the Will, published in 1754, is the American Calvinist's great work of philosophy. He wrote it against Arminian writers who taught that the will must be free from all motive to be moral. The book defends determinism joined to moral agency.

Edwards argues that the will always chooses as the strongest motive inclines it, and that this costs us no true liberty. A person is free, in his account, when nothing stops him from doing what he most wants. The argument's tight logic still anchors debate on freedom, sin, and responsibility.
ennemoser-history-of-magic-vol-1-1854:
Joseph Ennemoser gave magic a grave past in The History of Magic, Vol. I, in English dress from 1854. William Howitt turned the German text to English. Ennemoser was a healer who held that trance and dreams hint at deep laws of the mind. He traces rites from old tribes to the age of the church.

Dreams, spells, and wild cures get a fair, calm look. He treats the theme as fit for true study. The pair of tomes is the age's great past of magic. This first half lays the broad base. Howitt, who turned the text, was a poet and tale smith too. His smooth prose helped the dense German work find a wide English crowd.
ennemoser-history-of-magic-vol-2-1854:
Joseph Ennemoser brings his long past of magic to a close in The History of Magic, Vol. II, in English from 1854. William Howitt's turn of the German text fills this tome as in the first. The tale runs on through witch hunts, seers, and the trance cures of Ennemoser's own day and land.

He asks what part is fraud, what part is law of mind. His calm, grave tone sets the work past mere tales of spooks. Read with the first tome, it is the age's chief past of magic. Its reach spans two fat tomes. Ennemoser came from the Tyrol hills and healed the sick by trance. His own cures feed the last parts of this long, grave survey.
europmc-pmc10087054:
Mattsson-Carlgren and a large team test whether blood markers can predict memory decline before Alzheimer's disease symptoms appear, in a 2023 study. Alzheimer's builds up in the brain for years in a silent phase. How long that phase lasts varies a lot between people, which makes trial design and early care hard.

The team followed people with amyloid buildup but no symptoms, using blood tests over time. They asked which markers forecast later decline in thinking. Their results help sharpen the choice of patients for early treatment trials and future screening.
europmc-pmc10115554:
Thieblemont and a large trial team report dose expansion results for epcoritamab in large B-cell lymphoma that returned or resisted past care, in a 2023 study. Epcoritamab is an antibody given under the skin that grabs both T cells and cancerous B cells. By linking them, it directs T cells to kill the cancer cells.

Earlier dose-finding work had shown strong anti-tumor activity. This phase of the trial tested a set dose in more patients. The paper reports response rates and side effects in detail. Those results informed the drug's later approval path.
europmc-pmc10190754: A medical paper on the method of spread of gas gangrene into living muscle. The creeping gangrene. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
europmc-pmc10412454:
Gulen and colleagues showed in 2023 that a DNA alarm path drives inflammation in old age. Low-grade swelling is a hallmark of ageing and fuels decline. The path pairs two proteins, cGAS and STING, which sense loose DNA inside cells. Loose DNA can leak from worn cell power units.

When the team blocked STING, old human cells and tissues calmed down. In old mice, blocks cut swelling in many organs and in the brain, and tissue function rose. In the brain, the path woke microglia, the local immune cells, into states that harm nerve cells. Memory also fell when the path was forced on. The work marks the path as a drug target for ageing.
europmc-pmc1064854:
Leone and co-authors cut a gene in mice in 2005 to learn how the body manages energy. The gene makes PGC-1alpha, a helper that switches on genes for cell power units. Those units, mitochondria, burn fuel to make energy. Mice born without the helper lived, yet deep checks found faults in many systems.

Growth of the heart and slow muscle lagged after birth. Leone reports fewer, weaker power units in slow muscle, with less stamina as a result. Body fat rose with age, most of all in females. The mice could not hold body heat in the cold. After a short fast, fat clogged their livers. Brain tissue showed small hollow lesions as well.
europmc-pmc10772854:
Collins and co-authors opened a three-part series in 2024 on how to judge clinical prediction models. Such a model gives a person's risk of a disease or a future event. It weighs traits such as age, symptoms, and blood pressure. Doctors lean on these numbers for daily choices, so their accuracy is vital.

Most new models never reach real care, Collins notes. Small samples, overfitting, and patchy reports block the path. The core flaw is weak or missing tests of how a model fares in its target group. The piece lays out inner and outer validation, the checks done inside and outside the build data. It also urges tests of fairness across groups of patients.
europmc-pmc10920854:
Zhou and co-authors review a form of cell death driven by iron that may help fight cancer in this 2024 paper. Ferroptosis is a death path where iron sparks a build-up of harmful fats in cell membranes. It differs from the tidy cell death path called apoptosis. The body uses it to suppress tumours on its own.

Some cancer cells that shrug off standard therapy are highly prone to this death, the review notes. That makes it attractive for hard-to-treat cancers. Yet firing it can also blunt the immune attack on tumours, a real risk. The authors map its control paths and its talks with the tissue around tumours. They survey its use with immune therapy, radiation, and drug therapy. Markers to guide patient choice are discussed.
europmc-pmc11701654:
CZI Cell Science Program presents a single-cell data platform called CZ CELLxGENE Discover in this 2024 paper. Labs have now analysed single cells by the hundreds of millions, using high-throughput transcriptomic methods, which read gene activity cell by cell. The pooled knowledge could unlock insights into health and disease. Yet the sheer number of datasets and their varied formats block meta-analysis.

The platform hosts a growing, community-contributed corpus: over 93 million unique cells in all, the authors report. The data are curated, standardised, and tagged with consistent cell-level metadata. The collection is the largest of its kind, they state. It is available through a free online portal for exploration and modelling. The authors link the platform to new machine learning directions, including large language models applied to cell data.
europmc-pmc1269454:
Thomason and colleagues tracked delirium in non-ventilated ICU patients in 2005. Delirium is common in ventilated patients and predicts worse outcomes. Data for patients not on ventilators were scarce. The cohort held 261 medical ICU patients at a university hospital.

Nurses screened for delirium at least twice daily. Nearly half, 125 patients, had at least one delirium episode. Patients with delirium were older on average. Statistical models treated delirium as a time-based factor. Thomason tests whether delirium itself predicts longer hospital stay. The design separates delirium effects from illness severity. The study ran from February 2002 to January 2003. Nurses did the checks two or more times each day on the ward.
europmc-pmc1277854:
Shafer, Meyer, and Crofton reviewed pyrethroid insecticides and the developing brain in 2005. Pyrethroids hold 25 percent of the world insecticide market. Adult nerve effects are well characterized. Effects on developing brains were far less charted.

Newborn rats proved at least ten times more sensitive than adults. That gap held for two tested pyrethroids. Most others lack age-specific toxicity data entirely. The review covers 22 developmental studies in depth. Motor activity and a brain receptor density changed most often. Shafer flags sodium channel development as the key backdrop. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2005.
europmc-pmc1291354:
Ferwerda and co-authors tested two immune sensor systems against tuberculosis bacteria in 2005. Sensing the bacteria starts both rapid and learned immune responses. Toll-like receptors were the known sensors. A second sensor, NOD2, was their focus.

Cells with either receptor type responded to the bacteria. Mice lacking one receptor made over 50 percent fewer signaling molecules. Cells from people with a NOD2 mutation showed an 80 percent defective response. Both systems proved necessary, not backups for each other. Ferwerda establishes NOD2 as a core tuberculosis sensor. People with the NOD2 mutation showed the clearest defect.
europmc-pmc1395354:
Drummond, Ho, Phillips, and Rambaut introduced relaxed methods for dating family trees in 2006. Strict molecular clocks assume steady evolution rates. Unrooted models assume nothing about rates at all. Both extremes are biologically unrealistic, the authors argue.

Relaxed clocks let rates vary across branches in measured ways. The method estimates trees and divergence times under rate uncertainty. It also measures how clocklike a dataset actually is. Three large datasets showed no significant rate self-link in rates among branches. That undercuts models assuming rates are inherited smoothly. Datasets were placed on a clock fit scale for comparison. Yeast and bacteria sets were both in the test.
europmc-pmc1533854:
Scholars track citations to find landmark papers and gauge their own reach. Bakkalbasi and co-authors compared three citation tools in 2006: the long-standing Web of Science, plus newcomers Scopus and Google Scholar. They sampled articles from cancer and physics journals, from 1993 and 2003.

Counts differed by tool, field, and year. Web of Science led for 1993 cancer papers, at 45.3 citations on average. Scopus led for 2003 cancer papers, at 8.9. Web of Science led both physics years. Bakkalbasi shows that coverage gaps make counts depend on the tool chosen, so no single source tells the whole story.
europmc-pmc1550954:
Most surgical deaths in the UK strike a small high-risk group. Pearse and co-authors measured that group in 2006, using records from 94 hospitals over five years. They classed procedures with death rates of five percent or more as high risk.

Of 4.1 million operations, the high-risk group held just 12.5 percent of cases. Yet it accounted for 84 percent of all deaths, with a death rate of 12.3 percent. These patients stayed a median of 16 days in hospital. Pearse argues that spotting and resourcing this small group could save the most lives.
europmc-pmc1564154:
Comparing microbe communities across many sites needs tools that respect ancestry. Lozupone, Hamady, and Knight launched UniFrac in 2006, a free web tool for that task. It uses the family tree of microbes to judge how alike two communities are.

UniFrac can cluster many environments at once and test which ones truly differ. Applied to river, estuary, and ocean samples, it revealed patterns the first analysis had missed. Lozupone expects tree-based comparison to redraw the picture of microbe life in both nature and medicine. The tool needs only a web browser.
europmc-pmc1570054:
Extreme heat and cold kill, but not everyone faces equal risk. Medina-Ramón and co-authors scanned 7.8 million deaths in 50 US cities from 1989 to 2000. They flagged days beyond the 99th percentile of heat or the coldest one percent.

Older people, diabetics, black residents, and those dying outside hospitals were more prone to heat deaths. Cardiac arrest deaths spiked most on extreme cold days, rising about 14 percent in relative terms. Heart disease deaths in general rose more in cold than in heat. Medina-Ramón argues protection programs should target the groups and causes most at risk.
europmc-pmc1638054:
Arsenic in well water poisons millions in South Asia. Chowdhury and co-authors mapped the crisis in 2000 across Bangladesh and West Bengal, India. Forty-two districts in Bangladesh and nine in West Bengal held groundwater above the world limit of 50 micrograms per liter.

The team analyzed over 69,000 water samples. In Bangladesh, 59 percent topped the limit; in West Bengal, 34 percent. Hair, nail, and urine tests showed most sampled people carried arsenic above safe levels. About a quarter of examined Bangladeshis had arsenic skin lesions. After a decade of study, Chowdhury warns the seen harm is only the tip of the iceberg.
europmc-pmc1713254:
Transfer RNAs, the adapters that build proteins, are not spread evenly across the body. Dittmar, Goodenbour, and Pan measured them in 2006 with a new microarray holding 63 probes for nuclear and mitochondrial tRNAs. Levels varied widely among eight human tissues.

Brain expressed more nuclear tRNAs than all but one tissue, and more mitochondrial tRNAs than any other. Individual tRNA species showed tissue-specific patterns. tRNAs serving chemically similar amino acids rose and fell together. In some tissues, tRNA supply matched the codon usage of highly expressed local genes. Dittmar argues tRNA variety helps tune protein production by tissue.
europmc-pmc1885954:
Lam, Lamond, Andersen and co-authors timed in 2007 how fast new proteins arrive in the nucleolus, the cell's ribosome factory. There, ribosomal RNAs are made and joined with ribosomal proteins into ribosome subunits. The team fed cells isotope-labeled building blocks and tracked fresh proteins by mass spectrometry.

New ribosomal proteins flooded into nucleoli faster than other components, a pattern confirmed by filming tagged proteins in living cells. Bleaching and mass measurements suggested only a subset of the flood is actually built into ribosomes and shipped out. Blocking the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, made ribosomal proteins pile up in the nucleus but not outside it. Blocking RNA production first made the pile-up worse. Cells overproduce ribosomal proteins and destroy the surplus inside the nucleus.
europmc-pmc1914054:
Li, Sheils and co-authors tested in 2007 whether microRNAs survive in archived tissue blocks well enough to measure. Hospital archives hold vast formalin-fixed, wax-embedded samples, but fixing degrades and chemically modifies RNA, limiting gene studies. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA regulators that might resist that damage.

The team compared 160 microRNAs in matched cells preserved two ways: frozen fresh or fixed and embedded. MicroRNA from the fixed blocks amplified successfully with standard lab copying. Oddly, equal amounts of total RNA yielded higher microRNA readings from fixed cells. The likely reason is that cross-links formed during fixing trap large RNA, so more fixed cells are needed for the same total RNA, concentrating the small molecules. Overall, microRNA levels in fixed tissue tracked the frozen reference reliably.
europmc-pmc2000354:
Wu and colleagues profiled small regulatory RNAs in CD8 T cells in 2007. These immune cells move from naive, to effector, to memory states after meeting a target. MicroRNAs, tiny RNAs that tune gene activity, were suspected to shift during that change. The team compared antigen-specific cells at all three stages using three methods.

Seven microRNAs made up about 60 percent of all microRNAs found. Most were far more abundant than the rest. Overall microRNA levels fell in effector cells compared with naive cells. Levels tended to rise again in memory cells. One, miR-21, stayed higher in both effector and memory cells. The cloned RNAs also showed many end variations, suggesting new ways microRNAs are trimmed.
europmc-pmc2124854: A medical paper on changes in the proteolytic enzymes and anti-enzymes of the blood serum. The serum's enzymes. This article preserves that biochemistry. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2125154: Where polio struck and why was the question behind this epidemiology paper. The disease's patterns across populations. The article preserves that public-health research. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Preserved for study.
europmc-pmc2125254: A medical paper with a histological and chemical study of fatty matter of normal and cryptorchid testes. The tissue's fat. This article preserves that histology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2125454: A medical paper on intestinal obstruction and non-coagulable nitrogen of the blood. The blocked gut's chemistry. This article preserves that research. It waits for future eyes. It holds its historical place. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128354: Botulinum toxin kills in tiny doses, and this paper investigated exactly how Clostridium botulinum's poison does its work. The researchers traced the toxin's manner of action. The deadliest natural poison, studied. The article preserves that toxicology.
europmc-pmc2128454: A medical paper with studies on nasopharyngeal secretions from common cold patients. The cold's mucus. This article preserves that virology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2130954: A medical paper with studies on the oxidation-reduction of hemoglobin and methemoglobin. The blood's rust. This article preserves that biochemistry. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2131354: A medical paper on the role of the Thebesian vessels in the circulation of the heart. The heart's small vessels. This article preserves that cardiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131454: A medical paper with immunological studies in relation to the suprarenal gland. The adrenal immunity. This article preserves that endocrinology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2140554: A biology paper on the influence of electrolytes on the cataphoretic charge of colloidal particles. The charged colloids. This article preserves that biophysics. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2271054:
Walker and co-workers showed in 2008 that boosting chitin synthesis rescues the yeast Candida albicans from a new class of antifungal drugs. Echinocandins block production of beta-glucan, a main cell wall component, and normally kill this pathogen. Low drug doses instead triggered the fungus to make more chitin, the wall's other main scaffold, raising wall chitin content and reducing drug efficacy. Three signalling pathways mediated that compensation.

Activating those pathways let cells survive otherwise lethal drug levels. Survival worked even without two normally essential chitin enzymes, because a novel offset division wall formed and restored cell division. The findings anticipate a resistance route against echinocandins in patients. Encouragingly, combining echinocandins with chitin synthesis inhibitors synergised strongly, killing far better together. That pairing points toward combination therapies.
europmc-pmc2346554:
Duret and Arndt studied how recombination shapes the human genome in 2008. Recombination is the swapping of DNA between paired chromosomes when eggs and sperm form. Mammal genomes vary in GC content, meaning the share of the DNA letters G and C, across large regions.

They tracked neutral DNA changes in one billion letters of primate DNA outside genes. Regions near chromosome ends evolved toward lower GC content, while high-crossover regions evolved toward higher GC content, and crossover rate explained 47% of the pattern. The link was stronger for male than female crossovers, which argues against natural selection as the cause. They credited a neutral process called biased gene conversion, which favours G and C letters near recombination hotspots. It sits beside mutation, selection, and drift as a driver of genome change.
europmc-pmc2363254:
Chompret and colleagues studied inherited p53 mutations in childhood cancer in 2000. The p53 gene normally guards against cancer, and a faulty copy passed down in families can leave children exposed. The team screened children with solid tumors who had relatives with early or multiple cancers.

Of 268 children tested, 17 carried a germline p53 mutation, which is a fault present from birth. Thirteen had inherited it and four carried a brand-new mutation. Using family data corrected for how families were picked, they estimated lifetime cancer risk at 73% for male carriers. For female carriers the risk came to nearly 100%, driven largely by breast cancer. No low-risk version of these mutations turned up. The authors stressed that new mutations are not rare, so a clear family history is not required.
europmc-pmc2427054:
Driver and Noesselt surveyed how the senses influence each other in the brain in 2008. Classic neuroscience treated each sense, sight, hearing, touch, as a sealed module. Their review gathers human studies showing that the modules talk, early and often.

Brain scans and recordings now show meeting zones where signals from several senses converge. Some sit surprisingly close to the first processing areas for a single sense. Direct links may even join the primary cortices of different senses. What one sense reports can change both brain responses and conscious judgements about another sense, as when sound alters what people see. The authors weigh three wiring explanations: fast forward merging, relay stations in the thalamus, and feedback from meeting zones back to single-sense areas. They stress new methods can now separate these circuits.
europmc-pmc2515854:
Antao and colleagues introduced a software workbench called LOSITAN in this 2008 paper. Geneticists hunt for signs of natural selection by looking for genes whose variation between populations stands out from the genome-wide pattern. The standard tool for this, based on a statistic called Fst, was powerful but hard to run correctly.

LOSITAN wraps that method in a graphical interface that handles data import and export, estimates the neutral background level of variation, and draws the result plots. It also splits the heavy computation across processor cores, roughly halving run time on a dual-core machine. The authors argue the workbench makes selection scans practical for far more researchers, even on large population data sets.
europmc-pmc2582454:
Wang and colleagues showed in 2008 that glioma cancer stem cells depend on the protein c-Myc to keep growing. Malignant gliomas are among the deadliest cancers and contain a hierarchy of cells, topped by stem-like cells that renew themselves and rebuild tumours. Since c-Myc drives normal stem cells, the team compared its levels in glioma stem cells and ordinary glioma cells, then knocked it down with RNA interference.

C-Myc was far more abundant in the stem-like cells. Silencing it slowed their division, froze them in the resting phase of the cell cycle, and raised cell death, while ordinary glioma cells barely noticed. Stem cells with low c-Myc could no longer form spheres in culture or grow tumours in mouse brains. The authors propose targeting such core stem cell pathways against advanced cancers.
europmc-pmc2631154:
Atkinson, Morris, Ferrin, and Babbitt examined in 2009 whether drawing protein relationships as similarity networks can reveal functional patterns across huge protein families. The flood of new sequences outruns family trees and alignments, yet function is usually inferred from similarity. The team built networks where proteins are nodes linked by sequence similarity, then layered other information on top.

They tested the approach on three large groups: human GPCRs, human kinases, and the crotonase enzyme superfamily. Overlaying data such as known function exposed clear functional themes and flagged outlier proteins that break the pattern. Networks matched phylogenetic trees well in structure while handling far larger sequence sets. The authors define the method's limitations and argue it is an accessible way to generate testable ideas about how sequence relates to function.
europmc-pmc2653554:
Martin and colleagues traced in 2009 how a rare type of immune cell, called a MAIT cell, grows up in mice and humans. These cells guard body surfaces such as the gut. They all carry the same sensor and depend on a partner molecule called MR1, yet no one had found where they first appear.

Using special mice and a marker for the human cells, the team showed growth happens in two steps. The cells are first chosen inside the thymus, the school where immune cells mature, and this step needs MR1. They then multiply outside it, and that second step needs B cells plus normal gut germs. In human babies the cells are few and fresh at birth. Within years they expand greatly and take on a seasoned form, reaching a small but real share of blood immune cells.
europmc-pmc2675854:
Simon and colleagues described in 2007 BRB-ArrayTools, a software package that helps doctors and biologists analyze gene chip experiments soundly. Gene chips measure thousands of genes at once, and the flood of numbers traps the unwary: flawed analyses filled the literature. Expert statisticians with chip experience were scarce in most labs.

Built by statisticians at the National Cancer Institute, the package walks users through the full analysis, from raw data to building predictors that sort patients by outcome. It checks those predictors with complete cross-validation, a strict honesty test many papers skip. Links to public gene databases handle naming and pathway checks. An archive of over 100 published datasets, with patient details attached, lets users practice and compare. The tool also imports data straight from the main public archive of chip studies.
europmc-pmc2685454:
d'Erfurth and colleagues showed in 2009 that changing just three genes can turn meiosis, the sex-cell division that halves chromosome number, into plain mitosis in a plant. The result is seeds carrying the mother's full genome, exact clones. Farmers dream of such cloning, called apomixis, because a champion plant's traits could be kept forever through seed.

The team worked in Arabidopsis, a small lab weed. Meiosis differs from mitosis in three ways: chromosomes pair and swap pieces, sisters stay together at first, and the cell divides twice. They found a gene governing entry into the second division. Mutating it, plus one mutation killing the swapping and one freeing the sisters, removed all three differences at once. The triple mutant made diploid sex cells identical to itself. A major step toward engineered apomixis in crops, the authors say, is now in hand.
europmc-pmc2793254:
Parks, Cronn, and Liston tested whether reading whole chloroplast genomes could sort out close plant relatives that single genes leave muddled. Chloroplasts are the green cell parts that run photosynthesis, and their DNA changes slowly. Their 2009 study used fast parallel sequencing on thirty-seven pine family members.

Nearly complete chloroplast genomes, each about one hundred nine thousand letters long, settled thirty of thirty-three branch points with strong support. That was a clear gain over older work. Tests showed the whole genome was needed for the hardest, fast-splitting groups, and two gene regions carried an outsized share of the clues. A check of ninety-nine published plant trees suggested similar gains elsewhere.
europmc-pmc2825554:
Simó, Villarroel, Corraliza, Hernández, and Garcia-Ramírez reviewed in 2010 the retinal pigment epithelium. This cell layer at the back of the eye does far more than wall off the retina from blood. The layer ferries nutrients and water, soaks up stray light, and recycles the pigment that vision chemistry needs. It also eats shed pieces of light-sensing cells and secretes factors that keep the retina sound.

Research on diabetic eye disease has focused on nerve tissue damage and the inner blood barrier, the authors note. The pigment layer's failure, above all its secretory role, has drawn far less study. They argue new treatments should aim at this neglected layer before vision is lost.
europmc-pmc2832754:
Healy and colleagues, for the International LRRK2 Consortium, pooled worldwide data in 2008 on Parkinson disease caused by faults in the LRRK2 gene. Twenty-one centers joined to answer three questions: how the inherited form looks, which gene changes truly cause disease, and how likely carriers are to fall ill. Risk figures came from over a thousand mutation carriers in one hundred thirty-three families.

Six mutations passed the bar as proven causes. The commonest, called Gly2019Ser, appeared in one percent of lone cases and four percent of family cases, peaking in the Middle East. A carrier's risk of Parkinson disease reached about twenty-eight percent by age fifty-nine and seventy-four percent by seventy-nine. Symptoms ran milder than in ordinary Parkinson disease.
europmc-pmc2838754:
Habier, Tetens, Seefried, Lichtner, and Thaller studied in 2010 how much accuracy genomic breeding values in German Holstein cattle owe to close family ties. They separated that share from the share owed to lasting marker links. They used nearly thirty-nine hundred bulls typed at fifty-four thousand DNA markers, with daughter-based records for milk, fat, protein, and cell counts.

When the closest relative allowed between the training set and the test set was pushed further away, accuracy fell for every trait and both methods tried. A Bayesian averaging method drew far more lasting signal from marker linkage than a standard relationship-matrix method, especially with larger training sets. The authors warn that future candidates, lacking close kin in training, will score lower than early reports promised.
europmc-pmc2846954:
Bellera and colleagues warned in 2010 that a workhorse survival model in cancer research can mislead when a risk factor's effect changes over time. The Cox model assumes each factor shifts risk by a steady proportion throughout follow-up. With patients now living far longer, that assumption fails more often, and constant-effect summaries can hide early harm or late benefit.

The authors show the trap using nearly a thousand women treated for breast cancer and followed a median of fourteen years. Tumor grade's effect faded yet stayed strong. Hormone receptor status flipped sign: negative status raised the risk of spread early on, then turned protective later, which the standard model averaged into a misleading nothing. They urge routine checks for time-varying effects.
europmc-pmc2851054:
Kosten and George laid out in 2002 how chronic opioid use rewires the brain, and why those changes dictate treatment. Heroin and prescription opioids latch onto mu receptors that normally reward survival behaviors like eating, hijacking the pleasure system. Tolerance and dependence follow as the brain adapts, and deeper, longer-lasting changes drive craving and compulsive use.

Dependence chemistry fades within weeks of stopping, the authors explain, but addiction circuits can fire relapse months or years later, fed by stress, cues, and inherited vulnerability. Medications such as methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone act on the same systems with steadying effects. They work best, the authors stress, alongside psychosocial treatment rather than alone.
europmc-pmc2859054:
Yellow deposits called drusen build up in aging eyes and warn of macular disease, and Wang and colleagues measured in 2010 what drusen are actually made of. The team collected drusen with their covering cell layer from thirty-six donated human retinas soon after death. They weighed fats and proteins separately and identified proteins with a mass spectrometer, an instrument that sorts molecules by weight.

Fat and protein each made up a large share of each deposit, led by two fats named esterified cholesterol and phosphatidylcholine. Tiny fat-filled particles filled over a third of each deposit's volume. The protein list included several already tied to drusen, plus a few known from the covering cells, and one immune protein sat inside the deposits.
europmc-pmc2905354:
Carr, Cardwell, McCarron, and McConville pooled in 2010 every population study of myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease that weakens muscles by blocking the signal at the nerve-muscle junction. Fifty-five studies from 1950 to 2007 fed their meta-analysis. Together they covered one point seven billion person-years. The pooled outcomes were how often the disease starts, how many live with it, and how often it kills.

Pooled incidence came to about five new cases per million people per year, and prevalence to about seventy-eight per million. Rates for the two antibody-defined subtypes were also estimated. Frequencies varied widely even between similar populations, and they climbed in later, better-run studies. The authors read the rise as mainly better case finding, while leaving room for true environmental influences on onset.
europmc-pmc2923754:
Murdoch and Lloyd reviewed in 2010 the chronic inflammation at the heart of asthma, arguing the old single-story account no longer fits. Asthma was long told as one allergic pathway driving twitchy airways and structural remodeling. Human disease and animal models now show several immune flavors, some allergic, some not, converging on swollen, scarred, hyper-reactive airways.

The review walks through the key cells and messengers of the long phase of disease, where damage accrues between attacks. Against them stands a cast of endogenous brakes: regulatory cells and a family of pro-resolving mediators, molecules that actively end inflammation rather than merely blocking its start. Therapies that press the body's own resolution buttons, instead of carpet-suppressing immunity, are the frontier the authors highlight.
europmc-pmc2935454:
Dalloul led a large team that sequenced and assembled the genome of the domestic turkey in 2010, combining two newer sequencing platforms. Pairing Roche and Illumina machines gave an economical route into a genome that had stayed unread.

Reads from both platforms were merged with a physical map, a genetic map, and the chicken genome to place most sequence pieces onto turkey chromosomes. That placement supports comparisons across bird species and practical breeding based on genome position. Readers get the full assembly account plus early analysis of what the turkey genome contains.
europmc-pmc3021854:
Hook and colleagues published this review in 2010 on the microbes that make methane inside the stomachs of cattle and sheep. The rumen, the first stomach chamber, hosts these single-celled organisms. They are the only living things known to produce methane gas. Which kinds live there shifts with the food the animal eats and with where it lives.

Readers learn how methane forms during normal feed digestion and why it matters for both farm energy loss and the climate. The review weighs ways to cut those emissions, from changing feed mixes to adding fats, organic acids, and plant products. It also covers removing gut protozoa and using vaccines. Each option worked to a different degree in live animals.
europmc-pmc3090754:
Tadel, Baillet, Mosher, Pantazis, and Leahy presented in 2011 Brainstorm, a free program for analyzing the magnetic and electric signals recorded from outside the head. Such recordings, called MEG and EEG, track brain activity with fine timing but need heavy processing to locate where signals arise inside the brain. The program's specialty is estimating those cortical sources and aligning them with a person's own anatomy scans.

Brainstorm wraps both established and newer methods in a single graphical interface meant to be usable without programming. Data viewing, filtering, and source mapping flow through shared windows, and analyses can be replayed and shared between labs. The project is collaborative and open source, built by the user community over many years. Its stated aim is to connect working neuroscientists with the best available methods through a tool they can actually operate.
europmc-pmc3096954:
Prat and colleagues profiled in 2010 a recently recognized breast cancer subtype called claudin-low, filling in its clinical and biological portrait. Breast cancers sort into five gene based subtypes with different outlooks. Claudin-low tumors lack the markers of mature duct lining cells and instead carry signs of a shape shifting program, strong immune gene activity, and stem cell like traits.

Most are triple negative cancers, lacking all three standard drug targets, and they often show unusual growth patterns under the microscope. Their response to chemotherapy before surgery falls between two other subtypes. Widely used lab cell lines and several mouse models turned out to carry this same subtype, a useful accident for research. In a family tree of breast cell maturity, claudin-low sits closest to the mammary stem cell. The paper gives the field a working definition of the subtype.
europmc-pmc3244954:
Wei Wu, Quanguo He, and Changzhong Jiang reviewed magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles in this 2008 article in Nanoscale Research Letters. These particles respond to magnets and, once coated, can be steered and tracked inside the body, attracting wide use in biotechnology and catalysis. The review gathers the strategies for making them and dressing their surfaces.

The authors explain that practical use demands a combination of strong magnetism, stability, body-friendliness, and a reactive surface. Coatings range from organic polymers and biomolecules to silica and metals, each lending different functions. They walk through synthesis routes, structure, and magnetic properties of both bare and coated particles, then sketch applications. The closing sections weigh the field's main problems and challenges and point to where the technology is heading.
europmc-pmc3249054:
Charlotte Stagg and colleagues asked whether brain-chemistry scans reflect real synaptic activity, in this 2011 study in the Journal of Physiology. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy can estimate levels of glutamate and GABA, the brain's main excitatory and inhibitory messengers, and people differ in those levels. But whether a scan reading mirrors actual signaling was unclear, so the team compared scans with magnetic stimulation tests in the same volunteers' motor cortex.

Glutamate levels from the scan tracked a stimulation measure of overall cortical excitability, suggesting the scan does capture glutamatergic activity. GABA levels, by contrast, showed no clear relationship to stimulation measures of synaptic inhibition through either GABA receptor type. One less-understood stimulation protocol did track GABA. The authors suggest it may reflect background, extrasynaptic GABA tone.
europmc-pmc3323154:
Miller, Williams, Hobbs, and Wolfe tested whether a fatal deer disease can spread through contaminated ground, reporting in 2004. The disease, chronic wasting disease, is caused by prions, misfolded proteins that persist stubbornly in the environment. Whether deer must touch infected animals directly, or can catch it from soil tainted by dung, urine, or rotting carcasses, was unclear.

Healthy mule deer were placed in paddocks under three setups. Some shared space with live infected deer, others entered ground where infected carcasses had decomposed about two years earlier. A third group used paddocks vacated by infected deer over two years before. Deer caught the disease in some paddocks of every type, while control paddocks stayed clean. The results prove that prions lingering in the environment can infect deer long after the source animals are gone, complicating control efforts.
europmc-pmc3366754:
The World Health Organization Global Influenza Programme Surveillance Network analysed how H5N1 avian influenza viruses evolved in Asia during the 2004 to 2005 outbreaks. Nine Asian countries reported poultry outbreaks in 2004. By early 2005, 89 confirmed human infections had been recorded, 52 of them fatal. It was the largest human cluster since the virus emerged in 1997.

Genetic and antigenic analysis showed the viruses infecting people belonged to a clade that was drifting antigenically. These viruses resisted the older adamantane drugs but remained sensitive to neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir. The network's findings fed directly into antiviral stockpiling decisions and the selection of candidate vaccine strains.
europmc-pmc3367654:
Woolhouse and Gowtage-Sequeria surveyed the world's known human pathogens in 2005 to ask which ones keep emerging. Their updated count covered more than fourteen hundred species that can infect people. Over half of them also infect other animals, making them zoonotic in the broad sense.

Among the species classed as emerging or re-emerging, animal-linked ones appeared about twice as often as the rest. The authors compared viruses, bacteria, fungi, and other groups, and catalogued the drivers behind each new threat. Their results argue that watching animal hosts is central to catching the next outbreak early. The survey remains a basic reference for spillover research.
europmc-pmc3380054:
Edmondson and co-authors pooled studies in 2012 on post-traumatic stress disorder triggered by acute coronary syndromes, meaning heart attacks and unstable angina. A frightening cardiac event can itself cause lasting stress symptoms. The question was how often that happens and whether it worsens the heart's outlook.

Across twenty-four studies, about one patient in eight had serious stress symptoms after the event. Estimates swung widely, running higher in studies using screening questionnaires than in those using full diagnostic interviews. In the few studies tracking outcomes, symptoms came with about double the risk of another cardiac event or death. The authors call for firmer tests of that link.
europmc-pmc3437554:
Silva and colleagues showed in 2009 that a single protein, Nanog, is the gateway to the deepest form of pluripotency, the state where a cell can become anything. Nature builds that state in the early embryo's founder tissue, and lab reprogramming can rebuild it from adult cells. The team tested Nanog's role in both routes.

Fusing cells to make pluripotent hybrids worked only with Nanog present and pushing. In factor-driven reprogramming, partly changed cells stalled until Nanog arrived to complete the crossing. In the embryo, Nanog marks exactly the newborn founder tissue; without it, that tissue froze in a half-formed, unviable state. Nanog, they conclude, choreographs the ground state itself, in the womb and in the dish alike.
europmc-pmc3439854:
Astarita, Acton, and Turley reviewed podoplanin in 2012, a membrane protein whose jobs keep multiplying across development, immunity, and cancer. It appears in many tissues, from brain and heart to lymph vessels, and mice lacking it show how vital it is for building the heart, lungs, and lymphatic system. Labs already use it as the standard flag for lymph vessel cells.

Its best-studied act is clumping platelets through their CLEC-2 receptor, a pairing found nowhere else in the body. Tumors often raise the protein as they turn invasive, and high levels track with spread. Fresher work adds roles in T cells and dendritic cells of the immune system. The review gathers these threads into one map of a quietly central protein.
europmc-pmc3443254:
Jiao and a large team analyzed gene mutations across several hundred brain tumors in 2012 to sharpen the classification of malignant gliomas. Mutations in three growth regulators and a chromatin protein had just been found in certain glioma subtypes, but their reach was unmapped. The team typed them all against tumor type and patient outcome.

The chromatin gene ATRX was mutated in most lower-grade astrocytomas and secondary glioblastomas, traveling with IDH1 mutations. The other two genes clustered in oligodendrogliomas instead. Two combined signatures emerged, and patients carrying one lived a median far longer than the other group, who in turn outlived patients with neither. Even within single tumor types the signatures split outcomes. A three-way genetic label, they argue, should join the standard classification.
europmc-pmc3458854:
Fodor and colleagues followed the airway microbes of adults with cystic fibrosis in 2012 through flare-ups, antibiotic treatment, and calm periods. The disease clogs airways and breeds chronic infection, and flare-ups drive irreversible lung decline, yet what sparks them was unclear. Deep sequencing of sputum from twenty-three patients generated hundreds of thousands of reads across nearly two hundred microbial types.

Two known pathogens, Pseudomonas and Burkholderia, dominated most samples and rarely shared a patient. Other genera appeared in almost everyone. Antibiotics trimmed variety slightly but barely moved the community's shape, and flare-up samples looked much like stable ones. Flare-ups, they suggest, reflect spread of infection within the lung, not a new cast of germs. Sparse communities tracked with poor lung function.

europmc-pmc8106554: Wong-Rolle and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on unexpected guests in the tumor microenvironment (the tissue surrounding a tumor): microbiome (microbes living in the body) in cancer. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8309154: This 2021 review paper covers factors contributing to medication adherence in patients with a chronic condition: a scoping review of qualitative (interview-based) research. Introduction medication adherence continues to be a significant challenge in healthcare, and there is a shortage of effective treatments. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc8373954: This 2021 research paper covers etiological and epidemiological features of acute breathing infections in China. Nationwide prospective surveillance of all-age patients with acute breathing infections was conducted in China between 2009‒2019. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc8453354: Doctors and scientists took on head-to-head comparison of 8 plasma amyloid-β 42/40 assays in alzheimer disease in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8637554: Doctors and scientists took on elesclomol triggers copper-dependent ferroptosis (an iron-driven form of cell death) in colorectal (of the colon and rectum) cancer cells in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8837554: Doctors and scientists took on genome-wide (across all DNA) analysis of 102,084 migraine cases identifies 123 risk loci and subtype-specific risk alleles in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment.
europmc-pmc8851854: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at METABOLIC (energy-use): high-throughput profiling of germ genomes for working traits, metabolism (how cells turn food into energy), biogeochemistry, and community-scale working networks. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Clinics can put a tool like this to work right away, since the testing is already done.
europmc-pmc8884154: A fresh look at ultra-high sensitivity mass spectrometry quantifies single-cell (one cell at a time) proteome changes upon perturbation arrived with this 2022 research paper. Single-cell (one cell at a time) technologies are revolutionizing biology but are today mainly limited to imaging and deep. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9403754: This 2022 review paper covers the cost-effectiveness of digital health treatments: a systematic review (a review of every study) of the literature. Digital health treatments have significant to improve safety, efficacy (how well something works), and quality of care, reducing waste. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9403854: Bogenschutz and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on percentage of heavy drinking days following psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy vs placebo (dummy pill) in the treatment of adult patients with alcohol use illness. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9667854: A fresh look at global disparities in SARS-CoV-2 genomic surveillance arrived with this 2022 research paper. Genomic sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) is essential to track the evolution (gradual change) and spread of SARS-CoV-2, optimize. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9763654: A fresh look at global deaths linked to 33 germ germs in 2019: a systematic (thorough) analysis for the global burden of disease study 2019 arrived with this 2022 research paper. Reducing the burden of death due to infection is an urgent global public health priority. With firm counts in hand, planners can size the problem and track whether it grows or shrinks.
europmc-pmc9825554: Burley and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on RCSB protein data bank: transport of experimentally-determined PDB structures alongside one million computed structure models of proteins from artific. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9898554: A fresh look at learning local equivariant representations for large-scale atomistic dynamics arrived with this 2023 research paper. A simultaneously accurate and computationally efficient parametrization of the energy surface of molecules and materials is a long-standing goal. Clinics can put a tool like this to work right away, since the testing is already done.
europmc-pmc9908054: This 2023 research paper covers cohort profile update: the HUNT study, norway. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
feuerbach-essence-christianity-eliot-185:
Ludwig Feuerbach's Essence of Christianity appeared in English in 1854, translated by Marian Evans, who wrote as George Eliot. Feuerbach, a German philosopher, argued that God is a picture of human nature itself. The translation was Eliot's only work published under her real name.

Feuerbach held that qualities praised in God, such as love, wisdom, and justice, are human qualities projected upward. Religion, then, is humanity worshipping its own best image without knowing it. The argument shook German and British thought and fed later critiques of religion. Eliot's clear English carried the work into Victorian debates about faith, doubt, and what worship really means.
florence-worcester-chronicle-forester-18:
Florence of Worcester kept his chronicle in the twelfth century, and Thomas Forester's 1854 English version carries it to modern readers. The tale runs from creation to 1141. Norman conquest and the anarchy of King Stephen's reign form its grim late chapters.

A monk who lived through civil war tells of kings, battles, and portents. Castles rise, towns burn, and chroniclers count the cost in famines. The work stands as a base source for medieval English history. Forester's version, in a popular series, made the chronicle a household book for Victorians who wanted their past in the words of those who saw it.
frus-1861-d154:
Writing on 23 September 1861, William H. Seward kept William Dayton to the quiet autumn watch. The letter is document 154 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late September found no great turn in the war, and Seward's letters accept the lull. His note to Paris keeps the watch in place without fresh alarm. Such routine pages are the true bulk of the 1861 file, and its quiet strength. Routine pages like this one are the true mass of the 1861 record. Details of trade filled the small print where the blockade's fate was set. Quiet strength was the autumn's true policy.
frus-1861-d254:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 23 September 1861, addressed to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. It was printed as Document 254 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d54:
On 14 June 1861, Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London. The dispatch is document 54 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid June found Adams deep in the routine of notes and calls in London. The grand question of British recognition hung over each small task. His report shows the daily grind by which a great issue was held off, one meeting and one letter at a time. The daily grind in London was the price of keeping a great power neutral. Great issues are often held off by small tasks done well, day after day.
frus-1862-d154:
On 30 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed a dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, printed as Document 154 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter closed out a month of heavy mail between Washington and London.

September 1862 had brought Antietam and the emancipation plan, two events that reset foreign thinking about the war. British leaders put off any move to back the South, at least for the moment. Mail like this dispatch shows the steady pressure Washington kept on London while that choice hung in the balance through the autumn. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d254:
William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report on 21 February 1862, printed as Document 254 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris throughout this period.

Reports from Paris had a special flavor: Dayton dealt with a court where the emperor's wishes counted for more than public debate. He reported conversations, hints, and shifts of mood that rarely reached print in France. A February report like this one helped Washington judge whether Napoleon III meant to meddle in the war or only to watch it. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d354:
Edouard Thouvenel, the French foreign minister in Paris, wrote to Henri Mercier, his minister in Washington, on 19 January 1862. The instruction is printed as Document 354 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, among the French papers.

Thouvenel's letters were Mercier's orders, fixing the line France would take in Washington for weeks at a time. Seeing them in the American printed record lets readers watch French policy being made, not just received. This January instruction came as France settled into its solo course in Mexico and weighed the American war. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862.
frus-1862-d454:
John Lothrop Motley in Vienna received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 September 1862. It is Document 454 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Seward wrote on the eve of Antietam, with Lee in Maryland and the fate of the autumn campaign undecided. Motley, in Vienna, had to hold the Union's line at a court that watched and waited. Instructions sent at such a moment stressed resolve above all. The dispatch belongs to the mid-September cluster in which Seward wrote to nearly every post in Europe. He was preparing his ministers for either result on the battlefield. He was also preparing them for the emancipation order he knew was coming.
frus-1862-d54:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 28 April 1862, addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed as Document 54 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d554:
On 6 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister in Belgium. The instruction is Document 554 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Sanford was among the most active of Seward's ministers, traveling, reporting, and watching Confederate agents wherever they surfaced in Europe. Orders to Brussels in May 1862 came as Union arms advanced and the government's case abroad improved. Belgium's own stake was trade and its king's wide influence. Seward used Sanford's energy gladly, feeding him the arguments and news the Brussels post needed. The dispatch is part of a correspondence marked by unusual warmth and frequency for so small a mission.
frus-1862-d654:
Dated 21 October 1861, this letter went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Townsend Harris, the American minister in Japan. It stands as document 654 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Harris would soon leave the post he had held since the legation opened.

Seward wrote to guide the men who spoke for the United States abroad. A letter like this one set out views from Washington that Harris was to use in his talks with Japan's rulers. Read with the rest of the file, it helps show how a small mission kept its footing while its home government fought for its life.
frus-1863p1-d154:
The pair of 13 April 1863 for London opens with this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 154 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mid-April pairs from Washington split the brief as it stood after the raider's seizure: hold the gain, watch the yards, mind the tone. Seward fed Adams those points sheet by sheet. This letter opens the pair of 13 April. It is desk work of a high order, brief in form and heavy in what it guarded.
frus-1863p1-d254:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 30 July 1863. It appears as document 254 of the 1863 papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d354:
Writing in Washington on 8 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 354 in the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d454:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 9 April 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d54:
On 21 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to a Mr. Spence. Memminger was the Confederate secretary of the treasury in Richmond. The letter is document 54 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, among the Confederate papers printed in that volume.

The treasury's web reached into Britain, where agents and friends of the South worked on loans and sales of cotton. A letter like this one fed that web. It is dated the same week as Memminger's sheets to Mason in London, and it shares their theme: money, the South's scarcest weapon. Printed by the Union, it lets readers trace that hunt for cash in the foe's own words.
frus-1863p1-d554:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 6 June 1863 and wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d654:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 4 November 1863. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Each crossing of the Atlantic took the better part of two weeks, so these letters also show leaders acting on news that was already old. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d154: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt dated November 21, 1943 stands as Document 154 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It shares its date with two companions, written as the parties settled into Cairo on the conference's eve. The catalog record gives no topic for this note and assigns none should be made for it. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the other papers of that crowded day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d254:
