A meeting between Patrick Hurley and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek at Cairo on 23 November 1943 is covered by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. No official record of the substance of the conversation has been found; the appointment itself is shown by a letter from Hurley's aide to Harry Hopkins in the Hopkins Papers.

Interviewed by an editor in 1956, Hurley recalled that Madame Chiang was present. Chiang, he said, asked whether Roosevelt and Churchill were to meet Stalin, and Hurley answered that such a meeting was set, but not for Cairo. The two men also discussed the pending plan for American, British, and Chinese military cooperation in Burma.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d354:
A small errand at Tehran on 27 November 1943 is untangled by an editorial note in the volume. It concerns Admiral Wilson Brown's visit to the Soviet Embassy, about where President Roosevelt would live during the conference. The Log says Brown went to explain why the President had chosen the American Legation.

A letter written in 1954 by Minister Louis Dreyfus, who went with Brown, gives a fuller story. Roosevelt had in fact let it be known he would stay at the Soviet Embassy if Stalin invited him, and Dreyfus had passed that word to the Soviet chargé, Maximov. No answer from Stalin had come back. Maximov told the two visitors that he had no reply yet himself, but that since Stalin had already reached Tehran, the question would be put to him there.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d454: Historians prepared the editorial note cataloged as Document 454. It belongs to the Cairo-Tehran volume in the Foreign Relations series. Editorial notes give background, name key figures, and cross-reference nearby papers. Readers need that help across two conferences held weeks apart. Tehran brought Stalin together with Roosevelt and Churchill in late 1943. Cairo framed the talks that came before and after. The note links its neighbors into one story.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d54: On October 23, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt once more, and the message became Document 54 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Moscow Conference was in its middle days, and London was weighing what the talks would mean for the summit ahead. The record for this note gives the date and the names. Its contents are a matter for the printed text in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d554:
Prime Minister Churchill sent this message to President Roosevelt on March 3, 1944, one of two he sent that day. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, among the later correspondence the editors attached to the conferences' record.

March 1944 found the alliance deep in preparation for the invasion of France, with argument continuing over strategy in Italy and the Mediterranean. Churchill wrote to Roosevelt as his chief partner in all of it, sometimes several times a day. For readers, one of a pair of same-day messages shows the sheer tempo of the written partnership at the war's turning point.
frus-1944-quebec-d154:
H. Freeman Matthews recorded a conversation with British Ambassador Lord Halifax on August 26, 1944, and attached the aide-mémoire Halifax left with him. France wanted a larger role in the war against Japan, especially in Indochina. Eden needed answers for the French envoy Massigli before he left London on August 29, which made the questions urgent.

Two decisions were wanted at once: attaching a French military mission under General Blaizot to Southeast Asia Command, and basing a 500-man Corps Léger d'Intervention in India. The British paper would confine the mission to Indochina matters, bar the French from general strategy planning, and accept French forces only late in the war. Mountbatten, it notes, was prepared to accept both proposals.
frus-1944-quebec-d254: The United States Chiefs recommended a one-line order in C.C.S. 674/1, dated September 12, 1944. Effective 15 September, SCAEF would assume command of the Dragoon forces, following the plan Eisenhower recommended in Scaf 77. The Combined Chiefs approved dispatch at their 172d meeting that day. The message went out as telegram Facs 76 to Eisenhower and Wilson, executing the transfer Wilson had proposed and Eisenhower had shaped.
frus-1944-quebec-d54:
An assistant to the President's military aide, named Park in the heading, wrote to Naval Aide Wilson Brown on September 5, 1944. The message moved inside the White House's small military office. It appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Notes between the President's military staff settled the practical questions of a journeying wartime presidency: papers to be carried, officers to attend, and communications to be kept open. A week before Quebec, such details multiplied. For readers, the message shows the conference at its most workmanlike level, where success depended on aides whose names history mostly forgets.
frus-1945-50-intel-d154:
Dated 7 June 1946, this memorandum runs from the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers) to the National Intelligence Authority. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 154 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d254:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 15 December 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 254 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d354:
Dated 22 November 1948, this memorandum runs from the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong) to the Intelligence Survey Group. The State Department prints it as document 354 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d54:
Secretary Byrnes wrote to both Secretary Patterson and Secretary Forrestal on 10 December 1945. One letter to the two heads of the military departments shows the endgame of the autumn contest approaching. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

By December the rival plans had been cut down to a shape the president could accept. The secretaries were settling the last points among themselves. Byrnes writing to War and Navy together kept the talks at the top and in step. Readers should set this letter near Smith's November papers to Truman. Between them, the design of the National Intelligence Authority, announced six weeks later, becomes visible in the record before it was named.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d154:
Do it today, Churchill urged on 16 December 1944. This excerpt of his telegram 853 answers Roosevelt's questions about Poland from the day before. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Churchill thanks the President for his message and trusts he will carry out the proposal in it. The proposal is a note to Stalin asking him to postpone any firm action on Poland until the three leaders can get together. That suggestion, Churchill writes, is most valuable and also extremely urgent. His fear is close at hand: Stalin may at any moment recognize the Lublin Committee as the government of Poland.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d254:
General Deane reported the same Moscow military meeting to the Joint Chiefs on 15 October 1944. His top secret cable from the American military mission, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, names those present on all three sides. It is the staff record of the night Harriman described to the President.

Field Marshal Brooke opened with a fair survey of the war in Europe and in Italy, Deane writes, a good picture of British and American collaboration. Stalin suggested invading through Switzerland to outflank the Siegfried Line. On Italy, he said Soviet forces did not mean to advance westward through Yugoslavia. The allies, he thought, might join up in time in the neighborhood of Vienna. Churchill then summed up Britain's whole part in the war, ninety divisions in all.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d354:
Poland took over the plenary at Yalta on February 6, 1945, once voting in the world body had been covered, and Matthews's minutes follow the talk. Roosevelt spoke first. He said he came from a great distance, which gave him a more distant view of the problem. Six or seven million Poles lived in the United States, he noted.

He repeated his Tehran stand in favor of the Curzon line for Poland's eastern border. Poles, like the Chinese, wanted to save face, he said. Stalin broke in to ask who would save face — the Poles in Poland or the exiles. The exchange sets up the hardest fight of the conference.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d454:
Amended on February 10, 1945, this draft of the Declaration on Liberated Europe shows the text near its final shape. The Soviet Premier, the British Prime Minister, and the American President declare their shared accord. During the brief time of unrest in liberated Europe, the three states will align their policies.

The aim is to help peoples freed from Nazi rule, and peoples of the former Axis satellite states, solve their pressing problems by free means. Order in Europe and the rebuilding of home economies must come by steps that let freed peoples rule themselves. One typo — "considted" — survives in the draft, a mark of haste.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d54:
Two Allied ships needed to slip through the Turkish Straits before the Big Three met in the Black Sea. On 13 January 1945, Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt, in a personal and top secret telegram, about how to handle the passage. The message is part of the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences.

Churchill asks whether Turkey should be warned in advance. The ships could be called merchant vessels under the Montreux Convention, but Turkish officials could still stop and inspect them. He suggests telling President Inonu, at the last possible moment, only that heads of government would meet somewhere in the Black Sea.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d154:
The British Chiefs of Staff sent over their draft agenda for the Anglo-American staff conference on June 15, 1945. The memorandum, C.C.S. 880, is document 154 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The two staffs would meet beside the leaders at Terminal to plan the rest of the Pacific war.

The ten items are all about Japan: progress in the Pacific and Southeast Asia, an estimate of the Japanese situation, future operations, and British participation. They also cover command arrangements, Russian entry into the war, help from the French, Dutch, and Portuguese, a planning date for the war's end, and overall priorities. The British offer papers on their own role and on Southeast Asia command, and ask the Americans to cover operations and Russian participation. The list is marked purely provisional.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d254:
Admiral Leahy stated his Korea recommendation in a short undated note printed as document 254 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. The note, from the Truman Papers, is printed from the unsigned ribbon copy in the President's files.

Leahy recommends a four-power agreement. Upon Japan's defeat, Korea should be placed under a trusteeship composed of China, Great Britain, the Soviet Union, and the United States. The trusteeship should last as long as necessary for Korea to demonstrate its capacity to govern itself as a free and independent sovereign state. The single sentence gives the position the President's own chief of staff favored as the delegation sailed for Potsdam, matching the line the State Department papers had built.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d354:
Dutch and Belgian occupation of German land is traced in a memorandum by George Elsey, drawn from the Yalta record. At a full session on February 5, 1945, President Roosevelt had raised the Dutch floods. German forces had wrecked the dikes, and salt water had drowned large stretches of Dutch farmland.

Roosevelt thought Dutch farmers should receive, for a time, German land as compensation. The flooded fields, he said, would need at least five years before crops could grow again. He also felt the Dutch might claim a voice in the machinery controlling Germany. Elsey notes the President never developed the idea further at Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d454:
Northern Greece is the subject of an extract from MacVeagh's despatch No. 1213, written at Athens on June 23, 1945. He encloses a first report from Cromie at Salonika, dated June 15, together with a report by Captain McNeill that Cromie forwarded. McNeill's subject is partisan troop concentrations in Yugoslav Macedonia.

That matter, MacVeagh writes, is of extreme importance, in political and military terms alike, and it is most desirable to know the truth of it. He singles out McNeill's finding that no rise in autonomous Macedonian agitation inside Greece had been detected as a result. Greece, the report implies, had more to fear for the moment from the Bulgarian side.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d54:
President Truman thanked Churchill for accepting the July 15 meeting date in a top secret telegram sent June 7, 1945. It is document 54 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The message also reports back on the mission of Joseph Davies, Truman's envoy, who had just visited London for talks with Churchill and Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden.

Truman explains that duties at home, tied to the close of the fiscal year, made an earlier meeting impossible for him. He warmly agrees with Churchill's wish that the three leaders meet all at once, not in pairs. He adds that Davies's reports on the London talks were helpful, and thanks Churchill and Eden for their courtesy to his envoy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d554:
From Belgrade on July 10, 1945, U.S. charge Harold Shantz sent a top secret wire to Washington. It is document 554 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The wire passes on private words from Milan Grol. He was a non-communist minister in Yugoslavia's government.

Grol had given Tito a memo with three demands. The wartime assembly must be widened. A basic law must guard press, speech, and fair votes. The shape of the new regime must also be settled. Grol said all the non-communist parties backed him and would quit if he was refused. He hoped U.S. papers would ask why the assembly had not grown. The report shows the joint government close to breaking apart.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d654:
The Acting Secretary of State pressed for speed on the Tangier talks in a wire of June 23, 1945. Sent to Ambassador Caffery in Paris, it is document 654 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. News of the planned talks had already leaked widely.

Grew warns that the press coverage will prove deeply embarrassing if the Department cannot issue a statement soon. A decision on where the talks will sit is needed at the earliest moment. The Soviet government should be told as soon as the place is chosen. The message to Moscow would say that informal talks among the British, French, and U.S. governments were being held. It would promise that Moscow would be kept fully informed. Grew suggests the host government take the lead in sending it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1054: Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled Arthur Lane, the appointed ambassador to Poland, on July 31, 1945. The cable carries the text of a fresh Big Three agreement. It concerns the transfer of German populations into Germany, and its words later entered the conference Protocol. Lane must concert with his Soviet and British colleagues on passing the text to the Polish provisional government. The communication must be treated as strictly secret until the conference issues an official statement. Copies also went to the missions in Prague and Budapest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1154:
Charles Yost wrote a third memorandum for the Central Secretariat on 8 August 1945. The summit had ended six days before. The secretariat's chief still had files to sort, copies to certify, and the conference record to close in good order.

His series of notes traces the long tail of a summit. Leaders fly home; the paperwork stays behind until someone files it. Yost's office was that someone for the American side. This note is one beat in that closing work. Together, his memoranda show how a mountain of talk and paper became an archive that later readers could trust and use.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1254: Staff of the State Department wrote this internal memorandum on 25 July 1945. It moved inside the department, from desk to desk, as the summit ran abroad. Papers of this kind did the department's daily thinking while its chiefs sat at Potsdam. They fixed facts, framed choices, and kept a record of what was weighed, and why it mattered.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1354:
From London, Ambassador John Winant sent another cable to the acting secretary of state on 20 July 1945. It followed his message of two days before in the volume's Tangier and Spain papers. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Winant's seat in London made him a relay for British thinking on questions far beyond Britain itself. Spain and Tangier both touched British interests in the Mediterranean, so London's views reached Washington through him. Readers can follow how one embassy's reporting fed several files at once. The cable also shows the pace of July 1945, when no post, however senior, sent just one message and rested.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-154: This editorial note stands after document 710 without a number in the second Potsdam volume. The Foreign Relations editors placed such notes to keep a dense record readable. A note may supply a source, a date, or a pointer to a kindred text. Here it supports the reader among the final days' crowded staff papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-54:
Department of State minutes record the plenary session of July 21, 1945, opening at 5:15 p.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. President Truman opened the meeting by calling on Secretary Byrnes for a report.

Byrnes reported the morning's foreign ministers' meeting to the three leaders. He read the parts on the Council of Foreign Ministers and on German economic questions. He then turned to Poland, the session's hard core. The subcommittee on the Polish question had presented its report that morning. It had been unable to reach full agreement on the statement. The foreign ministers had tried the disputed points and failed as well. All agreed to refer the matter to the heads of government for final decision. Byrnes drew attention to the second paragraph, on transferring assets to the Polish provisional government.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d754:
The United States Chiefs of Staff recorded their joint view in this memorandum of July 21, 1945. Document 754 states the military chiefs' position in formal staff form. It dates from the Potsdam Conference's first week. The chiefs' agreed papers carried great weight with the President. The memo joined the second Potsdam volume.

A chiefs' memorandum differs from minutes. Minutes record talk; a memorandum states a settled line. Readers find the product of debate, not the debate itself. The document shows the military speaking with one voice at a key moment. Such unity strengthened the hand of the man they advised in the talks next door.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d854:
Collado wrote to Assistant Secretary Clayton and to the Secretary of State on July 18, 1945. Document 854 carries the financial office's view to the Department's top economic hands. Clayton was the Secretary's chief aide for economic affairs. Their channel handled the money side of the peace. The letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

Financial letters show the settlement's skeleton. Reparations, loans, and trade all passed across these desks. Readers see experts advising the men who would sign. The document also shows the Department's economic team working as a unit at the summit's start. Their quiet mail underpinned the conference's loudest arguments.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d954: American staff wrote these comments on July 30, 1945, answering three paragraphs of the Soviet reparations proposal of July 29. Their chief target is the Soviet wish to state capital removals in tons. Weight, they argue, cannot show the value or military weight of varied machinery. Tonnage quotas would invite stripping whole plants at random, sparking disputes and wrecking capacity Germany needs. Recurring reparations cannot be set before the sides agree on capacity to remove. The staff accepts the Soviet goods list as a basis for discussion.
frus-1955-57v16-d454: A 1955-1957 FRUS editorial note from the Suez Crisis volume. The 1956 crisis filled the pages. This note provides that context. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gao-gaoreports-b-297454: Wyse Technology took its January 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297654: Greater Pacific Aquatics took its February 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298454: Staab Construction took its September 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Builders get the same full hearing as everyone.
gao-gaoreports-b-298854: Advanced Technology Systems doubled its December 2006 protest — two case numbers, one tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298954: Northrop Grumman tripled its January 2007 protest — three case numbers, one defense fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles all three. The giant challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Triple filings get one thorough answer. Three dockets, one thorough answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-299054: Continental Staffing took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Staffing deals get the same full hearing as the hardware ones.
gao-gaoreports-b-299154: Palmetto GBA took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Health giants get the same fair hearing as the small firms.
gao-gaoreports-b-310454: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by KAR Contracting, LLC. The December 19, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-400154: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Commercial Window Shield. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-454: Unfunded mandate reform views varied in 2005, and GAO's report says opinions differed on the act's strengths, weaknesses, and improvement options. The review takes the poll. The states deserved the honest debate. The views were gathered. The states deserved the honest debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1054: The special counsels' spending got audited in 2006, and GAO's report grades the independent and special counsel outlays for the half-year. The findings deliver the formal opinion. The report shows even the investigators get investigated. The watchers got watched. The investigators got their own audit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-154: The national airspace transformation needed cultural change in 2005, and GAO's report says the overhaul required new thinking and balanced funding. The findings prescribe the shift. The report warns that the crowded skies deserved modern control. The change had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-454: The Army Corps' Mississippi classroom contract got a GAO look in 2006, and the report examines the Katrina-related deal. The findings review the procurement. The report warns that the storm's schoolrooms deserved honest bidding. The contract had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-54: Hospital quality data needed more rigor in 2006, and GAO's report says CMS needed tougher methods to ensure the public data were reliable. The findings demand the standards. The report warns that the patients deserved trustworthy grades. The methods had to be rigorous.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-554: Highway tolling was spreading in 2006, and GAO's report says states' expanding use illustrated diverse challenges and strategies. The findings map the trend. The report warns that the pay-to-drive wave needed honest accounting. The strategies had to be weighed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-654: Medicare drug benefit letters needed clarity in 2006, and GAO's report says communications to beneficiaries could improve. The findings demand the plain talk. The report warns that the seniors deserved understandable mail. The communications had to be clear. The seniors deserved understandable mail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-854: The visa waiver program needed a risk check in 2006, and GAO's report says stronger actions were required to assess and mitigate the dangers. The findings demand the scrutiny. The report warns that the open door needed a better lock. The risks had to be managed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1054: Cash for not plowing — GAO's 2007 report shows farm payouts tipping landowners toward turning grassland into cropland. The conservation dollars meant to protect soil were, perversely, nudging plows forward in some cases. The findings untangle a knotty trade: paying farmers well while keeping fragile land unplowed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-154: The financial cops were learning to share notes in 2007, and GAO's report says the consolidated-supervision agencies could sharpen how they measured themselves. The findings press for better scorecards. The report's timing proved prophetic: the storm was a year away.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-454: Homeland Security faced its GAO checkup again in 2007 — mission and management both on the exam table. The briefing notes real strides since the department's hasty assembly, plus the management tangles that would not loosen. The verdict: a work in progress, graded on a curve of its own making.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-54: Drug ads on TV needed a sharper watchdog in 2007, and GAO's report says the FDA's oversight of direct-to-consumer advertising wanted improvement. The findings target the hype. The report warns that the pill commercials should not outrun the science. The ads had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-654: The energy-saving prize was big but blocked in 2007 — GAO's report says real hurdles stood between America and serious efficiency gains. The findings map the barriers. The report frames negawatts as the cheapest power plant never built — if the nation could clear the path.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-54: Millions in bad contract payouts — that's what GAO found at the agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid in this 2007 report. Weak money controls let shaky bills get paid without a hard look first. The report maps where the checks failed and lays out fixes to guard two of the biggest pots of public money in the nation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-554: GAO published its findings on 2010 Census: Census Bureau Should Take Action to Improve the Credibility and Accuracy of Its Cost Estimate for the Decennial Census in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-754: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at peacekeeping: Thousands Trained but United States Is Unlikely to Complete All Activities by 2010 and Some Improvements Are Needed. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-854: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on defense Production Act: Agencies Lack Policies and Guidance for Use of Key Authorities. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-954: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at electronic Health Records: DOD and VA Have Increased Their Sharing of Health Information, but More Work Remains. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenthal-johan:
Johann Jacob Löwenthal (1810–1876) was a Hungarian chess master born in Budapest, profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and A. Porter. He held a civil post under Louis Kossuth, and when Kossuth fell he was expelled from Austria-Hungary. He emigrated to America in 1849 and settled in England in 1851.

At Manchester in 1857 Löwenthal defeated Anderssen for first place, and in 1858 he took first prize at Birmingham, though he lost a match with Morphy that same year. The article follows his second career as chess editor for London papers and “The Chess Players’ Magazine,” and notes his 1860 book on Morphy’s games. It also records that, under the influence of W. G. Ward, he became a Roman Catholic. For chess readers, the entry is a compact record of a top player turned writer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magdala-10254:
Magdala, a town in Galilee, is located and described in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. It is probably the birthplace of Mary Magdalene. A Talmudic saying claims the Romans destroyed it for its immorality. Jesus once sailed to it across the Sea of Gennesaret, the Gospels report.

The article weighs where the town stood. Some placed it on the eastern shore because of the boat journey. The writers judge the western shore more likely, near the modern village of Al-Majdal north of Tiberias. Rabbinic sources put it close to Tiberias, with a seminary, a synagogue, and a school. A few teachers of the Law were born there, including Rabbi Isaac and Yudan. The entry also warns that other place names built on Migdal, tower, are not quarters of Magdala. It is a careful exercise in sorting ancient geography.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandelstamm-leo:
Leon Mandelstamm, a Russian Hebraist and educator, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Zhagory in 1809, he learned rabbinic and secular knowledge under his father and brothers. His progressive views scandalized his wife's family at Keidany. He was forced to divorce after six months of marriage. He died at St. Petersburg in 1889.

The article follows his rise in Russian education. He graduated in philology at St. Petersburg in 1844, the first Jew in Russia to win that honor. When Lilienthal fled Russia in 1845, Mandelstamm took his place under Minister Uvarov. For twelve years he built Jewish schools, including the rabbinical schools of Wilna and Jitomir. He also controlled the candle-tax funds that paid for them, which made him hated by conservative masses. Later years softened that hatred. The entry shows the price of serving a government's school plan for the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-samuel-104:
Samuel Marx was chief rabbi of Bayonne in France. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was born at Dürkheim, in Bavaria, in 1817. He was a cousin of David Marx, the chief rabbi of Bordeaux. After his studies at the rabbinical school at Metz, he directed the Jewish religious school at Nancy and assisted that city's chief rabbi.

In 1843 he became rabbi of Saint-Esprit and Bayonne. He became chief rabbi three years later and held the post until his death in 1887. The entry is brief and rests mainly on his printed sermons. Among them are his installation address of 1846 and a sermon on the mezuzah. The list ends with an address for the centenary of Sir Moses Montefiore in 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-megillat-setari:
Megillat Setarim, the "concealed roll" of R. Hiyya, is the subject of a detective piece in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, by Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach. The roll supposedly lay hidden in Hiyya's house of study and held legal teachings he had recorded. Three maxims from it survive, quoted by Rab in the Talmud with the formula, "I found a hidden roll in the house of study of R. Hiyya."

Why hidden? Rashi's answer, that scholars secretly wrote down rulings because recording law was forbidden, is weighed and found wanting: the ban had already been lifted by Judah the Prince's written Mishnah. The article prefers a sharper explanation. Hiyya's roll gathered sayings Judah had excluded, plus corrections that contradicted him, and Hiyya kept it out of sight while the Prince lived, so as not to offend him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mende-10654:
Mende was chief town of the Lozère in France. It was once capital of the Gévaudan. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn give it a Jewish history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish community stood there in the twelfth century. The ruins of its synagogue could still be seen in 1904. After the expulsion of 1306, king and bishop quarreled over the spoils. In 1310 Philip the Fair yielded the Bishop of Mende a third of the confiscated Jewish property. He yielded a house too, one that had belonged to a Jew named Ferrier.

The article widens to the whole county. Jews lived at Marvejols, where the mystic Jacob ha-Levi dwelt about 1203. Jews lived at Villefort too, where the site of the old Jewish cemetery was still known. Even the map remembers them. It does so in villages called Salomon, Mont-David, Booz, Ruth, and Obed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-friederic:
Friederich Christian Meyer was a Jewish convert to Christianity who was born at Hamburg in the later seventeenth century and died in Belgium about 1738. Gotthard Deutsch and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. Baptized at Bremen, he spent thirty years traveling as a missionary to the Jews.

The article lists four of his works, all arguing his new faith. His Licht zu Erleuchten die Juden, printed at Leipsic in 1711, exalted Jesus, while a German pamphlet of 1713 set Moses and Jesus side by side to prove Jesus greater. A Hamburg work of 1719 blamed the length of the Jewish exile on the crucifixion, and a Hebrew treatise argued Jesus' divinity from the Prophets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minis-10854:
Minis is the family that helped found Jewish Georgia. Cyrus Adler and L. Hühner trace it generation by generation in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry published in 1906. Abraham Minis reached Savannah on July 11, 1733. He came with the colony's first Jewish settlers, weeks behind Oglethorpe himself. His name stands on the colony's earliest deed, a grant of town lots that December.

His son Philip was born at Savannah in 1734. He was called the first white male child born in Georgia. Philip bankrolled the Revolution as a merchant patriot. He also guided French troops at the siege of Savannah. The British answered by naming him in their Disqualifying Act of 1780. Later Minises presided over Savannah's congregation. They served in the War of 1812, the Confederacy, and the Georgia Hussars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montagu-sir-sam:
Sir Samuel Montagu was born at Liverpool on December 21, 1832. He was the banker who became Anglo-Jewry's one-man welfare state. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born Montagu Samuel; his parents reversed the names. He reached London in 1847. In 1853 he founded Samuel Montagu & Co., foreign bankers.

For over twenty-five years he sat at the center of the Board of Guardians, the Board of Deputies, and the United Synagogue. He founded the Jewish Working Men's Club. With Lord Rothschild he helped plant an industrial school in Jerusalem. In 1882 he went to Brody to inspect the refugee emigration. Russia answered his 1886 tour of its Jewish towns by ordering him out of Moscow within twenty-four hours.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-abrah:
Moses ben Abraham Abinu was a Christian who converted to Judaism and became a Hebrew printer and author. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Nikolsburg, he worked for two Amsterdam printers in 1686 and 1687. By 1690 he had a press of his own there.

In 1709 Moses set up a printing office at Halle in Germany. There he printed his Tela'ot Mosheh, a Judeo-German work on the Ten Tribes, in 1712. Two years later the king closed his press over anti-Christian passages, jailed him, and seized his books. Friends helped him escape to Amsterdam, where his children later became printers too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-solom:
Moses ben Solomon ha-Kohen Ashkenazi was a German tosafist who lived at Mayence in the twelfth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn. Though settled in Germany, he appears to have been born in France. He studied under Isaac ha-Zaken and, it seems, under Jacob Tam as well.

His pupils became leading rabbis, among them Baruch of Mayence, Eleazar of Worms, and Eliezer ben Joel ha-Levi. His responsa are mentioned in the Mordekai, and Asher ben Jehiel quotes his Sefer ha-Dinin. The entry is a knot in the web of teachers and pupils who carried Talmud study in the Rhineland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naamah-11254:
Naamah is a name carried by two women and one town in the Bible, and the Jewish Encyclopedia article treats all three. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote it. The first Naamah is the daughter of Lamech and Zillah and sister of Tubal-cain in Genesis. Some rabbis made her Noah's wife.

The second Naamah was an Ammonite, a wife of Solomon and the mother of King Rehoboam. The rabbis praised her righteousness, saying God had spared Ammon for her sake. The third Naamah is a town of Judah listed in Joshua, perhaps the home of Zophar the Naamathite. The entry gathers the rabbinic argument over whether the first Naamah was pious or an idol singer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-isaac-11:
Isaac Nathan was an English composer who carried music to Australia. Joseph Jacobs, Goodman Lipkind, Cyrus Adler, and Francis L. Cohen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Canterbury in 1792. He was meant for the ministry and studied at Cambridge. Love of music sent him to train under Corri instead.

Nathan sang at Covent Garden in 1816, but his voice was weak. He turned to composing and teaching music. He taught Princess Charlotte and served George IV as music historian. In 1841 he settled in Sydney and lectured there. He is best known for setting Byron's Hebrew Melodies to music. Six of those tunes found a place in synagogue use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-netter-justin-a:
Justin Arnold Netter was a French doctor of wide study. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Strasburg on Sept. 20, 1855. He trained in Paris hospitals from 1876 to 1884. He took his medical degree in 1883.

Netter became assistant professor in Paris in 1889. He served the Tenon and Trousseau hospitals in turn. In 1897 he took a chair of experimental anatomy. The Academy of Medicine elected him in 1904. Cholera service in 1892 won him the Legion of Honor. He wrote on lungs, meningitis, diphtheria, and plague. Typhus, cholera, and infantile scurvy also fill his studies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nishmat-11554:
Nishmat opens with the words, the soul of. Cyrus Adler and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is part of the morning liturgy for Sabbaths. On festivals it serves the same place in prayer. It leads up to the benediction after the Psalms.

The Mishnah calls it, with that blessing, Benediction of Song. The German form holds 340 Hebrew words in all. One line protests, beside Thee we have no King. Scholars see a later stroke against Christianity there. The heart of Nishmat thanks God for rain. Each drop of rain counts as its own benefit. Even mouths full of song, like the sea, fall short. That thanksgiving may predate the Temple's fall by centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oklah-we-oklah-:
Oklah we-Oklah is an old work on the Masorah, the Bible notes. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Masorah is the set of notes on the Hebrew text. This work gathers those notes and rules in one place. No one knows who wrote the work itself.

The work lists rare words and odd forms in the text. Some lists run by the first letters of words. Some run by the order of the Bible books. Its name comes from its first two words. Oklah stands in one verse of the Bible. We-oklah stands in a verse of Genesis. The book was praised as the most sound work on the Masorah. Gershom ben Judah made a copy of it by hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ordeal-11754:
The ordeal was a trial that called on God for proof. The board and Ludwig Blau wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It took the place of proof from men or from things. Its name comes from a word for judgment. In the Middle Ages, church and state both blessed its use.

The ordeal took many forms in those dark years. Trial by cross, by fire, and by water are named. Set forms of prayer were drawn up for its use. The rite spread wide among the Aryan peoples of Europe. It lives yet in India, the piece notes. Marks of it are found in the past of Israel too. Some see a mark in a verse of Exodus, the piece says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paulus-of-pragu:
Paulus of Prague was born Elhanan ben Menahem in Poland. He was born at Kholm about 1540 and died at Prague. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He converted to Christianity as a young man.

Paulus was baptized at Nuremberg and later baptized again at Chelm. He wrote German books in defense of his new faith. His best known work is Mysterium Novum, printed in 1580. In it he used gematria to find Jesus hidden in Scripture. He also printed the Book of Jonah in four languages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesahim-passove:
Pesahim is the Mishnah treatise on the Passover laws. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is the third treatise of the order Mo'ed. It runs ten chapters with eighty-seven paragraphs.

The opening chapters govern the hunt for leaven. They fix when leaven may be eaten and when burned. Later parts name the grains fit for unleavened bread. They list the bitter herbs for the table. Local custom rules the morning before the feast. The treatise also covers the paschal lamb in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pilsen-12154:
Pilsen is a Bohemian city with an old Jewish past. Gotthard Deutsch and Alexander Kisch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there in the fourteenth century. They had a synagogue and a burial ground. Jews formed large parts of nearby village life.

The city expelled its Jews in the 1500s. Only after 1848 could Jews settle there again. Village families moved in and formed a congregation. Their constitution won approval in 1859, a rare honor. A grand new synagogue rose in 1893. By 1904 the community counted 3,170 souls. Its yearly budget stood near 74,000 crowns then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollonais-gasto:
Gaston Pollonais was a French journalist born at Paris in 1865. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Désiré Pollonais, mayor of Villefranche. His mother was the writer Amélie Pollonais. About 1890 he began work for the papers.

Pollonais first wrote for a Belgian paper from France. He also wrote for Le Voltaire, Le Figaro, and Le Gaulois. For a time he edited the paper Le Soir. He then went back to Le Gaulois for good. In the Dreyfus affair he backed the nationalist side with zeal. In 1902 he became a Catholic. He also wrote plays for the French stage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pribram-przibra:
Alfred Pribram was an Austrian doctor born at Prague in 1841. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took his medical degree at Prague in 1861. He then worked at the city's general hospital. In time he joined the German university there as a teacher.

Pribram became a teacher of disease and cure in 1881. He also led the first medical clinic of the university. Before that he ran its dispensary for some years. His books and essays deal with fevers and their cure. One early work treats a returning fever in depth. The entry lists his many papers for the reader.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pyke-lionel-edw:
Lionel Edward Pyke was an English barrister of London. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Chatham in 1854. He died at Brighton in 1899. His father, Joseph Pyke, was warden of the Central Synagogue. Lionel was the second son of that house.

Pyke was schooled at Rochester Cathedral Grammar School. He read at London University and took two degrees. He joined the Inner Temple as a student in 1874. In 1877 he was called to the bar at last. He made his life in the London courts from then on. In 1880 he took a seat on a council of his people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rami-b-ezekiel-:
Rami b. Ezekiel was a Babylonian amora of the third generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the younger brother of Judah b. Ezekiel. Judah founded the academy at Pumbedita.

The article says Rami studied under his father Ezekiel. Against his brother's view, he left Babylon for Palestine. At Bene-Berak he found the land rich, as Scripture promised. Later he returned home to Babylonia. There he corrected sayings his brother cited from Rab and Samuel. The entry gives a family dispute with real weight for Talmud study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reichenberg-126:
Reichenberg is a city in Bohemia where Jews long faced a ban. Gotthard Deutsch and Alexander Kisch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. No Jews could live there until a law in 1860. That law lifted Austrian limits on Jewish residence.

The article says about thirty families settled first. A synagogue opened in a rented house in 1861. Town and state officials attended its opening. The congregation gained legal standing in 1862. A cemetery followed two years later. Before that, burials went to distant Turnau. A burial society aided poor sick members as well. By 1869 the congregation counted ninety families. The entry shows a community built from scratch in one decade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenhain-jakob:
Jakob Rosenhain was a German pianist born at Mannheim on December 27, 1813. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He died at Baden-Baden on March 21, 1894, after a long musical career.

A one-act piece by Rosenhain, Der Besuch im Irrenhause, scored a hit at Frankfort in 1834. His later operas met a cooler welcome from audiences. In Paris he joined J. B. Cramer in founding a school for piano playing. After 1863 he left opera behind and gave himself to instrumental music. His works include three symphonies, one of them called Im Frühling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sama-b-rakta-13: Sama b. Rakta was a Babylonian amora of the sixth generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a contemporary of Rabina I, with whom he disputed a point of law in Kiddushin. He also passed on a saying of Rab Awia in Baba Mezia. He is probably the R. Sama who sat with Rabina before R. Ashi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-and-yate:
Samuel and Yates are two families that led Liverpool's Jewish congregation in the early nineteenth century. Joseph Jacobs wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. Both lines trace back to Strelitz, in Germany.

Ralph Samuel was born, probably at Strelitz, on November 22, 1738. Samuel Yates, also of Strelitz, married into the Abrahams family there. Three Yates daughters married three sons of Ralph Samuel in time. Those marriages fused the two houses into one combined family. Later members reached Parliament, among them Herbert Samuel, seated in 1902. Stuart M. Samuel served the Home for Jewish Incurables and a workingmen's club.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schefftel-simon:
Isidore Singer and Felix Perles wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Simon Baruch Schefftel. He was a German Hebraist. Schefftel was born on June 14, 1813, at Breslau. He died on March 9, 1885. In 1848 he settled at Posen as a merchant. He retired from business in 1871. Then he gave his years to one great work.

Schefftel wrote a large Hebrew commentary on the Targum Onḳelos. That Targum is the classic Aramaic rendering of the Pentateuch. His son-in-law Joseph Perles published the book after his death. It appeared at Munich in 1888 as Bi'ure Onḳelos. The commentary holds many fine critical and word-by-word notes. It stands as one of the key reference works on the Targum Onḳelos.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemaiah-of-tro:
Shemaiah of Troyes was a tosafist of the early twelfth century and a pupil of Rashi. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He likely married into the family of Samuel ben Meir. His glosses appear across several Talmud tractates.

Legal writers cite Shemaiah as a casuist on hard questions. He probably compiled the book called Sefer ha-Likkutim. Rashi's Sefer ha-Pardes, as it survives, seems his compilation too. He merged Rashi's original with another work, Sefer ha-Orah. His commentary on Middot was printed in the 1522 Talmud. The entry shows a pupil who preserved his master's teaching by editing it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sihin-13654:
Sihin was a large, populous city in the territory of Zebulon's tribe. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. It stood near Sepphoris in the Galilee region. After Jerusalem's destruction the city lost its importance.

From then on it was called merely Kefar Sihin, a village name. Josephus mentions a place that may be the same town. His Sogane sat near Sepphoris in his war account. The Talmud names the city under several variant forms. Its vessels were said to match metal in durability. A fire once broke out in a notable's house there. The entry gathers scattered mentions to keep a faded Galilean city on the map.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simons-david-13:
David Simons was a Dutch jurist born at The Hague on November 3, 1860. Isidore Singer and E Slijper wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied law at the University of Leyden. He took his doctor's degree there in 1883. He then set up as a lawyer in Amsterdam.

In 1897 Simons became professor of penal law at Utrecht. His doctoral thesis dealt with freedom of the press. It had won the university gold medal in 1882. He wrote a handbook on criminal procedure, in its third edition by 1901. He also began a textbook of Dutch criminal law. From 1902 he edited the Weekblad van het Recht.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-edward-:
Edward Solomon was an English musician and composer born in London in 1856. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was largely a self-taught musician in his craft. He gained a strong name as a composer of light opera. He had a gift for pleasing melody and bold orchestration.

He conducted many comic operas in London theaters. He wrote opera bouffes much like the Gilbert and Sullivan works. Billee Taylor, produced in 1880, was an early success. Claude Duval and The Red Hussar followed in quick order. The Nautch Girl and The Vicar of Bray also drew crowds. He died in London in January 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spices-13954:
Spices are aromatic plant substances used in food, salves, and perfumes. Emil G Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Ancient Jews knew almost no condiments except salt for food. Even cinnamon was used only in unguents and like mixtures. Aromatic herbs served mainly in mulled wine at table.

Nearly all perfume ingredients were vegetable in ancient Israel. One exception was shehelet, from a mussel of the Red Sea. It formed one part of the Temple incense blend. Burned alone it smells foul, but it gives pungency to mixtures. Galbanum, another incense part, worked in the same way. Oils were drawn from gums by boiling them in fats.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stobbe-johann-e:
Otto Stobbe was a Christian historian of the Jews born in 1831. Joseph Jacobs and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Königsberg on June 28 of that year. He studied philology, history, and law at Königsberg. He died at Leipsic on May 19, 1887.

Stobbe taught German law at Königsberg, Breslau, and Leipsic. His 1866 book studies Jews in medieval Germany. It was the first to treat them from a strict legal standpoint. He traced links between Byzantine and Carolingian treatment of Jews. The book became a standard and was reprinted in 1902. Though Christian, he helped collect sources on German Jewish history. The entry honors a fair-minded legal historian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sylvester-james:
James Joseph Sylvester was an English mathematician born in London in 1814. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on September 3 of that year. He studied at Liverpool and at Cambridge. He died in London on March 15, 1897.

Sylvester placed second in Cambridge's math tripos in 1837. His Jewish origin barred him from taking the degree. Only in 1872 did Cambridge grant it after the Tests Act. He taught at London, Virginia, and Woolwich in turn. At Johns Hopkins he founded the American Journal of Mathematics. Oxford made him its geometry professor in 1883. The Royal Society gave him its Royal and Copley medals. The entry honors a scholar who beat a rigged gate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarshish-14254:
Tarshish is a far maritime land named in the Bible. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Genesis lists Tarshish as a son of Javan. Like its kin names, it denotes a country. Prophets place it among earth's remotest regions.

Jonah fled toward Tarshish from God's presence. Isaiah names it among places that never heard of God. Any great sea-going ship was called a ship of Tarshish. The phrase did not mean the ship sailed there. Solomon and Jehoshaphat owned such fleets in the texts. Tarshish traded in silver, iron, tin, and lead. Jeremiah and Ezekiel record that commerce. A precious stone also bears the Tarshish name. The entry gathers every thread of an elusive place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thebes-14354:
Thebes, the famed Greek city and capital of Boeotia, had a notable Jewish past. Samuel Krauss wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. No documents prove Jews lived there in ancient times. Still, Jews lived all across Greece, including nearby Athens and Corinth.

Benjamin of Tudela gives the first firm report. He found more than 2,000 Jewish families in Thebes. Their silk and purple work was the finest in Greece. Many studied Mishnah and Talmud at a high level. Named scholars led the community in his day. After his account, the record falls silent. The entry shows both the wealth and the gaps of the evidence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tortoise-14454: Tortoise renders the Hebrew word zab in the Authorized Version at Leviticus 11:29. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Some commentators also read tortoises into a word in Hosea. Old versions, Greek and Syriac, back that reading. Two land tortoise species live in Palestine. Several water tortoises live there too, Emys caspica being most common. The Talmud uses zab for the toad as well. It even tells of a water-snake born from toad and snake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tyre-14554:
Tyre, chief city of Phoenicia, traded and warred with Israel across centuries. Emil G. Hirsch and W. Max Muller wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. King Hiram befriended both David and Solomon. He sent Lebanon wood and skilled workmen for their building. Solomon paid him in grain and Galilean land.

Tyrian ships sailed for Solomon from Red Sea ports. Tyre grew immensely rich on commerce, Ezekiel shows. Prophets cursed its flourishing slave trade in particular. Tyrian merchants sold fish and wares in Jerusalem. The city stands for all Phoenicia in several psalms. Sidon claimed Tyre was merely its later colony. Ethbaal of Tyre fathered the infamous Jezebel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vecinho-vizino-:
Joseph Vecinho, also spelled Vizino, served Portugal's king as doctor and scientist. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Vecinho lived at the end of the fifteenth century. He studied math and the stars under Abraham Zacuto. King John II trusted his skill greatly.

The king sent Vecinho to the Guinea coast to measure the sun. In 1484 Columbus laid his western plan before the king. Vecinho sat on the panel that judged it. The panel said no, and Columbus blamed the Jew Joseph. Still, Columbus used Vecinho's translation of Zacuto's star tables on his voyage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weissmann-chaje:
Marcus Weissmann Chajes was an Austrian scholar and editor. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Tarnow, Galicia, in 1830. Rabbis trained him for a rabbinical career. At age ten he wrote Hebrew letters in verse. At fifteen he versified the Polish revolt's failure.

In 1872 Weissmann Chajes founded a Lemberg journal. Maggid Mishneh covered Jewish history and Hebrew literature. Only four numbers of it ever appeared. He then settled in Vienna and edited other journals. His books gather Talmudic proverbs in rhymed verse. He also wrote elegies, glosses, and parables. His index serves readers of the Jerusalem Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wise-isaac-maye:
Isaac Mayer Wise (1819-1900) was the best known Reform rabbi in the United States. Cyrus Adler and David Philipson wrote his long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Bohemia, Wise reached New York in 1846 and soon led a synagogue in Albany.

At Albany he brought in family pews, sermons in English, a mixed choir, and confirmation. A split there led his friends to form a new synagogue for him. In 1854 he moved to Bene Yeshurun in Cincinnati, Ohio. He stayed there for the last forty-six years of his life. The entry treats him first of all as an organizer. It credits him with building strong groups that shaped Jewish life in America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zalinski-moses-:
Moses G. Zalinski (born 1863) was an American soldier of the supply corps. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in New York city, he was schooled in its public schools. He joined the ranks as a private man in 1885.

In 1889 he rose to second lieutenant of the Second Artillery. He left the Artillery School with his class in 1894. The next year he rose to first lieutenant in a new corps. In 1898 he was made a captain of the supply arm. Since 1903 he has been based at Washington in that role. He holds the rank of major in the supply corps now. The short entry rests on the American Jewish Year Book. It gives a plain chain of posts and ranks in order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zhitomir-jitomi:
Zhitomir is a Russian city and the chief town of Volhynia. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is one of the old towns of the realm of Russia. It came to Lithuania in the year 1320 by rule.

In the mid 1400s it stood as a chief town of that realm. As late as the mid 1600s few Jews lived there at all. The sack of 1648 left no tale of Jews in its fall. When the town came to Russia in 1778, Jews thrived there. It grew to be a hub of the Hasidic move in the south. In 1861 its Jews stood at more than thirteen thousand souls. The town held one great synagogue and twenty-six small ones. By 1891 its Jews had grown to more than twenty-four thousand.
keller-green-henry-1854:
Gottfried Keller, the Swiss writer, published Green Henry in German in 1854 and 1855. The text here comes from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, since no English translation is in the public domain. Heinrich Lee, nicknamed for his green coat, tells the story of his own youth and failed hopes.

Heinrich dreams of painting, drifts to Munich, and learns how thin his talent runs. Love, money trouble, and pride delay his return to his patient mother in Zurich. Keller drew the tale from his own life, softened by humor and hindsight. The novel ranks beside Wilhelm Meister among German artist novels. Its rich village and city scenes made it the great Swiss novel of growth.
king-american-eclectic-dispensatory-1854:
John King compiled The American Eclectic Dispensatory in 1854, a huge guide to the plant remedies of his school. King taught in Cincinnati, a center of eclectic medicine, which chose the best cures from every system. His book tells doctors what each drug is, how to prepare it, and when to use it.

Roots, barks, and herbs fill the entries, many of them native American plants little known in Europe. King gives doses, cautions, and the forms a medicine might take, from teas to extracts. For historians, the volume is the dispensatory of American botanical practice, a full shelf of plant lore in one binding.
king-henry-vi-part-1-pg2254:
Under a dead march, Shakespeare's King Henry VI, Part 1 brings Henry the Fifth's funeral on stage. Bedford speaks first, asking night to replace day in the sky. Comets should brandish their crystal tresses, he says, and scourge revolting stars. Those stars, in his charge, consented to Henry's early death.

Gloucester, the Protector, then takes up the praise of the dead king. His brandished sword blinded men with its beams, Gloucester recalls. His arms spread wider than a dragon's wings in battle. His eyes, full of wrathful fire, are recalled with equal awe. Together the speeches present Henry as a lost and unmatched ruler.
kircher-oedipus-aegyptiacus-vol3-1654:
Kircher sums up Egyptian wisdom in the third volume of Oedipus Aegyptiacus, in Latin from 1654. Real learning and fancied lore stand side by side in the vast close. The work forms the last great monument of Renaissance Hermeticism, splendid in dress and mistaken in many of its bold decipherments of the ancient signs.

No other book shows the old magical world view so fully arrayed. Kircher's Rome workshop drew reports from missions across the globe for it. Engravers, printers, and patrons all served his boundless design for years. Readers leave with awe at the scale of the attempt, if not belief in its answers.
l-alchimie-et-les-alchimistes-ou-essai-h:
Louis Figuier's essay on alchemy and the alchemists first reached readers in this 1854 French edition. Its full subtitle calls it a historical and critical essay. The subject is hermetic philosophy, the old thought behind alchemy.

Figuier was a trained chemist and doctor who wrote much popular science. His other books explained steam engines, railways, and electric machines. Here he turns that clear style on alchemists and their claims. The edition helps readers see alchemy judged by a working nineteenth-century scientist. Figuier writes for curious general readers, not for adepts. He treats marvels with caution while honoring their hold on the mind.
lazarillo-de-tormes-1554:
The Life of Lazarillo de Tormes is an anonymous Spanish tale dated 1554. This old English version was drawn out of Spanish by David Rowland. Its title page calls it a pleasant history.

Lazarillo serves many masters, one after another. A blind man is the first and sharpest of them. Hunger teaches the boy cunning as he grows. Each master exposes a new kind of greed or pride. The tale founded the picaresque novel, a form built on rogues and survival. Rowland's old English keeps the tale's rough, comic bite. Later rogue novels across Europe copied Lazarillo's pattern.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The February 1876 Lippincott's continues its century series. American progress forms the second paper on the centennial theme. Edward C. Bruce concludes his Up the Thames journey. F. A. Hillard offers a poem, The Poet's Pen.

Emma Lazarus contributes Fra Aloysius among Sketches of India. Mrs. Linton advances Leam Dundas through chapters twenty-one to twenty-four. Lady Barker's letters arrive from South Africa. Robert Wilson concludes his two papers at the old plantation. A sylvan search and Mirza-Schaffy songs were listed for March readers. Medical education in the United States joins the monthly gossip.
mental-alchemy-1854:
B. Brown Williams, a medical doctor, published Mental Alchemy in New York in 1854. The publisher was Fowlers and Wells of Clinton Hall. Williams divides his subject into twelve chapters. His title page lists the topics: mind, the nervous system, psychology, magnetism, mesmerism, and diseases.

The book treats mental and nervous illness through the popular sciences of its day. Magnetism and mesmerism then stood at the border of medicine and showmanship. Williams writes as a practitioner explaining these forces to lay readers. The work preserves a moment when psychology was still forming as a separate field.
murchison-siluria-1854:
Roderick Murchison, a British geologist, named the Silurian system after an ancient Welsh tribe. His Siluria, published in 1854, sums up years of fieldwork in Wales and beyond. It is the founding text for one great slice of earth's past.

Murchison maps the old rock layers and the fossils that mark them. He traces the same system through England, Europe, and America. The work fixed the order of the oldest fossil-bearing rocks and gave geology a firm time scale. Later disputes over its borders only showed how central the book was. Welsh hills and quarries supply many of his best proofs.
nerval-daughters-of-fire-1854:
Gérard de Nerval published Daughters of Fire in 1854, his linked stories, here in English translation for readers. The set holds Sylvie, Émilie, and Octavie, the dreamlike heart of French Romanticism in its late flower. Nerval, who walked a lobster on a blue ribbon in Paris, wrote these tales between spells of madness.

Sylvie, the crown of the set, shuttles between a village girl, a dancer, and a lost actress in Valois. Memory and present blur until the narrator cannot tell which love, or which year, he truly inhabits at all. Octavie and Émilie mix travel, theatre, and occult longing in Nerval's limpid, haunted prose of dream and waking. He hanged himself in 1855, weeks after the book appeared, and France slowly learned what it had lost in him. Proust and the surrealists later claimed these tales as scripture.
noizet-memoire-somnambulisme-1854:
Francois-Joseph Noizet studies the magnetic sleep in his memoir on somnambulism, in French from 1854, though written back in 1820. The French general treats mesmerism with a soldier's order and a scholar's care. His early account ranks among the first scientific treatments of the strange sleep and its claimed wonders of sense.

He reports trials, failures, and puzzles without the showman's gloss. Publication waited decades while the subject ripened around his manuscript. Psychology might have grown faster had his road been taken sooner. The memoir stands as a road not taken in the field's history, sober proof that the magnetic sleep drew serious minds early.
nott-gliddon-types-mankind-1854:
Josiah Clark Nott and George Robins Gliddon published Types of Mankind in 1854 in Philadelphia. Nott was an Alabama physician and Gliddon a popular lecturer on Egypt. Their large, illustrated treatise argued for polygenism, the claim that human races were created separately and unequally.

Chapters on skulls, ancient monuments, and natural history built a case that served the defense of slavery in America. The book was a bestseller and a scientific scandal at once, praised by slaveholders and attacked by clergy and later scientists. Modern scholars cite it as a foundational text in the history of scientific racism. It is kept and studied as evidence of how science was bent to serve bondage.
openalex-w2100316154:
Jens Vindahl Kringelum, Claus Lundegaard, Ole Lund and Morten Nielsen worked on computer prediction of antibody binding sites. Their paper appeared in PLoS Computational Biology in 2012. Antibodies latch onto targets at spots called B-cell epitopes. Finding those spots guides vaccine design. Lab mapping is slow and costly.

Computer methods had shown only moderate success. The authors argue that test data understated performance. Many real binding spots were never mapped in benchmarks. That made good predictions look wrongly false. They improved both the method and its testing. Cleaner benchmarks gave fairer performance scores. Better prediction tools can speed vaccine work. They also help design diagnostics and immune therapies.
openalex-w2147818954:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this measurement in Physical Review D in 2012. They measured how often W and Z bosons are produced in proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. These rates are basic tests of the standard model and of our picture of the proton's inner parts.

The team used early collision data from 2010, studying decays to electrons and to muons. They report total rates plus rates split by the direction of the particles produced. Precision reached a few percent, and electron and muon results were combined into one joint measurement. The numbers were compared with the best quantum chromodynamics predictions. Agreement tests the proton structure maps used across particle physics.
openalex-w2337283254:
Sigbjørn Lien, Ben Koop, Simen Sandve, and colleagues published this genome study in Nature in 2016. They present a high-quality reference genome for Atlantic salmon. Eighty million years ago the salmon family doubled its whole genome. Salmon still live with the aftermath, returning slowly to ordinary paired inheritance.

The assembly spans nearly three billion DNA letters. Reading it, the team mapped how the doubled genome was edited ever since. They tracked which duplicate genes survived, which were lost, and where chromosomes rearranged. Their patterns challenge the view that this return to normal pairing was gradual and orderly. They also question how duplicate genes usually divide old jobs or invent new ones after genome doubling.
openalex-w2529724154:
Christian Tomás Schmiegelow, J. Schulz, and Henning Kaufmann, with colleagues, reported this experiment in Nature Communications in 2016. Light beams can carry a twist, called orbital angular momentum, beyond their usual spin. Twisted light already drives tiny particles in circles and stirs quantum gases. The team asked whether that twist could pass into a single bound electron.

They aimed a vortex laser beam at one laser-cooled calcium ion held in a trap. The beam excited an atomic transition inside the ion. Their measurements demonstrate the transfer of optical orbital angular momentum to that bound electron. The work also shows how the twist changes which atomic transitions are allowed. That gives physicists a new way to probe single atoms using structured light.
openalex-w2767671054:
The ATLAS Collaboration searched for dark matter in this 2018 paper in the Journal of High Energy Physics. It uses proton-proton data from 2015 and 2016 at thirteen TeV, the LHC's highest energy. The target signature is one energetic jet plus large missing momentum. Invisible particles, like dark matter candidates, would carry that momentum away unseen.

Events needed a hard jet above a high threshold and no electrons or muons. Several signal regions imposed rising demands on the missing momentum. Counts in every region agreed well with Standard Model predictions. The null result became exclusion limits on several theories. Pair-produced dark matter candidates, large extra dimensions, and squeezed supersymmetry scenarios all lost ground. Each empty search narrows the hiding places left for new physics.
openalex-w2790924554:
Kelly Brener-Raffalli, Camille Clerissi, and Jeremie Vidal-Dupiol, with colleagues, studied coral partnerships in Microbiome in 2018. Their host is Pocillopora damicornis, a reef-building coral found across warm seas. A coral is a holobiont: animal plus algae plus bacteria living as one. Which partner shapes the microbes, the host's lineage or the local environment, was the open question.

The team sampled two coral lineages across Djibouti, French Polynesia, New Caledonia, and Taiwan. Those sites span different thermal regimes. Sequencing identified the algae and bacteria living in each colony. One algal type dominated in cooler sites, another in warmer ones. Geography itself explained very little of either community. Host lineage constrained bacteria more, while temperature tracked the algae more strongly. The title states the verdict: thermal regime and host clade, not geography, drive these assemblages.
openalex-w2888543854:
Kristian A. Thygesen, Joseph S. Alpert, and Allan S. Jaffe chair the group behind the fourth universal definition of myocardial infarction, out in 2018. Heart attack diagnosis needed one global standard as blood tests grew far more sensitive. This document, from cardiology's major societies, updates the shared definition. It separates heart muscle injury from actual infarction.

Injury means a cardiac troponin value above the ninety-ninth percentile of healthy people. Injury is acute when troponin rises or falls across measurements. Infarction requires that acute injury plus clinical proof of blocked blood flow. Proof includes symptoms, ECG changes, new Q waves, or imaging showing fresh muscle loss. The types of infarction are defined for different causes and settings. A shared definition makes trials comparable and diagnoses consistent across hospitals. This fourth edition is the reference clinicians worldwide now cite.
openalex-w3185925954:
Johann Bell, Inna Senina, Timothy Adams, and colleagues examine what climate change means for tuna-dependent Pacific Island nations. Warming seas are shifting tuna from island waters toward the high seas. Island governments earn large shares of their revenue from fees paid by foreign fleets fishing in their waters. If the fish move, that income moves with them.

The team modelled three tuna species across the waters of ten Pacific Island states out to the year 2050. Under high emissions, tuna biomass in those waters falls, and catches drop by about a fifth. Access fee income falls too, cutting some government budgets hard. Under lower emissions the losses shrink sharply, tying climate policy directly to island finances.
openalex-w4362717754:
David Montero, César Aybar, Miguel Mahecha, and colleagues present a standardised catalogue of spectral indices for satellite Earth observation, in Scientific Data in 2023. Spectral indices are simple formulas that turn satellite light readings into measures of the land. The most famous, NDVI, gauges vegetation greenness from red and near-infrared light. Hundreds of such indices now exist, scattered across papers with clashing names and definitions.

The catalogue gathers the indices in one checked, standard form. It records each formula and its intended use, from vegetation and water to soil and snow. Variants that correct for soil brightness or haze are included too. One trusted list should make studies easier to compare and reproduce, and help new users choose the right index.
openalex-w7133323154: Irregular heartbeats can hide in young, healthy-seeming adults. This study screened 403 adults aged 18 to 40 with questionnaires to spot silent atrial fibrillation. The authors linked the findings to heart-risk profiles and quality of life. A cardiology study of catching a quiet rhythm disorder before it causes harm.
openalex-w7160150454: Chilled near absolute zero, a samarium compound lines up its magnetism in a strange pattern. This lab paper used neutron and muon probes to catch two back-to-back magnetic shifts, at 2.8 and 0.9 kelvin. The team mapped the oddball order. A deep-freeze physics study of magnetism's strangest layouts.
openalex-w7204102154: Bleeding inside the brain needs surgery, but how much cutting is best? This review pits small-hole techniques against opening the skull for sudden brain bleeds. The authors compare how well each works, how safe each is, and which patients gain most. A brain-surgery review of doing less to save more.
openalex-w7204804154: Wasting muscles signal trouble in advanced cancer. This study tested whether bedside bioimpedance and simple strength tests can flag muscle decline tied to survival in chemotherapy patients. The authors evaluated the quick screens. An oncology study of simple tests with grave meaning.
openalex-w7214940554:
Luanderson Manoel Pereira Neto II, Beatriz Baptista Marques Nogueira, and Marina Mattar analyzed inequalities in hospital deaths from Alzheimer's disease in Brazil from 2016 to 2025 for a 2026 study. Using national hospital system data for people aged sixty and over, they compared death rates by sex, race and skin color, and age group in a descriptive time-series design.
