Hospital mortality rose across the period. The oldest patients, those aged eighty and over, died at the highest rates, followed by younger elderly groups. Black Brazilians recorded the highest rates, above white and brown populations, with a sharp peak in one recent year. Rates for men and women were similar overall, though women's rate moved above men's by the final year. The authors conclude that age and race mark relevant inequalities in who dies in hospital with this disease.
openalex-w7215058054:
Ana Flávia Santos de Castro and Cleber Cezar da Silva surveyed Brazilian graduate research, in a 2026 article, on school psychology. It covers the field after a 2019 law placed psychologists and social workers in basic education. Searching thesis and dissertation banks for work from 2019 to 2025, they chose twenty studies and read thirteen closely on how the profession is practiced and seen in schools.

The literature shows a practice centered on the single child and on blame. Students and families are blamed for school problems and treated as ill, and the psychologist is cast in a clinician's role. Putting the law in practice faces obstacles in regulation, hiring, working conditions, and unclear duties. Yet the studies point to critical practices shared across professions and fitted to each school's reality. Building school psychology, the authors conclude, takes public policy and practice that open education up, not formal placement alone.
openalex-w7221153354:
Ana Maria de Sousa Costa and three co-authors reviewed Brazilian research on nursing and violence against older people, publishing an integrative review in 2026. Abuse of the elderly takes many forms and is heavily underreported, which hides its true scale; the authors ask where nurses stand in spotting it and setting protection in motion.

Nurses, they find, are central to early identification, to educating and guiding families and caregivers, and to the compulsory reporting that triggers the protection network. Humanized welcome, active listening, and teamwork with other professions round out the role. The authors conclude that qualified nursing strengthens both care and public policy for the dignity of older Brazilians.
personal-narrative-of-travels-to-the-equ: Another volume of Humboldt's immortal travel narrative, carrying his South American explorations ever deeper into the unknown. Volcanoes climbed, rivers mapped, and nature studied with tireless zeal fill these pages. The great naturalist's masterpiece rolls on. Jungles, savannas, and Andean heights pass before his ever-curious eyes.
philo-yonge-vol1-1854:
Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher of the first century who read the Torah through Greek philosophy. Yonge's 1854 first volume of his complete works in English appeared in Bohn's Classical Library. It made Philo's full range open to Victorian readers for the first time.

Philo treats the stories of Genesis as allegories of the soul while holding fast to Jewish law and worship. His idea of the Logos, the divine word that orders the world, bridges Greek thought and later Christian theology. This volume holds his accounts of creation and the lives of the patriarchs.
philo-yonge-vol2-1854:
Volume two of Yonge's Works of Philo Judaeus, published in 1854, holds Philo's allegorical commentaries on Genesis. Here Philo reads the creation story and the lives of the patriarchs as maps of the soul. The great treatises on the creation and on the virtues stand in this volume.

Abraham's journey becomes the soul's schooling, Sarah and Hagar become wisdom and its handmaid, and each command hides an inner sense. Yonge's plain Victorian English keeps Philo's dense Greek argument readable for students without the language. The volume shows Philo's fusion of Torah and Platonism at its most inventive.
philo-yonge-vol3-1854:
Volume three of Yonge's Philo, published in 1854, gathers the historical and apologetic works. Philo steps out of allegory here to defend his people before Rome and record their recent past. The Life of Moses and the Embassy to Gaius anchor the volume.

The Embassy tells how Philo led a Jewish delegation to the emperor Caligula after riots against the Jews of Alexandria. His account is an eyewitness record of Jewish life under Roman power at a moment of crisis. Historians prize this volume beside the allegories, since it preserves facts found in few other sources.
philo-yonge-vol4-1854:
Volume four of Yonge's Philo, published in 1854, completes the first English Philo with the Questions and Answers on Genesis and Exodus. Philo poses a question on a verse, then answers it on two levels, the literal and the allegorical. The form shows his classroom method at work.

Why did God plant a tree in Eden, why did Cain build a city, and what do the plagues of Egypt mean? Each answer turns law and story into teaching on the soul's growth and God's care. With this volume, English readers gained the whole surviving Philo in their own tongue.
plos-pone-0000054:
Mathijs Baens, Heidi Noels, Vicky Broeckx, and co-authors exposed a flaw in a beloved lab tool in a 2006 paper. EGFP, a glowing green protein from jellyfish, is attached to other proteins so scientists can watch them move inside living cells. Labs worldwide trusted it as a passive tag that changes nothing.

The team found the dark side of that title: EGFP shows defective polyubiquitination, meaning the cell's tagging system for disposing of proteins handles it abnormally. A marker that bends the very process under study can mislead experiments on protein breakdown, a field central to cancer and brain disease. The paper is a caution that tools are part of the experiment.
plos-pone-0000154:
Elene R. Valdivia, Yajun Wu, Lian-Chao Li, and colleagues published this plant biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies a group-1 grass pollen allergen, a protein that also drives many hay fever cases. In maize, the authors test how this allergen affects pollen competition, the race between pollen grains to fertilize a flower.

A protein best known for making people sneeze turns out to matter in plant reproduction too. The authors measure its influence on which pollen wins. The work links an allergen's biology to plant breeding and to the spread of genes through maize populations, including questions about gene flow from crops.
plos-pone-0000254:
Per Unneberg and Jean-Michel Claverie published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tries a tentative mapping of interactions between chromosomes that are triggered by transcription, the reading of genes. Their data come from chimeric EST and mRNA sequences, messages that appear to join pieces from different chromosomes.

Chromosomes were once pictured as separate territories that rarely touch. Evidence of transcription-driven contact between them challenges that picture. The authors sift public sequence data for signs of such contact. The paper is exploratory, mapping a phenomenon that later work with new methods would test.
plos-pone-0000354:
Andy M. Reynolds and Mark A. Frye published this insect behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fruit flies track odors in free flight, zigzagging toward a food smell through moving air. The authors show this free-flight odor tracking is consistent with an optimal intermittent, scale-free search. Such a search is a pattern of bursts and pauses with no single characteristic scale.

A scale-free search is the best strategy when targets are sparse and clues are patchy. Showing flies match that optimum links their flight control to search theory. The result interests both biologists and engineers building small flying robots that must find odor sources.
plos-pone-0000454:
Yoshan Moodley and Michael W. Bruford argued for joining two fields to save Africa's wildlife, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Molecular biogeography uses DNA to map where species and their populations came from and how they are related across landscapes. The authors laid out a framework for conserving pan-African biodiversity built on that evidence.

Africa's wildlife crosses borders that conservation plans often respect more than animals do. DNA maps can show which populations are unique, which are connected, and where protection matters most. The paper is a call to integrate genetics into conservation decisions across the whole continent, rather than reserve by reserve.
plos-pone-0000554:
John Stephen Yap, Chenguang Wang, and Rongling Wu built a computational method described in PLOS ONE in 2007. It maps genes that shape how organisms handle heat. Thermal performance curves chart how well an organism grows or moves across temperatures. Their approach performs functional mapping of quantitative trait loci, the genome regions that regulate those curves.

A curve, not a single number, is the trait: genes may shift its peak, width, or height. Mapping such dynamic traits needs math that treats the whole curve at once. With climates warming, knowing which genes set thermal limits has direct ecological and agricultural stakes.
plos-pone-0000654:
Nathalie van der Velde, Bruno H. Ch. Stricker, Jos R. T. C. Roelandt and colleagues asked whether heart ultrasound can predict falls in older people. European and American guidelines call for echocardiography in patients with syncope, meaning fainting. Half of older adults with syncope present with a fall. Yet no published data had addressed heart scan findings in older fallers.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study set out to determine whether echocardiographic abnormalities mark those at risk. Falls injure and kill many older adults, so any test that flags risk early has value. The study tests whether a scan already used for fainting can do double duty for fall prevention.
plos-pone-0000754:
Renata Freitas, GuangJun Zhang and Martin J. Cohn found an old pattern of gene activity in shark fins, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The evolution of limbs from fins required new distal structures, the digits at the far end. In four-limbed animals, genes at one end of the HoxD cluster switch on in two distinct phases during limb development. The second phase builds the digit region.

Shark paired fins, the authors show, also display this biphasic Hoxd expression. That pushes the distal limb domain's origin far back, before fins became limbs. Sharks are not primitive leftovers here; their development preserves the ancient program that digits later inherited.
plos-pone-0000854:
Stephanie D. Shaw, Sutapa Chakrabarti, Gourisankar Ghosh and colleagues trimmed a splicing factor and found it still worked, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Serine/arginine-rich proteins, called SR proteins, are essential splicing factors. They carry one or two RNA-recognition motifs and a tail rich in arginine and serine, the RS domain. SR proteins bind splicing enhancers in the RNA and were thought to promote splicing from that position, using the RS domain.

Deleting the N-terminus of the SR protein SF2/ASF permitted splicing independent of the RS domain, their title reports. A part thought indispensable turns out dispensable after trimming. Results like this revise the mechanics textbooks give for splicing.
plos-pone-0000954:
Dietmar Dirnberger and Klaus Seuwen tested whether human frizzled receptors can talk to a yeast mating pathway, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Frizzled receptors span the cell membrane seven times, like the large GPCR family, but they are classed as atypical members. Yeast mating runs through a classic GPCR system, making yeast a handy test bed.

By placing human frizzled receptors into that system, the pair could watch for signaling in a clean setting. Yeast offers a blank background, free of the many partners found in human cells. Results from such swaps help sort which receptors truly couple to G proteins, a question with direct drug relevance.
plos-pone-0001054:
David Plachetzki, Bernard Degnan and Todd Oakley traced how new protein partnerships arose in animal eyes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Biologists increasingly understand the genetic bases of change in form. The origins of traits built on brand new protein interactions, though, remain largely undocumented.

Opsins are the light catching proteins of vision, and their partners decide what an eye can do with light. The team analyze opsin evolution across animals to catch new interactions as they arose. A documented origin is worth more than a plausible story. Their case gives eye evolution a rare before and after record.
plos-pone-0001154:
DNA barcoding uses a short stretch of DNA to identify a species, much as a barcode identifies a product. Chodon Sass and colleagues tested whether proposed barcodes work for cycads, an ancient group of plants, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Barcodes are most needed when a specimen lacks the features used for visual identification.

The authors evaluated the candidate marker sequences for telling cycad species apart. Reliable barcodes could become a forensic tool for conservation, since many cycads are endangered and traded illegally. Their tests show how well the proposed markers perform in this plant group.
plos-pone-0001254:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is the most common motor neuron disease, currently incurable, with treatment largely limited to supportive care. Katrina Gwinn and colleagues survey the genetics of the disease in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They also call for a new era of collaborative gene discovery. Family history raises the risk of ALS, and many inherited causes had already been found.

The authors argue that progress now depends on groups pooling samples and data, since each individual cause is rare. Their piece is a perspective on how ALS research should organize itself. It reflects a shift toward large consortia in human genetics.
plos-pone-0001354:
In mature neurons, the genes for MHC class I are repressed. These genes encode the immune system's identity-display molecules. Neurons are normally invisible to immune patrols in this respect. Julie Miralvès and colleagues studied a repressor behind that silence, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. MeCP2 is a protein that binds methylated DNA and represses genes; its own gene's mutations cause Rett syndrome.

The authors report that high levels of MeCP2 depress MHC class I expression in neuronal cells. The MHC genes are rich in the CpG sites MeCP2 reads. Their finding links a famous neurodevelopmental protein to immune invisibility in the brain.
plos-pone-0001454:
Tadashi Nomura and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on what makes the mammal cortex unique. The cortex has six neat layers of nerve cells, built in a set order as the embryo grows. No other class of backboned animal has a true match for it. The team asked which growth traits make this layered build possible.

They point to the pattern of nerve cell birth and to the level of a guide protein called Reelin. Both traits prove vital for a mammal type cortex to form. The work helps explain how a new brain design arose in evolution. It also frames why faults in these steps cause grave brain ills.
plos-pone-0001554:
Hoau-Yan Wang, Maya Frankfurt, and Lindsay Burns published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on opioid tolerance. Very low doses of opioid blockers can boost pain relief and cut tolerance. They do so by stopping a switch in how the opioid receptor links to its cell partners. Where the blocker binds to force that was not known.

The team show the blocker binds a protein called filamin A with high strength. That bind is the grip that stops the switch. A named grip gives drug teams a clear target. Drugs built on it could hold pain relief longer with less dose gain and less dependence.
plos-pone-0001654:
Marta Pires de Miranda and co-authors dissected a virus protein that hijacks B-cell signals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Gammaherpesviruses set up lifelong latent infections in B cells, the antibody-making cells of the immune system. To do so, they switch on pathways that normally sit below the B-cell receptor. One such viral tool is m2, a protein of murine gammaherpesvirus 68.

The team shows that m2 gathers several cell proteins at once, a multi-docking assembly. It bends the Fyn and Vav signaling pathway to the virus's ends. The full text gives the binding tests and the signals they recorded. Knowing how a virus imitates the cell's own switches helps explain how these infections persist for life. The question also bears on the human gammaherpesviruses.
plos-pone-0001754:
Emma L. Meczes, Kathryn L. Gilroy, Katherine L. West, and their co-authors studied a tail piece of a DNA-handling enzyme in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Type II DNA topoisomerases are essential enzymes that solve tangles arising as DNA is copied and read. They pass one double helix through a temporary break in another, powered by ATP.

The team measured the impact of the human enzyme's C-terminal domain, its tail region, on activity. The full text gives the enzyme assays with and without the tail and what changed. These enzymes are targets of major cancer drugs, so knowing which parts control activity can help design drugs and explain resistance.
plos-pone-0001854:
Lieven Thorrez, Katrijn Van Deun, Léon-Charles Tranchevent, and their co-authors warned against a common lab shortcut in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Housekeeping genes are needed in every tissue, since their expression is required for cell survival, integrity, or duplication. They are commonly used as reference genes to normalize gene expression data, on the assumption that they are expressed at constant levels.

Using ribosomal protein genes as the test case, the team shows that assumption can fail: reference genes vary more than users expect. The full text gives the expression data across tissues. Bad normalization quietly distorts thousands of published gene measurements, so this cautionary tale has unusual reach.
plos-pone-0001954:
Francois van Loggerenberg and co-authors described the work of building a high-risk HIV study group in South Africa, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The group, part of the CAPRISA 002 study of acute infection, follows people at high risk so that new infections can be caught early. Such groups are the base for vaccine and prevention trials.

Between August 2004 and May 2005, the team enrolled the cohort and recorded its health and social profile. They also report new infection rates and the hard parts of keeping such a group intact. Honest accounts of these hurdles help later trials plan for real life.
plos-pone-0002054:
Sanjeev Mahanta and co-authors found the smallest piece of a cancer-linked protein that drives growth, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, MUC1, is made in abnormal form on many solid tumors. On healthy lining cells it clusters at the top face only; on cancer cells it spreads over the whole surface. A direct link from that change to cancer growth had been elusive.

The team whittled MUC1 down to a minimal fragment. As the title states, that fragment alone mediates the growth of cancer cells. A small active piece is a cleaner drug target than a huge protein.
plos-pone-0002154:
Melissa Bowlin and Martin Wikelski measured the true flight costs of migrating songbirds, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Migrant birds, bats, and insects tend to have more pointed wings than species that stay put. Pointed wings and low wing loading were thought to save energy on long flights. Low wing loading means low body mass per wing area. The idea had never been tested directly.

Bowlin and Wikelski report that pointed wings, low wing loading, and calm air each cut the cost of migratory flight. Their tests turn a long-held guess about wing shape into measured fact. The results help explain why long-distance migrants look the way they do.
plos-pone-0002254:
Lina Guerra and co-authors used a bacterial toxin to find a key player in the response to DNA damage, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When adherent cells meet DNA-damaging agents, such as the bacterial cytolethal distending toxin or radiation, they switch on the small protein RhoA. RhoA builds stress fibers and delays cell death, but the signals between damage and RhoA were missing.

The team identifies Net1, a factor that activates RhoA, as a key effector in that response. Filling in the chain from DNA damage to cell survival helps explain how cells buy time to repair themselves. How cancer cells may abuse the same delay.
plos-pone-0002354:
Ziyin Li and co-authors found a new passenger complex that guides cell division in a parasite, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Aurora B kinase is a key part of the chromosomal passenger complex, which steers chromosome segregation and the final split of one cell into two. In Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind sleeping sickness, an Aurora B relative was known but its partners were missing.

The team identifies a novel chromosomal passenger complex in the parasite. They also show it takes a unique position during cytokinesis, the final split. A division machine that differs from the human one is attractive for drugs that must kill the parasite, not the patient.
plos-pone-0002454:
In 2008, Desmond and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Chris Desmond, Ruth M. Bland, Gerard Boyce, and others. Its subject is scaling-Up Exclusive Breastfeeding Support Programmes: The Example of KwaZulu-Natal. Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for six months is the mainstay of global child health.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002554:
A research team led by Stoel reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Berend C. Stoel, Terry M. Borman, and others. Its subject is a Comparison of Wood Density between Classical Cremonese and Modern Violins. Classical violins created by Cremonese masters, such as Antonio Stradivari and Giuseppe Guarneri Del Gesu.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002654:
Jayabalan M. Joseph led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the actinome of dictyostelium discoideum in comparison to actins and Actin-Related proteins from other organisms. Authorship is credited in the record to Jayabalan M. Joseph and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Actin belongs to the most abundant proteins in eukaryotic cells which harbor usually many conventional actin isoforms as well as actin-related proteins (Arps). Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002754:
Chiara Pastori led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was arterially perfused Neurosphere-Derived cells distribute outside the ischemic core in a model of transient focal ischemia and reperfusion in vitro. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Chiara Pastori, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Treatment with neural stem cells represents a potential strategy to improve functional recovery of post-ischemic cerebral injury. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002854:
Thomas A. Terleph led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was response properties of the auditory telencephalon in songbirds change with recent experience and season. The catalog record names Thomas A. Terleph first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The caudomedial nidopallium (NCM) is a telencephalic auditory area that is selectively activated by conspecific vocalizations in zebra finches and canaries. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002954:
Paul Makidon, Anna Bielinska, Shraddha Nigavekar and co-authors tested a new hepatitis B vaccine form in animals in 2008. Hepatitis B stays a major global health problem despite safe, effective vaccines. Current vaccines need cold storage and three shots, which restricts use where clinics are scarce.

Their candidate uses a nanoemulsion, a mix of tiny oil droplets, given through the nose as a mucosal vaccine. Pre-clinical evaluation means testing before human trials. Published in PLOS ONE, the work explores a form that could ease delivery in the developing world if later trials support it.
plos-pone-0003054:
Paul Medina, Ryan Worthen, Lawrence Forsberg and co-authors studied dendrite upkeep in neurons in 2008. Neurons need precise control of their inner skeleton: microtubule tracks carry cargo in axons and dendrites, while actin organizes synapses. Their unique shape makes neurons especially sensitive to faults in that system.

The actin-binding protein Capulet genetically interacts with the microtubule motor kinesin to maintain dendrite homeostasis, the title reports. Pairing an actin factor with a microtubule motor shows the two systems cooperate. Published in PLOS ONE, dendrite stability underpins learning circuits and their disorders. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003154:
Georgiy Bobashev, Robert J. Morris and D. Michael Goedecke examine airport networks in epidemic models in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Models of global spread for flu, SARS and tuberculosis often treat a sample of international airports as the network that carries disease. Yet there was no agreement on how that sample should be chosen.

The authors study sampling choices and the topology, or shape, of an international airport network. Readers see why the airports picked can change what a model predicts. The work matters for planners who rely on such models to judge how fast a new infection might travel around the world.
plos-pone-0003254:
Natasha Webb, Geoff Connolly, Judy Tellam and colleagues reassess a virus pathway claim in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Previous studies had indicated that Epstein-Barr virus can modulate the Wnt pathway in virus-infected cells, and that this effect is mediated by the viral oncogene latent membrane protein 1, or LMP1. The team reassessed the role of LMP1 in regulating expression of various pathway components.

The title reports that Epstein-Barr virus modulation of the Wnt pathway is not dependent on LMP1. Readers see a causal credit reassigned after a direct check. Such corrections keep virus cancer research from building on the wrong viral protein.
plos-pone-0003354:
Ingrid Masse, Laurent Molin, Laurent Mouchiroud and colleagues find a new lifespan factor in worms in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The PTEN tumour suppressor encodes a phosphatase, and its daf-18 orthologue in Caenorhabditis elegans negatively regulates the insulin and IGF-1 DAF-2 receptor pathway that influences lifespan in worms and other species. The team set out to identify new DAF-18 regulated pathways involved in lifespan.

The title reports a novel role for the SMG-1 kinase in lifespan and oxidative stress resistance in C. elegans. Readers get another gene in the ageing network beyond insulin signaling alone. Worm lifespan genes often nominate pathways later found in mammals.
plos-pone-0003454:
Bahareh Vali and co-authors studied liver damage in people with two viruses in this 2008 paper. Hepatitis C harms the liver faster when HIV is also present. The immune reasons for that speed-up were unclear. The team looked for HIV-specific T cells inside the liver.

They examined patients co-infected with hepatitis C and HIV-1. T cells aimed at HIV were indeed found gathered in liver tissue. Fighters meant for one virus may add harm in the other's organ. That misplaced buildup could help explain the faster liver disease. Co-infection care must treat both viruses as one joint problem, not two separate ones.
plos-pone-0003554:
Magali Saint-Geniez and co-authors studied a growth factor's role in vision in this 2008 paper. VEGF is famous for building blood vessels, healthy and diseased alike. Evidence hinted it also acts directly on non-vascular cells. Anti-VEGF drugs are now widely used in eye care.

The team showed endogenous VEGF is required for visual function. It supports survival of Müller cells and of photoreceptors, the light sensors. Blocking VEGF too hard could starve the retina it should save. The finding urges care in dosing eye treatments. The same drugs also treat some cancers and lung diseases at higher stakes.
plos-pone-0003654:
M. Ángeles Serrano and Paolo De Los Rios published this network study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Flow networks move things along directed paths from input points to output points. Their large-scale shape decides how well the whole system works. The team asked what makes such networks efficient.

They studied percolated landscapes, where paths appear once enough links are in place. Their analysis links the layout of these networks to how much they can carry and how they change over time. The results apply to systems as unlike as water in rock and goods on roads.
plos-pone-0003754:
Ulrich Kirk published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. How much we like an object depends in part on the setting around it. Neuroimaging work had often studied context and perception, but less so beauty. Kirk used fMRI to watch aesthetic judgment at work.

He examined how the brain handles the link between an object and its context during judgment. The same image could please more or less depending on its frame. The study shows taste is not just in the object; the brain builds it from object and context together.
plos-pone-0003854:
Karim Hnia, Cécile Notarnicola, Pascal de Santa Barbara, and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Gastrokine-1 is a protein known from the stomach lining, and its role in smooth muscle cells was a mystery. To study it, the team first needed the native protein in pure form.

They established a protocol to purify gastrokine-1 from freshly dissected chicken gizzard smooth muscle. Then they characterized its biochemical properties, some of them unexpected. The groundwork sets up future study of what this protein actually does in muscle tissue.
plos-pone-0003954:
Joep P. M. Derikx, Dick A. van Waardenburg, Geertje Thuijls, and co-authors studied gut barrier loss during surgery in 2008. A leaking gut barrier is tied to complications after operations. Most study of that loss came from belly surgery itself. The team asked whether major surgery elsewhere also breaks the barrier.

Their PLOS ONE article followed twenty children having spinal fusion surgery. Spine surgery does not open the abdomen at all. Signs of gut barrier loss still developed in these patients. The finding widens concern about gut leakage to many major operations. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004054:
Elaine J. Gavin, Bo Song, Yuan Wang, and co-authors weakened a DNA protein in colon cancer cells in 2008. Their group had found Orc6 levels highly elevated in colon tumors. Orc6 also rose after treatment with the drug 5-fluorouracil. Those links made Orc6 a candidate drug target.

Their PLOS ONE article lowered Orc6 in human colon cancer cells. The cells then grew more sensitive to 5-fluorouracil and cisplatin. Pairing a target blocker with standard drugs could improve response. The work points to a combination strategy worth further testing. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004154:
Lane Yoder published this theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brain's wiring is so vast and tangled that exact, fully specified networks have rarely been explored. As a result, how the pattern of synaptic connections shapes the way the brain handles information is poorly understood.

Building on a recently proposed model of the retina, Yoder designs explicit logic circuits, networks written out connection by connection. He tests whether such circuits can tell one neural state from another. The work offers a concrete way to link wiring diagrams to the computations a brain circuit performs.
plos-pone-0004254:
Makoto Honda and colleagues published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Narcolepsy is caused by the loss of most neurons that make hypocretin, also called orexin, the brain chemical that keeps us awake. The loss is believed to result from an autoimmune attack, but what actually kills the cells is unknown.

The team studied IGFBP3, a binding protein for growth factors, in relation to hypocretin. They report that IGFBP3 colocalizes with hypocretin and regulates it. A regulator sitting alongside the missing chemical gives researchers a new lead on the narcolepsy puzzle.
plos-pone-0004354:
Lina Rodahl and colleagues published this tumour genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Several regulators of endocytic trafficking, the system that sorts cargo inside cells, have lately been named tumour suppressors in Drosophila. These include components of the ESCRT machinery, which packages proteins for disposal. Breaking ESCRT subunits leads to enlarged cells and tissue overgrowth.

The team report that disrupting Vps4, an ESCRT partner, and JNK function in Drosophila causes tumour growth. Two systems that seem unrelated, waste sorting and stress signalling, collide in this route to cancer. The flies make the genetics fast and cheap to test.
plos-pone-0004454:
Waves moving through flowing material behave in ways that matter for blood clotting, model Elena Ermakova, Emmanuil Shnol, Mikhail Panteleev, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many living and chemical systems carry traveling waves of excitation. In real settings the medium itself moves, as blood flows or as fluids stream through reactors.

The team studied two-dimensional waves in a channel with a smooth, curved flow profile. They used the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, a classic math stand-in for excitable tissue. Their results show how flow bends, speeds, or breaks up the waves as they travel. That insight reaches beyond math: clots form in flowing blood, and wave behavior in a stream helps decide where a clot grows and when it stops.
plos-pone-0004554:
Software that mines the medical literature for protein partnerships is presented by Min He, Yi Wang, and Wei Li in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tool is called PPI Finder. Published biomedical papers are growing so fast that no one can read them all, so text mining tools are needed to manage the overload automatically. One common job is extracting protein-protein interactions from PubMed abstracts.

Existing tools mostly hunted interactions by matching patterns or names. The authors set out to build a mining tool for human protein interactions with a fuller approach. Protein partnership maps are basic infrastructure for biology: they show which proteins work together. Automating their extraction from papers keeps those maps growing at the speed of publication.
plos-pone-0004654:
Eight villages in a secluded corner of Sardinia are far more different genetically than expected, report Giorgio Pistis, Ignazio Piras, Nicola Pirastu, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Isolated populations are prized for gene studies because their uniformity can make disease genes easier to find. But population isolates should not be assumed homogeneous, even when communities look alike.

To design association studies well, researchers must understand how history and isolation molded each community. Using genome-wide high-density SNP analysis, the team found high differentiation among the eight villages. Neighbors separated by hills and old marriage customs carry distinct genetic profiles. Gene hunters who treat them as one pool risk false leads; those who respect the structure gain a sharper tool.
plos-pone-0004754:
Tobias Wiedemann and colleagues showed that early immune response to stomach bacteria sets up later pre cancer change in gerbils, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Infection with Helicobacter pylori that can inject a toxin linked protein raises risk for severe stomach disease. The injection system and its cargo are key to that added risk in humans.

The team tracked infection over time in Mongolian gerbils, a good model for stomach disease. Early immune events predicted later changes that can lead toward cancer. The link argues for early treatment to cut long term risk. It also maps steps where intervention might help.
plos-pone-0004854:
Lijing Xing and colleagues linked phosphate tagging of wheat lectin VER2 to vernalization induced signaling and motility, in PLOS ONE in 2009. O-GlcNAc modification of proteins mediates stress response and motility in animal cells. The plant lectin concanavalin A can raise nuclear modification levels, yet function of modification in wheat vernalization. The cold requirement for flowering, remained unclear before this cellular study.

VER2 phosphate tagging connects cold sensing to cell movement. Vernalization prepares winter wheat for spring flowering. Molecular steps could improve crop timing. Climate shifts make such knowledge valuable. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004954:
In type 2 diabetes, pancreatic beta cells fail and die. These cells make the body's insulin. Fatty acids are part of what harms them. Glucose makes that fat-driven harm worse, for unknown reasons. Etti Bachar and co-authors investigated the pairing in PLOS ONE in 2009.

They used the fatty acid palmitate on beta cells. Glucose amplified the stress it caused in the endoplasmic reticulum. That structure is the cell's protein-folding workshop. The effect ran through a signaling complex called mTORC1. The chain links high sugar, fat and a named pathway. It gives diabetes research a clearer target for protecting beta cells.
plos-pone-0005054:
Myelodysplastic syndromes are bone-marrow disorders. They can turn into leukemia. Telling low-grade from high-grade cases shapes treatment. Xiaorong Yang and colleagues built a tool for that task in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used SNP arrays, which read DNA variation across the genome. Copy number aberrations were their signal.

A new algorithm, called CMA, finds the aberration patterns. Pattern selection then boosts power and discrimination. The method separates low-grade from high-grade syndromes. Genetic fingerprints become a diagnostic aid. The tool sharpens care for marrow disorders. It is a step toward precision medicine. Better grading means patients get treatment matched to their risk.
plos-pone-0005154:
Chickpeas tolerate drought better than many crops. A protein called CaZF helps them. Deepti Jain, Nilanjan Roy and Debasis Chattopadhyay studied it in yeast. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. CaZF comes from a drought-tolerant chickpea variety. It also gives salt tolerance to tobacco plants. Salt-sensitive yeast mutants were their test bed.

CaZF rescued the yeast through two known stress pathways. It also worked parallel to them, on its own route. The pathways are the HOG pathway and the calcineurin pathway. A plant switch plugs into yeast machinery and adds its own. The finding reveals a portable stress-tolerance tool. Moving such genes could harden crops against salt and drought.
plos-pone-0005254:
Malaria vaccines are urgently needed, and one candidate is built on a parasite surface protein called AMA-1. Spring and colleagues ran an early-phase trial of that vaccine, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Volunteers got the protein mixed with one of two booster systems.

The trial checked safety, the strength of the immune response, and signs of protection. Comparing the AS01B and AS02A boosters head to head shows which partner works better with AMA-1. Early trials like this one decide which vaccine recipes deserve large field tests. Malaria kills most in young children, so each step that moves a safe vaccine dose closer to field trials in Africa counts for a great deal.
plos-pone-0005354:
Wnt5a is a signaling protein best known for guiding development before birth. Its pattern in adult human skin had not been fully studied. Romanowska and colleagues mapped that pattern in PLOS ONE in 2009, along with two of its receptors.

Wnt5a showed layer-specific expression in adult skin, sitting in set layers rather than throughout. It was also upregulated in psoriasis, the scaly autoimmune skin disease, and it synergized with type 1 interferon. A development signal returning in diseased skin is a clue to what drives psoriasis. Psoriasis is not just a skin rash. it links to joint pain and heart risk, so a skin signal that teams up with an immune signal may flag the cases most in need of strong care.
plos-pone-0005454:
Watcharee Chokejindachai and David Conway set out a plan for malaria gene hunting in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Some forms of the malaria parasite cause far worse illness than others. To find the gene changes behind that, workers need many markers spread across the parasite's large genome.

The authors argued that Thailand was a good place to start the search. They laid out a case-control method that compares parasites from severe and mild cases. A clear plan matters because a weak search wastes samples, while a sharp one can point to the genes that make malaria deadly.
plos-pone-0005554:
Celia Perales, Rubén Agudo, and Esteban Domingo studied virus killing by mutation overload in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Some drugs kill viruses by raising their mutation rate until they cannot copy faithfully. A risk is that the virus evolves resistance to the mutating drug, as it does to normal drugs.

The team used a virus strain already resistant to one such drug, ribavirin. They showed that a second, different mutating treatment could still wipe it out. The result supports pairing mutating drugs so that resistance to one does not save the virus.
plos-pone-0005654:
Kelly Haston, Joyce Tung, and Renee Reijo Pera studied a gene in mouse germ cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Germ cells follow a special path: they multiply, travel to the gonads, reset their gene marks, and finally become eggs or sperm. Little was known about some steps of that path.

The team studied a gene called Dazl in the earliest germ cells, both in animals and in dishes. They found that it keeps the cells able to take any path and runs their genetic and marking programs. Faults there could underlie some infertility.
plos-pone-0005754:
Daniel Wiswede and co-authors tested in 2009 whether the body's own emotion signals change how the brain handles its mistakes. The embodiment idea holds that feelings involve the face, posture, and gut, not just the brain. Smiling or slumping can nudge what a person feels.

The team measured the brain's error signal while manipulating these body cues. That signal, seen after a slip, shows how the brain monitors performance. If body state shifts it, then emotion reaches deeper into basic control than assumed. The results link feeling and self-monitoring in a way lab tasks rarely capture.
plos-pone-0005854:
Heather Maughan and Rosemary Redfield traced in 2009 how a bacterium's talent for eating stray DNA evolved. Haemophilus influenzae can take up DNA from its surroundings and splice matching pieces into its own genome. Most incoming DNA is destroyed; a lucky fragment can bring new traits.

The pair reconstructed how this competence arose and changed across the species' history. The ability is costly to keep, so its persistence implies real benefits. Their history helps settle why sex-like gene swapping exists in bacteria at all. It also informs how resistance genes may move through this respiratory pathogen.
plos-pone-0005954:
Food can act almost like a drug when the dose is right. Ismayil Ahmet, Edward Spangler, Barbara Shukitt-Hale and colleagues tested blueberries in a 2009 PLOS ONE study with rats. They asked whether a diet rich in blueberries could guard the heart when blood flow is cut and then restored, an injury called ischemic damage.

Harmful oxygen byproducts play a big part in that injury, and simple lab-made antioxidants have given mixed results at best. A whole food offers a broader mix of guards. The title states the outcome: the berry-fed rats' hearts were protected. The work supports the idea that diet can brace the heart before injury strikes.
plos-pone-0006054:
Losing one copy of a gene can matter as much as losing both. Isabel Rubio-Aliaga, Gerhard Przemeck, Helmut Fuchs and colleagues proved that for the gene Dll1 in adult mice in 2009. Dll1 belongs to the Notch pathway, an ancient signaling route that patterns embryos and renews tissues. Their PLOS ONE paper maps the full set of effects in grown animals.

The half-dose mice showed a complex mix of changes across metabolism and immunity. A single missing copy thus ripples far beyond the embryo where Notch first acts. The catalog of effects helps predict what milder Notch flaws might do in people, and it warns that adult health can rest on gene doses set before birth.
plos-pone-0006154:
The Parkinson's drug L-dopa fills in for missing dopamine, but its help may stop at movement. Thomas Jubault, Laura Monetta, Antonio Strafella and colleagues tested that boundary with brain scans in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses fMRI during a set-shifting task, after overnight withdrawal, to see which brain networks L-dopa restores in Parkinson's disease.

L-dopa restored activity in the motor cortico-striatal loop but did not modify the cognitive network, the title reports. A drug that fixes motion and leaves thought loops untouched matches what patients describe. The split guides honest counseling and pushes the search for separate treatments for Parkinson's thinking troubles.
plos-pone-0006254:
Known protein shapes lag far behind known protein sequences, by more than two hundred to one. Michael Lee and colleagues built PSPP, a structure prediction pipeline for computer clusters, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Predicted shapes fill part of that gap and guide drug and vaccine design.

The pipeline spreads prediction work across clustered machines to gain speed. Faster shape prediction means more proteins can be modelled for study. Each model is a hypothesis about how a protein works. The tool helps labs with modest resources attempt predictions that once needed specialist centres.
plos-pone-0006354:
Infection during pregnancy raises the offspring's risk of schizophrenia and autism. Qi Li and colleagues modelled that risk with prenatal immune challenge in mice, reported in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The most consistent brain abnormality in schizophrenia patients is enlarged lateral ventricles, the brain's fluid spaces.

Magnetic resonance imaging checked whether the mouse model shows matching brain and behaviour changes. Linking an early immune event to later brain structure supports the developmental theory of schizophrenia. A valid model lets researchers test prevention ideas. It also clarifies timing: harm may begin long before symptoms.
plos-pone-0006454:
Kathy Cai and colleagues linked two gene switches to ovarian cancer types in PLOS ONE in 2009. The GATA family of transcription factors guides how cells take on their roles in embryos and organs. Two members, GATA4 and GATA6, are often lost in ovarian cancer. That loss was proposed to explain how these tumors change character.

Their title reports that loss of GATA4 and GATA6 marks the histological subtypes of ovarian cancer. The loss also comes before the change of normal surface cells into cancer. An early, type-specific marker could aid diagnosis. It also suggests the switches help keep ovarian cells in their normal state.
plos-pone-0006554:
Oluf Røe and co-authors profiled genes in a rare chest cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malignant pleural mesothelioma is considered an almost incurable tumor with increasing incidence worldwide. It usually develops in the parietal pleura, from mesothelial lining cells. The team compared genome-wide profiles of mesothelioma with parietal and visceral pleura tissue.

Their aim was an emerging gene portrait of the tumor. Knowing which genes define mesothelioma can improve diagnosis, which is often late. It may also reveal drug targets. Comparing tumor to both pleural layers prevents mistaking normal layer differences for cancer changes.
plos-pone-0006654:
George Hinkal, Neha Parikh, and Lawrence Donehower timed tumor suppressor loss in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Inactivating mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene occur often in progression of human cancers. The p53 protein inhibits outgrowth of nascent cancer cells through anti-proliferative mechanisms. The team used timed somatic deletion of p53 in mice.

Their title reports the timing reveals age-associated differences in tumor progression. Losing p53 young versus old does not give the same cancers. Age context shapes what a mutation does. That insight matters for interpreting cancer risk across the lifespan.
plos-pone-0006754:
Lora L. Shadwick and colleagues rebuilt the family tree of certain slime molds in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protosteloid slime molds make tiny fruiting bodies of stalk and spores. They were classically grouped with other slime molds as Eumycetozoa. The larger supergroup in question is Amoebozoa. Whether the classical grouping holds was unsettled.

The team sequenced a ribosomal RNA gene across many species. That gene, called SSU rDNA, is a standard family-tree marker. Their phylogeny tested whether Eumycetozoa equals one true branch. The answer reshapes how slime mold groups are named and related. Clear trees help every later study of how these organisms evolved.
plos-pone-0006854:
Karen L. Wozniak and her team probed how mice beat a grave fungus in PLOS ONE in 2009. The fungus is Cryptococcus neoformans. It strikes men and women whose immune shield is weak. It can cause dire lung illness and brain illness. Past work gave mice a tame strain of the fungus. That strain made interferon gamma, and the mice were safe when the wild fungus came.

In that lung model, the team asked what does the guarding. Which parts of the immune force truly keep mice safe? The reply could guide vaccine design for the frail. Those with weak shields need guarding most, yet vaccines work worst in them. The mouse work shows what a win looks like.
plos-pone-0006954:
Andrew Haddow, Carl Jones, and Agricola Odoi examined disease risk reporting in PLOS ONE in 2009. Focal arboviral infections strike only a subset of a population. These mosquito and tick borne infections pose overlooked problems for risk assessment. Reported risk can shift a lot with the group chosen as the population at risk.

The authors measured how much risk estimates vary under different choices. They also looked at how those choices affect the search for spatial patterns. Their point is practical. A risk figure can mislead if the at-risk population is drawn carelessly, and control programs may aim at the wrong places.
plos-pone-0007054:
Christopher Hale, Sean Sun, and Denis Wirtz settled a cell mechanics question in PLOS ONE in 2009. Einstein first linked random thermal forces to how small particles move in fluid. Later work on actin networks hinted that living cells add non-thermal forces. The role of actomyosin, the cell's contractile machinery, was disputed.

The team measured cell stiffness using microrheology, tracking tiny probes inside cells. They resolved how much actomyosin contraction drives the readings. The answer matters for reading cell health from mechanical tests. Tumor and stem cells are often judged partly by how soft or stiff they feel.
plos-pone-0007154:
Alexandra-Chloé Villani, Mathieu Lemire, Edouard Louis, and colleagues tested a fever gene in bowel disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The MEFV gene causes familial Mediterranean fever when faulty. It builds pyrin, a regulator of the inflammasome, the platform that activates inflammatory signals. Pyrin interacts with the product of another inflammation gene, NLRP3.

The team asked whether MEFV variants change risk of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Both are chronic inflammatory bowel diseases. Shared inflammatory machinery makes the question sensible. A confirmed link would tie periodic fever biology to common bowel disease in a useful way.
plos-pone-0007254:
Anna M. Mileo, Claudia Abbruzzese, Stefano Mattarocci, and colleagues studied a cancer virus protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human papillomavirus type 16 is a classic high-risk virus. Such viruses cause nearly all cervical cancers, and their E6 and E7 genes are usually active in those tumors.

The authors examine the E7 oncoprotein and its partner GST P1, a detoxifying enzyme. They report that E7 interacts with GST P1 and enhances its role in cell survival. That interaction may help infected cells live longer, giving the virus time to push them toward cancer.
plos-pone-0007354:
Nga T. Lao, Alan P. Maloney, John F. Atkins, and colleagues built reporter systems to study a translation quirk in plants in 2009. Translation usually stops at the first stop codon in a message. Many viruses, and some cell messages, contain stop codons that some ribosomes read through instead, adding another amino acid.

That readthrough can produce extended proteins with new functions. The authors present versatile dual reporter gene systems for plants. The systems measure how often readthrough occurs. Their PLOS ONE tools help researchers study a process viruses exploit and cells sometimes use deliberately.
plos-pone-0007454:
Adam Margolin and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the math behind modern protein measurement. New machines now let biologists count thousands of proteins in a single test. That flood of data feeds a broad view of how cells work. Yet the tools for making sense of the data had lagged far behind the machines. The team set out to close that gap.

They built a new framework based on empirical Bayes methods. The approach borrows strength across many measurements at once, which steadies the results when data are noisy. Sounder math means the protein counts can support firmer claims about how cells behave. The framework is built for the large data sets such machines now produce as a matter of routine. It helps turn raw machine output into results biologists can trust.
plos-pone-0007554:
Michela Traglia and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was Val Borbera, a valley in the northwest Apennines of Italy whose people have lived apart for a long time. Such groups are prized for gene hunting. They share one stable setting, carry a narrower range of gene variants, and show long linked stretches of DNA. The team set out to describe this large group in full.

They measured how strongly traits run in the valley's families. The work shows why such a group gives gene hunters an edge. A well-mapped group like this becomes a natural lab for the study of common disease. The paper lays the base: who lives there, how they tie to each other, and what their genes can show. Later work in this valley stands on that base.
plos-pone-0007654:
Thomas Bettecken and Edward Trifonov published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the code that packages DNA into chromatin. It is widely accepted that DNA's own sequence strongly governs how it wraps. DNA spools around proteins called nucleosomes, and certain two-letter combinations favor particular positions on the spool. That packaging code is layered over the code for proteins. The team catalogued the repertoires of those positioning dinucleotides.

A catalogue of the signal pairs refines our reading of the chromatin code. Different genomic regions carry different mixes of the signals. Those mixes help explain why some DNA wraps tightly and other DNA stays open. Open and closed packaging decides which genes a cell can use. The study is an inventory paper, and inventories of codes are how codes get cracked.
plos-pone-0007754:
Taylor Chomiak and Bin Hu published a theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks what insulation thickness is best for nerve fibers in the rat brain. A fatty coat called myelin wraps many fibers and speeds their signals. The g-ratio compares the fiber's inner width to its full outer width.

That ratio serves as a standard index of healthy myelination. Myelin is complex to build and is often hit by injury and disease. The authors use theory to find the optimal g-ratio for rat central fibers. A firm target value helps researchers judge damage and repair in myelin diseases.
plos-pone-0007854:
Renata Goncalves and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how a blood meal reshapes a mosquito's flight muscles. The mosquito is Aedes aegypti, a carrier of dengue and yellow fever. Digesting blood releases products that can harm cells.

Flight muscle mitochondria, the cell's power plants, sit at the center of the story. After blood feeding, their function changes in a measurable way. Those changes are reversible once digestion ends. The muscle must keep the mosquito flying to find its next meal. The study shows how a blood feeder balances energy and damage.
plos-pone-0007954:
Francine Matthys and colleagues judged a standard retreatment plan for tuberculosis in PLOS ONE in 2009. The World Health Organization's Category II plan is the usual second try when TB comes back or a first course fails. Their patients lived where many TB strains no longer yield to first-line drugs.

Outcomes under the standard plan were poor in that setting. When strains resist the main drugs, a fixed recipe that assumes they still work will miss often. The authors' data press for drug testing up front and for plans matched to local resistance, rather than one recipe for all places.
plos-pone-0008054:
Yingjie Wu and colleagues bred a better gene-cutting mouse for PLOS ONE in 2009. Modern mouse genetics rests on tools that delete or swap genes in chosen tissues. One such tool, FLP, worked sluggishly in its older forms, wasting time and mice.

An improved form, FLPo, was placed in the most common lab mouse strain. The new line cuts its target DNA cleanly and with high success. A trusty, fast deleter line speeds nearly every mouse study that needs a gene removed, which is to say much of modern biomedicine.
plos-pone-0008154:
Derek Murphy and colleagues mapped where a childhood cancer's master gene grips the genome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuroblastoma arises from young nerve tissue and is a major cancer killer of children. Extra copies of the gene MYCN mark the worst cases.

Across the genome, the MYCN protein bound at spots marked by distinct DNA motifs, and often near zones where DNA was heavily methylated, a silencing tag. The combined map shows how an overgrown master gene rewires a cell. Each stronghold it holds is a place where treatment might pry it loose.
plos-pone-0008254:
Nicasio Mancini and colleagues studied hepatitis C antibodies in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Hepatitis C virus comes in several genotypes that differ in surface proteins. Some human antibodies can neutralize many types at once. They target spots on the E2 surface protein that stay conserved across genotypes. Such antibodies are central tools for understanding virus and host interplay.

Finding them in infected people would support vaccine and treatment design. Antibodies aimed at conserved spots are harder for the virus to escape. The team examined whether infection itself elicits these broad antibodies. Their answer informs strategies for prevention and therapy.
plos-pone-0008354:
Johannes Hirrlinger and colleagues presented a gene control tool in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. DNA recombination systems such as Cre/LoxP let researchers regulate genes in living animals. Precise targeting of one cell type at one time point has remained challenging. Spatial control often comes at the cost of timing control. The team split the Cre protein into fragments to solve this.

Their Split-CreERT2 system restores Cre activity only when fragments complement each other. A drug trigger adds control over timing. Together these switches allow finer experiments on gene function. The tool serves genetics studies that need exact timing.
plos-pone-0008454:
Severine Mazaud Guittot and co-authors study the GATA4 gene in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. GATA4 makes a factor that switches other genes on and off. It is needed for the growth and work of many organs. Yet how the GATA4 gene itself is controlled was little known. The team focus on the start region of the gene.

They find that the gene can use more than one first exon. An exon is a coding piece spliced into the final message. The same first pieces are used across species. That shared pattern hints they matter for control. The work clarifies how a key organ gene is switched on.
plos-pone-0008554:
Matthieu Chalopin and co-authors find a target for red wine compounds in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Diets rich in polyphenols are linked to lower cardiovascular risk. Polyphenols are plant compounds abundant in red wine and fruits. Their vascular protection is generally accepted. Yet the molecular targets for those effects remained unknown. The team study the endothelium, the inner lining of blood vessels.

They identify estrogen receptor alpha as a key target on the endothelium. Red wine polyphenols act through that receptor to protect vessels. The receptor is best known for mediating estrogen hormone effects. Its new role connects diet, hormones, and heart health in one pathway.
plos-pone-0008654:
Hai Li and co-authors analyze a chitinase domain in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Chitinases are enzymes found across archaea, bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals. They break down chitin, the second most abundant carbohydrate in nature after cellulose. Chitin forms insect shells and fungal cell walls. Many chitinases contain an insertion domain that helps bind chitin. The team perform sequence and structural analysis of that insertion domain.

They reveal two conserved motifs involved in chitin binding. Those motifs appear across distant species, marking them as essential. Knowing the binding motifs aids design of antifungal and insecticidal enzymes. It also clarifies how nature recycles a vast chitin pool.
plos-pone-0008754:
Paul ThiamJoo Tan, A. T. Heiny, Olivo Miotto, and colleagues sifted flu pieces for vaccine building blocks. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seasonal flu vaccines chase a virus that changes its coat yearly. Epitope-based vaccines would instead target pieces that T cells recognize. Such pieces must stay stable across many viral strains. They must also fit common human immune types.

The team checked H1N1 epitope candidates for conservation and variety. Strong candidates appear in most strains yet vary little. A vaccine built from them might work across seasons. Their shortlist guides the search for longer-lasting flu protection.
plos-pone-0008854:
Rebecca Baker, Claire Kent, Rachel Silbermann, and colleagues probed a disputed family of gene switches in mouse breast tumors. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The PEA3 family of Ets factors shows up at high levels in many breast tumors. Some reports cast them as tumor promoters. Others suggest they might restrain tumors instead. Mice whose mammary tumors are driven by Wnt1 gave a clean test.

Changing PEA3 factor activity in those tumors revealed their true contribution. Evidence from a defined model beats correlations from mixed human samples. The verdict helps decide whether drugs should block or boost these factors. Breast cancer biology gains a firmer fact.
plos-pone-0008954:
Jean-François Pombert and Patrick Keeling read the power-plant genome of a parasitic alga, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Helicosporidium is an alga that lost its green colour and its ability to feed on sunlight. Instead it lives as an obligate parasite inside insects and other small animals. Its cysts burst open inside the host and release a thread-like cell.

The pair sequenced the DNA of its mitochondria, the cell's energy-making parts. That genome is stripped down compared with free-living algae. Comparing it shows what a parasite can throw away once a host feeds it. The genome adds a data point to the story of how parasites evolve.
plos-pone-0009054:
Ryota Matsuo and co-authors reported a slug brain healing itself after injury, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Adult mammal brains recover poorly from damage, which makes stroke so hard to treat. The land slug Limax offers a different model for smell processing. Its higher olfactory centre handles the slug's sense of smell.

After that centre was injured, it recovered on its own. The team describes the regrowth as a novel mode of regeneration. Function returned along with structure over the following weeks. A simple animal that rebuilds a brain centre may teach principles mammals lack.
plos-pone-0009154:
Claire Shovlin and co-authors found a second source of a key clotting protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Factor VIII is the protein missing in haemophilia A. Too much of it, conversely, predicts repeat blood clots in veins. High levels also track with pulmonary hypertension driven by local clots.

The liver was thought to be plasma factor VIII's source. Endothelial cells, the vessel lining, also process the protein, the team showed. They even make alternatively spliced versions of its message. A vessel-wall source could explain clots forming exactly where they do.
plos-pone-0009254:
Georgina Thorborn and co-authors published this HIV immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In HIV infection, regulatory T cells, the immune system's brakes, decline in number. That loss was blamed for the uncontrolled immune activation that drives disease. But the story may be more subtle than cell counts alone.

The team studied people with HIV who had no symptoms yet. They measured not just how many regulatory cells remained, but how their targets respond. Effector T cells had grown more sensitive to suppression by the regulators. That extra sensitivity compensated for the reduced regulator numbers. Balance, it turns out, can be kept even with fewer brakes.
plos-pone-0009354:
Feng Wang and co-authors published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the germ behind tuberculosis, lives inside human cells and resists study. New tools are needed to speed drug and vaccine work against it. The team built one such tool.

They developed a way to insert unnatural amino acids into the germ's proteins. These are building blocks that nature never uses, placed at chosen spots by genetic tricks. A tagged protein can be lit up, tracked, or fished out of the cell. The method gives tuberculosis researchers a handle on proteins inside a stubborn pathogen.
plos-pone-0009454:
Jameson Miller, Miles Parker, and Robert Bourret built a computer model of a bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2010. Escherichia coli swims toward food and away from harm. It steers with a chain of signals inside the cell. Groups of receivers on its surface sense chemicals and pass the news inward.

Their model treats each molecule as an agent that follows simple rules. Thousands of agents act at once, as in a real cell. The team could then watch the steering system work step by step. The model offers a test bed for ideas about one of the best known signal chains in biology.
plos-pone-0009554:
Shinichi Sunagawa, Cheryl Woodley, and Monica Medina sampled threatened corals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Corals host rich communities of microbes on and inside them. Deep sequencing of DNA from such samples had shown that microbial diversity was once underrated. The team read the DNA in samples from corals at risk. They looked for kinds of microbes not seen elsewhere.

The samples held a wealth of microbial life, much of it rare. A few kinds dominated, while many appeared only in traces. The authors argue that threatened corals shelter microbial habitats that science has barely explored. Saving reefs thus saves more than the corals themselves; it saves whole unseen worlds.
plos-pone-0009654:
Bruno Vellutini and Alvaro Migotto documented the early life of a sea biscuit in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sea biscuits are flattened sea urchins that burrow in sand. The species studied is Clypeaster subdepressus. Its development from egg to juvenile had not been fully recorded. The team raised the animals in the lab and followed each stage in detail.

Their account covers the embryo, the swimming larva, and the young juvenile after settling. Stage by stage drawings and timings give a full atlas of its growth. Such atlases let scientists compare how related urchins build their bodies. They also fill a plain gap in marine biology for this group.
plos-pone-0009754:
Honey bees face many stresses, and chemicals inside their own hives are one of them. Christopher Mullin and colleagues measured pesticide levels in North American apiaries. Their survey appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Apiaries are places where beekeepers keep colonies of honey bees. The team found high levels of miticides, chemicals used against hive mites, plus other farm chemicals. Residues build up in wax and pollen that bees live on. Beekeepers themselves apply some of these chemicals to save their colonies. The findings raised hard questions about what chronic exposure does to bee health.
plos-pone-0009854:
Prostate cancer often spreads to bone and changes how bone grows. Murali Ravoori and colleagues measured that bone response in mice without cutting the tissue. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bone response is a key sign of how the disease advances.

The team combined in vivo micro-CT scans of living mice with ex vivo scans and DXA after death. Micro-CT builds detailed three-dimensional images from X-rays. Together the methods quantified how much mineralized bone the cancer produced. Noninvasive measures let researchers follow the same animal over time.
plos-pone-0009954:
Alcohol makes fruit flies hyperactive, and two neurons may drive much of that buzz. Eric Kong and colleagues traced the circuit behind the response. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fruit flies are a standard model for alcohol research.

A pair of dopamine neurons targets the D1-like receptor DopR in the central complex. Dopamine is the brain's reward and movement signal. Activating that path promotes ethanol-stimulated locomotion in Drosophila. A two-neuron circuit is a clean model for how alcohol moves behavior. The central complex is a brain hub for movement control.
plos-pone-0010154:
Caitlin McCabe, Sue Goldie, and David Fisman weighed a treatment plan for pregnant women with HIV in 2010. Suppressing the virus in late pregnancy prevents transmission to the baby. Directly observed therapy, where staff watch each dose, improves that suppression. Their PLOS ONE study projected both effectiveness and cost for the third trimester.

Cost-effectiveness analysis asks whether the health gained is worth the money spent. Watched therapy costs more to deliver than handing over pills. If it prevents enough infant infections, it may be the better buy. Their model was built to make that judgment for health systems.
plos-pone-0010254:
The authors were Catarina Hioe, Terri Wrin, Michael Seaman, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested antibodies against a loop on the HIV surface. The V3 loop on the virus envelope protein gp120 was once called HIV's main neutralizing domain. It was later dismissed as too variable between strains to serve as a useful antibody target for vaccines.

New structural and chemical data suggested V3 still holds conserved features. The team showed monoclonal antibodies against V3 neutralized many HIV-1 subtypes broadly. A variable target that still yields broad protection could change vaccine design assumptions.
plos-pone-0010354:
Michael Waterston and Christopher Pack asked whether magnetic brain stimulation sharpens vision, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The method, called rTMS, pulses magnetic fields through the skull. At some settings it was thought to dull the stimulated brain area briefly. Researchers often treated it as a reversible, virtual lesion for experiments. Waterston and Pack tested that assumption on visual tasks.

After stimulation, subjects actually got better at telling visual stimuli apart. That result cuts against the simple dulling story. If pulses can improve performance, many past experiments need a second look. The finding also hints at uses for boosting perception. Either way, the study warns against easy labels for a complex tool. What rTMS does may depend on task and timing.
plos-pone-0010454:
Elena Gómez-Díaz and Jacob González-Solís mapped a seabird food web in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used chemical tracers, and they included the birds' parasites. Food web studies often leave parasites out, though they are everywhere. Parasites feed in varied ways, making their place in the web tricky. Stable isotope analysis reads diet from tissue chemistry, offering a way in. The team applied it to a seabird colony and its parasites.

Isotopes placed each parasite at a feeding level relative to its host. Some parasites feed higher than expected, effectively preying on predators. Including parasites changes the web's shape and its energy accounting. That matters for predicting how webs respond to species loss. The study argues parasites deserve seats in food web science.
plos-pone-0010554:
James Stapleton and James Swartz built a cell-free screen to find better hydrogen-making enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzymes called [FeFe] hydrogenases make and split hydrogen gas. That talent could serve renewable fuel systems. Natural versions, though, are fragile and easily damaged, which has blocked engineering. Screening improved versions inside living cells is slow and awkward. Their plate-based screen works without cells at all.

In tiny wells, enzyme variants could be made and tested in parallel. Speed lets researchers try many designs and keep the best. Cell-free methods trade living complexity for control. If sturdier hydrogenases emerge, biohydrogen gets closer to practice. This study supplies the sieve for that search.
plos-pone-0010654:
Marcela Dávila López and colleagues used gene order to find linked genes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neighboring genes are usually shuffled apart over evolution. Pairs that stay neighbors across many species are probably kept together for a reason.

Scanning whole genomes, the team found gene pairs whose order survived across eukaryotes. Those pairs often worked in the same process and were switched on together. Order itself became a clue to function for poorly known genes. The approach turns genome maps, which labs already have, into a guide for experiments they have not yet run.
plos-pone-0010754:
Ryan Boyko and Andrew Marshall tested ape counting methods with computer simulations, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Great apes are shy and hard to count directly. Survey teams instead count the nests apes build each night and convert nest counts into animal numbers. The conversion rests on guesses about building and decay.

The simulations modeled an orangutan population building nests over time. Different survey methods were then graded against the known true count. Some common methods drifted far from the truth under plain conditions. Knowing which methods hold up matters, since survey numbers decide where scarce conservation money goes.
plos-pone-0010854:
Jie Dong, Guoqian Jiang, Yan Asmann and co-authors published this development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs are tiny molecules that fine-tune how much protein a gene makes, and they help shape growing organs. How whole networks of them behave while a lung forms was poorly mapped, so the team tracked them across mouse development.

They profiled both microRNAs and gene messages at every recognized stage of lung growth, from early embryo to adult, and matched the results against protein data. More than a hundred microRNAs rose and fell in clear time patterns, forming distinct groups. Dong and colleagues chart how these small regulators may coordinate with the genes they target. The map gives lung researchers a framework for studying birth defects and lung tumors alike.
plos-pone-0010954:
Manuel Gonçalves, Josephine Janssen, Maarten Holkers and co-authors published this cell fusion methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells merging with each other underlies fertilization, muscle building, and bone maintenance, and also plays roles in disease. Measuring those fusion events quickly and sensitively, in many kinds of experiments, was an unmet need.

Their system is a genetic switch split across two cell populations, delivered by lentivirus carriers so it works in dividing and non-dividing cells alike. Only when two cells fuse does a recombinase enzyme complete the switch and turn on a reporter. Gonçalves and colleagues designed the two modules for flexible pairing. A clean on-off signal for fusion lets researchers screen for genes and drugs that promote or block cell merging.
plos-pone-0011154:
Kowarsch, Marr, Schmidl and colleagues mapped RNA targets in PLOS ONE in 2010. Small RNAs tied to disease act in many signaling paths, but their effects shift by tissue. The team carried out a tissue focused analysis of which genes these small RNAs target in human pathways.

Their maps show that control by these RNAs depends strongly on context. The same RNA can matter in one tissue and do little in another. That insight matters for precise medicine, since drugs aimed at these RNAs must hit the right tissue. It should help design treatments with fewer off target effects elsewhere in the body.
plos-pone-0011254:
Vitzthum, Scutaru, Musial-Bright and colleagues mapped tobacco smoke research in PLOS ONE in 2010. Secondhand smoke, called environmental tobacco smoke, has been studied worldwide for decades. Using counting methods for science itself, the team charted where that research concentrates and where it is thin.

Their equalized maps show the global shape of the field at a glance. Funders and policy makers can see which countries and topics dominate and which are neglected. Such a bird's eye view helps direct money to gaps that matter for nonsmokers' health. It is research about research, used to steer future work.
plos-pone-0011354:
Aric Gregson and co-authors looked in 2010 for immune cells that might protect transplanted lungs. After a lung transplant, many patients develop a scarring condition that slowly blocks the small airways and is the main limit on long-term survival. The team searched lung grafts for regulatory T cells, a type that calms immune attack.

Patients whose grafts held a specific set of these calming cells were protected against the scarring syndrome. The cells carried two markers that together singled them out from other T cells in the graft. Finding a protective cell type gives transplant teams a possible early sign of who is safe and who is at risk. It also suggests that boosting such cells could one day help grafts last longer.
plos-pone-0011454:
Nima Dehghani and co-authors used source modeling in 2010 to ask whether two common brain recordings see the same sleep events. Sleep spindles are brief bursts of activity during deep sleep that help lock in memories. They are recorded both by EEG on the scalp and by MEG, which senses the brain's magnetic fields, and the two traces do not match neatly.
