Modeling where each signal comes from in the cortex, the team found the two methods pick up different generators of the same spindles. The tools are therefore not interchangeable windows on sleep but complementary ones, each favoring different sources. Sleep researchers who combine both gain a fuller picture than either gives alone. The paper is a caution against treating a familiar brain wave as one simple thing.
plos-pone-0011554:
Mark Anderson and Charles Ferree argued in 2010 for a change in what conservation saves first. As climate shifts, species will move, vanish, or arrive in new places, making any reserve picked for today's species a gamble. The authors proposed saving the stage instead: the varied rocks, soils, slopes, and landforms whose diversity generates and shelters living diversity in any climate.

Geology changes slowly, so a reserve network chosen for geophysical variety should keep offering many kinds of habitat whatever the climate does. Species can then sort themselves across a rich stage rather than being stranded on a poor one. The reframing is strategic, not poetic: it turns an unknowable bet on future species into a durable bet on future options. Land trusts and agencies can act on it now, with maps that already exist.
plos-pone-0011654:
Chandan Goswami and co-authors studied a sensory channel called TRPV4 in cultured cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. TRPV4 lets calcium and other ions into cells and responds to physical force. Both the channel and the cell's inner skeleton, the cytoskeleton, have been tied to how cells sense touch and pressure, and to heightened pain.

The team showed the channel and skeleton influence each other in both directions. TRPV4 interacts with the actin and microtubule networks, and those networks in turn tune the channel's behaviour. That two-way control helps explain how cells convert mechanical signals into chemical responses.
plos-pone-0011754:
Sandhya Das and co-authors tested both forms of an immune call signal, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rapid movement of neutrophils from blood vessels to infection and injury sites is critical for resolving inflammation. The chemokine CXCL8 is central to recruiting them, and it occurs both singly and in paired form.

Working in living animals, the team showed both the single and paired forms are essential for neutrophil recruitment. Neither form alone could do the job fully. That two-key requirement reveals a finer control on calling in immune reinforcements than a single signal would allow.
plos-pone-0011854:
Far Chiang, Hannah Kuper, and Robert Lindfield led a rapid survey in 2010 of blindness that could have been avoided in the Occupied Palestinian Territories. No recent figures existed for how common blindness and poor vision were among people aged fifty and older there. Their survey was designed to produce answers quickly enough to guide real services.

Field teams examined older adults and recorded both the scale of vision loss and its causes. Many causes of blindness, such as cataract, can be treated or prevented when services reach people in time. A clear count of where the need sits helps eye care programs spend scarce staff and money where they will restore the most sight.
plos-pone-0011954:
Isabelle Laporte and co-workers studied in 2010 how the return of wolves changes the behavior of elk and cattle sharing the same range. Wolf predation and harassment of livestock are a central conflict in wolf conservation. Wild elk answer wolves with anti-predator behavior, but cattle, shaped by breeding, may not.

Comparing how elk and cattle respond clarifies where livestock losses come from and which husbandry steps actually help. Behavior, not just killing, is the channel: fear alone can move herds, change grazing, and raise costs. Evidence on that channel gives ranchers and conservationists something more useful than slogans on either side of the wolf debate.
plos-pone-0012054:
Phillip Cassey and co-workers compared in 2010 bird eggshell colors across museum collections to study why they vary so much. Eggshell diversity has inspired many adaptive explanations, from camouflage to signaling. Progress was blocked by three problems, starting with measuring color reliably in a way birds themselves would see.

Working with museum eggshells gave the team a comparative sample no single field season could gather. Standardized color measurement across species lets hypotheses about climate, nesting habits, and predators be tested fairly. Museum drawers, often dismissed as stamp collections, here serve as a century-deep data set on evolution's palette.
plos-pone-0012154:
Caroline Hall, Rachel Kassel, Robert Tacke, and co-authors studied how hepatitis C virus quiets the immune system, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Few viruses are better at staying for life once they infect a person, and this one often ends in lasting liver disease. A key part of its trick is weakening the T cells that should clear it, helped by regulatory T cells that calm immune attacks.

The team showed liver cells carrying the virus can push ordinary T cells to become regulatory ones, using a calming signal the infected cells release. That is a direct route by which the virus builds its own shelter. Naming it suggests ways a future therapy might lift the calm and let the immune system finish the job.
plos-pone-0012254:
Olga Rivero, Andreas Reif, Julio Sanjuán, and co-authors tested a brain development gene's link to schizophrenia in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, AHI1, is needed to build parts of the human brain, changed quickly during human evolution, and sat in a chromosome region that family studies had tied to schizophrenia. Those clues made it a natural suspect for a case-control test.

Comparing patients and healthy controls, they weighed whether the gene's variants raise the risk of the disease. Genes that guide brain building are strong suspects when thinking goes wrong, but suspicion is not evidence. Careful association studies, including ones that come back negative, are how psychiatry sorts real risk genes from near misses.
plos-pone-0012354:
Michael Behnke, John Wootton, Margaret Lehmann and co-workers mapped gene activity across the fast growth cycle of Toxoplasma gondii in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Toxoplasma is a widespread parasite that infects people and animals and can harm unborn babies and weak immune systems. In its fast form, called the tachyzoite, the parasite builds new copies of itself in a tightly timed cycle.

The team found that the cycle runs on two coordinated sets of genes that switch on in waves, one set handling the standard cell cycle and the other building parasite parts. That two-track program explains how the parasite times growth so precisely. It also exposes steps that drugs might block to stop infection.
plos-pone-0012454:
Danielle Ulanet and Douglas Hanahan studied a tumor guard's loss in a staged mouse cancer model, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The guard, p19 Arf, senses abnormal growth signals and usually calls in p53, the famous tumor suppressor. The authors asked what else happens when Arf is lost as tumors form step by step.

Losing Arf flipped the angiogenic switch early — tumors built blood vessels sooner — and sped tumor initiation through both p53-dependent and independent routes. Extra vessels feed faster growth, so the loss is doubly dangerous. The work helps explain why tumors lacking this guard behave so aggressively and resist single-pathway drugs.
plos-pone-0012554:
Daisuke Yamamoto, Kaori Shima, Kou Matsuo and colleagues tested a polyamine blocker in oral cancer cells, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Gene activity is set partly by methyl tags on DNA and on histone tails; cancers often misplace those tags. Blocking polyamine production — a growth chemistry — was known to affect methylation, and a protein called antizyme carries out part of that block.

Raising antizyme stripped methyl marks from genome DNA and from a key histone site in the oral cancer line. Removing silencing marks can wake protective genes that cancer shut off. The mechanism suggests antizyme pathways as a fresh route to epigenetic cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0012654:
Hong, Chung and Kim worked out a better way to compute how tightly small peptides grip SH3 domains. These domains pass signals inside cells by grabbing short peptide pieces on other proteins. Knowing the grip strength helps predict which proteins will pair up in a cell's signal web.

Their 2010 method combines many protein shapes and many peptide templates instead of relying on one of each. Real proteins flex, so averaging over shapes should match reality better. Sharper grip predictions help map cell signalling and design drugs that block bad pairings.
plos-pone-0012754:
Dawes, Kuzevski, Bettelheim and co-authors surveyed mobile drug-resistance packages in E coli from people and animals. Class 1 integrons are gene traps that collect resistance genes and pass them around between bacteria. Their 2010 study screened more than five hundred E coli samples of human and animal origin.

They charted a particular form in which a segment called IS26 has cut out part of the integron's conserved tail. Such cuts can reshape which resistance genes the trap keeps and spreads. Tracking these forms shows how resistance travels between farms, clinics and the wider environment.
plos-pone-0012854:
Stelzer, Schmidt, Wiedlroither and co-authors reported a small water animal that gave up sex and shrank. Asexual lines should enjoy a head start, since every individual can reproduce, yet they rarely last in nature. Their 2010 study follows a tiny metazoan lineage that took that path.

The lineage lost sexual reproduction and became dwarfed compared with its sexual relatives. Its fate tests theories about why sex persists despite its costs. Tiny animals with both kinds of relatives offer rare, clean comparisons for that old question.  Its relatives still reproduce both ways for comparison.
plos-pone-0317254:
Erin Ingalls and colleagues interviewed seventeen recreational runners who had ended a daily running streak of at least one hundred days. Run streaking, running at least a mile every single day, is praised for building strong habits. The researchers wanted the other side of the story: what breaking such a streak feels like and whether it can backfire.

Some runners admitted they had run through injuries and treated the streak as a burden before it ended. Afterward, many felt sadness, anger, or disappointment, and some described a grieving process, though relief appeared too. The pain was sharpest for runners most attached to their streak, a warning for habit programs built on never missing a day.
plos-pone-0329054:
Jair Alonso Góngora-Bendezú and colleagues checked the lungs of four hundred Peruvian workers who had recovered from COVID-19 and who regularly work at high altitude despite living at sea level. All had confirmed past infection, and each took a careful breathing test in twenty twenty-four. The team looked for lasting damage and for which workers were hit hardest.

More than seven in ten workers showed abnormal breathing patterns, most often a mixed pattern that stiffens and narrows the airways at once. Risk climbed with obesity, other illnesses, years of breathing workplace fumes, years of altitude exposure, and having had severe COVID-19. The authors urge steady lung monitoring for this workforce, with closest attention to those carrying several of these risks at once.
plos-pone-0337254:
Cesilia Charles and colleagues surveyed health workers at Katavi Regional Referral Hospital in Tanzania in mid 2025. They wanted to know how well staff follow basic steps that stop infections from spreading in the hospital. Close to two hundred doctors, nurses, and lab staff took part, using questionnaires and checklists during visits to wards.

Average compliance sat below seventy percent, and fewer than four in ten workers reached the high level. Doctors scored lower than nurses. Workers did better when they felt motivated, had regular supportive supervision, and worked where an active infection committee existed. Soap and water were still missing in many latrines, which helps explain the gap.
plos-pone-0338854:
Min Kyu Yang, Seong Jung Ha, and Ho-Seok Sa sort out a confusing eye condition in PLOS ONE in 2026: inflammation that swells only the muscle pair lifting the eye and eyelid. They reviewed fifty-eight patients with this isolated pattern and asked which diseases caused it and how the causes could be told apart on examination and scans, since treatment differs sharply by cause.

Thyroid eye disease accounted for about two thirds of cases and an unexplained muscle inflammation, idiopathic orbital myositis, for most of the rest; only two patients had the IgG4 related form. Tendon involvement on imaging strongly favored the myositis group, while limits on looking downward clustered in thyroid disease. Myositis patients whose lid drooped were diagnosed faster and responded better to steroids. The comparison gives eye specialists a practical checklist for a rare presentation.
plos-pone-0339554:
Mojisola Fasokun and co-workers link loneliness with self-reported thinking decline among adults in the United States. Their 2026 study uses national survey data collected over eight years. Close to eighty-six thousand adults answered questions on how often they feel lonely. They also said whether their memory or thinking has slipped.

The chance of reporting thinking decline rose step by step with loneliness. Adults who always felt lonely reported decline nearly half the time, against about one in ten among those never lonely. The gap ran wider for women at the loneliest level. Age and background changed the picture little. Treating loneliness as a health risk, the authors argue, belongs in brain-health planning.
plos-pone-0341754:
Raksha M Narasimhan, Crystal S Taswell, and co-authors looked back at women treated for early breast cancer that had spread to a few nearby lymph nodes. After mastectomy, doctors still debate whether radiation to the chest wall helps these patients live longer or stay cancer free. Their 2026 review covered women treated at one center over more than two decades.

Only fifty-seven patients fit the study, and about two in five received radiation. Radiation was not linked to better survival or fewer recurrences, even in the aggressive triple-negative type. Hormone therapy did help, while having more involved nodes predicted worse outcomes. The authors say treatment choices should rest on each patient's tumor traits and overall therapy, though the small group limits firm answers.
plos-pone-0343754:
Checking newborns for hidden disease is expanding, and gene-based screening could soon test for hundreds of conditions at birth. Camille Level and colleagues surveyed about sixteen hundred forty French parents on whether such expansion feels acceptable, in this 2026 PLOS One study run through maternity wards and an online panel.

Parents weighed an expanded test panel against a genomic version, rating feelings, expected benefit, and fairness. A trade-off exercise probed what they would accept in exchange for more information. The team used an established acceptability framework to separate enthusiasm from ethical unease. Their findings aim to guide French policy so growth in screening keeps public trust.
plos-pone-0343954:
Meng Wang and four colleagues build a network that names the style of a painting. Their 2026 study tackles a slippery computer vision problem. Style cues scatter across a canvas, tangled with subject matter and background. The proposed network reads the whole composition and local brushwork together. Four modules share the labour: encoding style features, generating attention maps, learning by contrast, and checking attention counterfactually. That last module asks what the prediction would lose without each highlighted region.

Counterfactual checks suppress flashy but irrelevant regions. Contrastive training pulls fine-grained styles further apart in the model's internal space. Tests ran on public art datasets, including the large WikiArt collection. Interpretability is the selling point alongside accuracy. Curators and heritage managers need systems that show their working. A classifier that points to the brushstrokes behind its verdict is far more useful for digital archives than one that merely announces a label.
plos-pone-0344454:
Zahra Cheraghali and Mohsen Rostamy-Malkhalifeh tackle a management problem: in organisations run from a centre, which handful of branches or units lifts the whole system's performance most? Standard efficiency scoring rates each unit on its own, ignoring how much a unit matters to the group. Some newer fixes can produce impossible or runaway answers unless constants are guessed in advance.

Their new model picks a set of outstanding units of a chosen size in one optimisation, needs no preset constants, and is guaranteed to return a feasible, bounded answer. Two real-world datasets were used to show the method works in practice. The authors frame it as a decision-support tool for headquarters teams deciding where praise, investment, or replication efforts will pay off most.
plos-pone-0345354:
Csaba Varga charts where highly pathogenic bird flu struck wild waterfowl and poultry across the United States from 2022 into 2025, in a single author PLOS ONE study published in 2026. The H5N1 strain that reached North America in early 2022 spread unevenly, and understanding its clustering could sharpen farm defenses. Varga analyzed public detection records at county level and scanned for places and times with more cases than chance would predict.

Wild birds logged more than seventeen thousand detections across nearly fifteen hundred counties. Four species, mallards, Canada geese, green winged teal, and snow geese, supplied about forty percent of them. Poultry outbreaks hit turkey farms hardest, then egg layers, broilers, and ducks. Several spillover waves moved from east to west, with wild bird detections sometimes preceding nearby farm outbreaks. The timing links give poultry regions a warning signal worth watching.
plos-pone-0345554:
Megan Dreher and colleagues separated two ways music is supposed to help runners: rhythm and motivation. They replaced music with its ingredients. Their 2026 study had fifteen adults run on a treadmill in three conditions. One was silence. One used a flashing visual metronome matched to their stride. One added a non-rhythmic motivational speech to the metronome. Sensors tracked trunk movement and balance, and runners rated their effort.

Both stimulus conditions trimmed perceived effort slightly, shy of statistical significance. The combined condition measurably steadied the trunk. It reduced sway acceleration in every direction compared with the metronome alone. The design offers researchers a clean way to test which part of music does the work. Early evidence credits motivational content with real biomechanical calm.
plos-pone-0345854:
Faraz Sarmeili and colleagues benchmarked ranking methods that order cancer drugs by likely benefit for a given cell line. Ranking fits the real task better than predicting exact response values. Their 2026 study compared six ranking loss functions and five ways of describing drugs across two large screening datasets.

List-based losses led on both early and overall ranking quality. Mixing molecular fingerprints with basic chemical descriptors improved results further. The team added attention maps and an explanation tool that flagged genes and drug fragments behind each ranking. The explanations separated two breast cancer subtypes and highlighted known active parts of real drugs. Sarmeili and colleagues present the work as a step toward ranking tools doctors can inspect.
plos-pone-0347854:
Takafumi Ishii, Takashi Kojima, Yusuke Yasuda, and Kazushi Fujimoto present a way to compute entropy, the measure of disorder, for small local regions inside rubber-like materials. Rubber's springiness comes from entropy in its tangled molecular network, but local entropy changes had resisted calculation. Their method counts the states available to atoms from how they jiggle in molecular dynamics simulations.

Tested on simulated polymer networks, the computed entropy agreed qualitatively with thermodynamic expectations and with values from established integration techniques. The method works for the whole system and for local patches around cross-links. The authors offer it as a tool for understanding why elastomers stretch and snap back.
plos-pone-0348054:
Sahar Abed and Abdolrazagh Hashemi Shahraki led a hunt for a virus that kills drug-proof bacteria. The target germ causes pneumonia and resists last-resort drugs. The team found the virus in hospital wastewater. They named it Halo KS-7. Gene reading, done with help from AI tools, mapped its makeup. Tests ran in dishes and in mouse wounds.

The virus hit the target germ hard. It worked best at body heat and in salty settings. It broke bacteria open after a short wait of about twenty minutes. Mouse wound tests tracked healing and tissue health. The team calls the virus a strong hope for treating a germ that badly needs new foes.
plos-pone-0348354:
ZhiPeng Wu proposed a new weather forecasting method in 2026 that blends graph networks with a diffusion model. Standard computer models of the atmosphere are costly and strain against its chaotic behaviour, while many learning methods miss how conditions vary from place to place.

The method maps weather onto graphs at several scales to catch local and wide patterns, then lets a diffusion model trace how conditions evolve over time in a compressed form. On real data sets it beat leading rivals in accuracy and speed, doing especially well for temperature, air pressure height, and wind. Sharper cheap forecasts aid farms and disaster planning.
plos-pone-0348954:
Aya Sugiyama and co-workers follow how long COVID-19 symptoms lasted across pandemic waves in Hiroshima, Japan, comparing adults and children. Their 2026 study extends an earlier group to nearly twenty-seven hundred people infected between twenty twenty and twenty twenty-four, asking about thirteen symptoms and how long each hung on.

Adults fared worst in the Delta period, when close to half still had symptoms at six months. Later variant periods left fewer adults affected, and children's rates ran far lower throughout. Symptoms lasting past two years rarely cleared after that, though children's remaining symptoms did not disrupt daily life. Younger age sped recovery most. The long tail of illness shrank with newer variants but never vanished.
plos-pone-0349254:
Ryota Yamamoto and co-authors tested whether brain responses to flashing patterns can measure the eye's focusing power objectively, useful for patients who cannot report what they see. Twenty-one students viewed checkerboard patterns and the same boards rotated into diamonds while the team blurred their vision with lenses in steps and recorded the brain's electrical reply. The replies were compared with each student's own measured focusing range.

The brain signal's height shrank as blur grew, even when its timing held steady. Diamond patterns predicted focusing power more accurately and tracked the students' own measurements more tightly than upright boards. The authors trace this quirk to how vision favours horizontal and vertical lines over slanted ones. They propose the diamond test as the better candidate for an objective focusing exam.
plos-pone-0349354:
Kimia Taki and colleagues optimized a venturi tube reactor that pasteurizes milk without heat, using collapsing bubbles to kill germs. A venturi tube narrows a pipe so fast-moving liquid forms cavitation bubbles; their violent collapse destroys bacteria while the milk stays cool. The team used fluid dynamics simulations and a statistical design method to tune the tube's throat size, length, and angles.

The tuned design maximized turbulence in the cavitation zone while keeping energy losses and pressure drop low. In experiments the reactor cut E. coli counts by nearly three orders of magnitude, while milk fat, protein, and lactose stayed essentially unchanged. Heat-free pasteurization that keeps fresh flavor and nutrition intact is a long-sought goal for small dairies.
plos-pone-0349554:
Arshad M Khanani and colleagues ran a multi site trial of a cooling device that numbs the eye before injections into the eye. Many patients need repeated eye injections and dread the pain. Eighty patients who had long used numbing drops or gel tried set cold doses, from minus ten to minus fifteen degrees for ten to twenty seconds.

Pain fell most with the shortest cold dose, ten seconds at the colder setting, with average scores staying low across visits. A longer dose at the same cold hurt more on average. Mild surface marks appeared in one group but not the other. Cold numbing can ease eye injection pain, the trial finds, when dose is kept brief.
plos-pone-0349654:
Han and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, build a vision model that can tell whose sheep is whose on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Overgrazing is wearing down the grassland, and knowing which flock grazes where would help balance herds with grass and settle disputes between herders. Sheep carry natural color patterns on their backs, and the team trained a segmentation model to read them.

Their model upgrades a strong existing design with three additions. A module reads the scene at several scales. Another keeps meaning consistent. A third rebuilds fine detail when enlarging the output. On a purpose-built data set of sheep in varied light and backgrounds, it beat its base model on every score. It also held up on a public benchmark and small test sets. The authors offer the tool for precision grazing management on fragile high grassland.
plos-pone-0349754:
Kétlin Fagundes Teixeira, Ana Carolina Cadore-Rodrigues, and co-authors tested how surface preparation affects the fatigue strength of zirconia ceramic used for dental crowns. Crowns fail by cracking after years of chewing, and how the ceramic is treated before cementing may decide its lifespan. Their 2026 lab study prepared ceramic discs with five treatments, from sandblasting with different grits to glazing, then cemented them with thick or runny resin cements and flexed them to failure.

Surface treatment mattered greatly, while cement thickness did not. Glazing produced the strongest discs, with smooth, even surfaces. Coarse sandblasting performed worst and left the deepest defects, while fine sandblasting and glaze-plus-acid landed in between. The authors conclude that gentle glazing beats aggressive roughening for long-lasting zirconia restorations.
plos-pone-0349854:
Alexandra Poeschla and co-authors tracked a fungal infection marker in Ugandan outpatients with advanced HIV from 2017 to 2022 in work published in 2026. Cryptococcal disease kills many such patients, and a blood antigen test can catch it before symptoms, as national screening expanded.

More than four hundred adults tested positive. Their immune counts were very low, and the median marker level sat at a mid range tied to risk. Over the years the share already on HIV treatment at screening fell, while marker levels drifted up without a clear trend. The data show screening reaching people later, a gap programs must close.
plos-pone-0349954:
Xiao-Ying Huang and Xiang Zheng studied a combined inflammation score in critically ill patients with high blood fats in 2026, using a large intensive care database. The score folds four blood cell counts into one number meant to capture immune strain.

More than twelve thousand first time intensive care patients were followed for deaths at one, three, and six months, plus kidney injury and delirium. Higher scores meant higher death risk at every horizon, with risk climbing sharply past a clear threshold. The top quarter fared worst. A score from a routine blood count could help flag fragile patients on day one.
plos-pone-0350454:
Liping Wu and colleagues assessed the reliability of a key valve system in coal gasification plants in 2026, using a blend of two artificial intelligence methods. The lock bucket valve works under harsh conditions, and its failure can halt a plant.

A learning network first tuned the starting numbers of a dynamic risk model that tracks how failure chances shift over time. The tuned model then judged the system forward and backward. Without upkeep, predicted reliability after three hundred hours was very low, and maintenance lifted it greatly. The optimised model gave more cautious estimates than the untuned one, a warning against rosy assumptions.
plos-pone-0350554:
Simon de Gans and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One observational study of how medical teams work together for patients with several chronic conditions at once. The researchers filmed and recorded two kinds of treatment meetings: interprofessional meetings, where specialists pursue one shared patient-centered goal, and multidisciplinary meetings, where each specialist mainly argues their own field's case.

The interprofessional meetings sat people around a table with a designated chair and a relaxed, learning-friendly tone, while multidisciplinary meetings used a theatre layout with more passive listeners and disease-centered talk. Clinicians who attended both formats joined in far more actively in the interprofessional ones. The authors distill their observations into nine practical keys for better collaboration, aimed at hospital teams drowning in complex patients.
plos-pone-0350854:
Asma ElAdel, Imen Filali, and Mourad Zaied published this 2026 study of artificial intelligence screening for diabetic retinopathy, serious eye damage from diabetes that blinds when caught late. Eye specialists remain the gold standard but are slow and scarce. Their model uses a compact vision transformer, an attention-based design good at linking distant parts of a retinal image.

The system was built to grade disease severity and flag likely cases quickly for human review. ElAdel pitches it for pre-screening and telemedicine, especially where ophthalmologists are few and diabetes is rising.
plos-pone-0351054:
Xiaoyuan Jin and colleagues built a light vision model that spots faults on power line insulators even in fog. Fog blurs small cracks and dirt marks, and drone photos add busy backgrounds. Their model cleans fog noise, lifts faint fault marks, and blends detail at several scales while staying small enough for field gear.

On a fog data set the team built, accuracy reached a solid mark with under three million settings to tune. Scores held up on two public fog sets and on a clear weather road scene set as well. Light weight matters here: a model that runs on a drone can flag faults during flight instead of after landing, cutting inspection time for power crews.
plos-pone-0351154:
Lucas David, Nicolas Pellerin, and Michaël Dambrun adapted a questionnaire on selflessness and self-centeredness so it can measure a single day rather than a person's general character. A trait version already existed, splitting selflessness into four parts and self-centeredness into three. Three studies, with hundreds and then over a thousand respondents, checked whether the daily version keeps that shape.

The daily scale did reproduce the seven-part structure, and its scores lined up with mental health, relationships, and care for the environment in ways theory predicts. Days on which people felt more selfless differed measurably from self-centered days. A day-level tool lets researchers ask how these states rise and fall with events, sleep, or practice, and whether nudging a single day can nudge a life.
plos-pone-0351254:
Semin Kazazoglu and four colleagues developed this 2026 PLOS One questionnaire measuring how dehumanized academics feel by their own universities. Managerial, metric-driven governance has raised complaints that scholars are treated as numbers rather than people. Working with two samples of Turkish academics totaling nearly six hundred, the team built and tested a scale for this perception.

The final thirty-four-item scale splits into two dimensions: feeling devalued and feeling treated as a mere instrument. Statistical checks showed the scale is highly consistent and mostly succeeds at measuring something distinct from neighboring concepts. The authors offer it to researchers and university leaders as a diagnostic tool for spotting where institutional practices make staff feel less than human.
plos-pone-0351554:
Scott W Gill and colleagues studied health understanding among people held in prisons in New South Wales, Australia. They used answers from a standard health literacy survey given to more than four hundred people. Grouping methods sorted people with like strengths and struggles. Interviews with ten people inside added daily detail about getting care.

Grouping found fourteen distinct profiles for the whole sample, and nine for people who identified as Aboriginal. Staff and advocates then helped shape twenty three short portraits, each standing for one profile. The portraits show that average scores hide wide differences. Care and health teaching can fit real needs better when they start from these varied profiles instead of one score for everyone.
plos-pone-0351754:
Fadi Al Zoubi and six colleagues adapt an evidence-based practice questionnaire for Hong Kong clinicians. Their 2026 study imports a tool built for recent Canadian therapy graduates. Evidence-based practice means blending research, expertise, and patient values. Measuring it fairly requires wording that survives translation and culture. First came translation into the local language and back again, scrutiny by an expert panel, and probing interviews with thirty-six providers. Then two hundred forty-eight clinicians completed the final version.

The tool's structure survived the journey. Its two models cover six ideas, from actual use of evidence to knowledge, confidence, attitudes, and resources. Statistical modelling checked that items behaved consistently and treated groups fairly. One model needed only language adjustments. Hong Kong's health system employs thousands trained across many traditions. A validated measure lets educators see whether evidence habits are spreading, rather than assuming imported questionnaires mean the same thing abroad.
plos-pone-0352154:
Carly Lightstone and five colleagues interview patients in the raw days after losing a leg. Their 2026 qualitative study sits in a vascular surgery service. The patients had peripheral arterial disease and chose planned, primary amputations. Interviews ran five to ten days after surgery. The premise is that adjustment begins long before the operation. A patient's emotional state approaching amputation shapes recovery, rehabilitation, and quality of life afterwards. Understanding that inner process is the study's aim.

Conversations were analysed thematically for recurring patterns. The authors frame psychological support as part of surgical care, not an afterthought bolted on later. Surgeons deciding with patients about amputation hold more than a technical choice. Fear, grief, identity, and hope all sit in the consultation room. By documenting patients' own accounts so soon after surgery, the study gives care teams language and timing for support that patients will actually recognise as help.
plos-pone-0352254:
Hayato Ishii and six colleagues mine breast cancer data for prognostic signals in this 2026 study. Their focus is the genes that build junctions between cells. Those junctions hold epithelial tissue together, and their failure has long been tied to cancer spread. The team analysed one hundred seventy-nine junction genes across breast cancer subtypes. Two large datasets supplied the discovery material. An independent Scandinavian cohort provided validation.

A combined junction signature predicted survival within subtypes. High scores meant poorer outcomes nearly everywhere. The effect bit hardest in Luminal B and basal-like tumours, the aggressive kinds. High scores also forecast recurrence inside the first five years. Such tumours switched on matrix and scaffolding pathways, as if loosening their moorings. Single-cell data showed which cells carry the signature genes. A junction-based score could help oncologists spot, early, the patients whose cancers are likeliest to return.
plos-pone-0352454:
Qianyao Yuan and colleagues compared scans and tissue features of a rare lung cancer that mixes two cell types in one tumor. Adenosquamous carcinoma grows both gland-like and flat squamous cancer cells, behaves aggressively, and is hard to name before surgery because its scans resemble either parent type. The team reviewed twenty-seven such cases against forty each of the two pure types.

Against squamous cancers, the mixed tumors sat more often toward the lung's edge and showed more pleural pulling, spiky borders, and spread to lymph nodes. Measures built from these traits separated the groups usefully. For surgeons and radiologists, the work lists concrete scan clues worth weighting when a lung mass could be this mixed, harder-to-treat cancer rather than a commoner one.
plos-pone-0352654:
Guan and colleagues designed a soft robot gripper for holding odd-shaped objects in a 2026 study. Soft grippers bend gently, but they can be too floppy to hold firm. Their design pairs a rubber-like material that bends when voltage is applied with a printed star-pattern support that adds stiffness without blocking sideways bend.

Computer models tested how stretching the rubber and squeezing the support changed the bend. A built version with two rubber layers was then checked in trials against the models. Tuning those two settings gave stronger, more controlled bending. The design points toward gentle robot hands that can still hold their shape under load.
plos-pone-0353154:
Liyun Su, Linke Hou, and Jiaodi Liu present this 2026 PLOS One engineering paper on a flexible version of the Stewart platform, the six-legged device that moves flight simulators and precision machines. Their design adds piezoelectric elements to correct tiny motion losses in the telescopic legs. The hard problems are calculating leg lengths for a desired pose and, harder still, working backward from leg lengths to pose.

For the backward problem they trained a neural network enhanced with a stronger fitting algorithm, using exact formulas to generate its training data. In simulations the network predicted platform pose with errors under half a percent across the whole workspace. The authors say the approach beats both the classic iterative method and standard neural networks, supporting ultra-precise positioning in robotics and measurement.
plos-pone-0353354:
Gang Chen, Qinjuan Zhong, and Ning Tang test whether tiny parcels shed by a medicinal herb can fight stomach cancer, in this 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory study. The herb is danshen, long used in Chinese medicine. From it the team purified exosome-like nanoparticles — microscopic bubbles carrying small RNA molecules — and fed them to human stomach cancer cells growing in dishes.

The cancer cells swallowed the parcels and slowed down: they survived less well, formed fewer colonies, and migrated less. Sequencing catalogued the RNA cargo, which appears to drive the effect. Plant-derived parcels are attractive because they are cheap and naturally tolerated, but the authors stress this is dish-level evidence, far from a treatment.
plos-pone-0353554:
Zhang and Hedayati Marzbali, in a 2026 study, ask what makes residents of old Chinese villages satisfied with tourism in their home places. Reviving traditional villages through tourism is a favored path to rural renewal, but residents' feelings can make or break it. The team surveyed people in three traditional villages in Yongzhou.

Two ideas guided the work: whether tourism met what residents expected, and how attached residents felt to their place. Higher expectations were linked to lower satisfaction, a letdown effect. Feeling that tourism brought real value carried the good effects of place pride and attachment into satisfaction. Age mattered: older residents were more satisfied, and several links between feelings and satisfaction differed by generation. The authors advise planners to keep promises modest, share value visibly, and design tourism with each generation in mind, so villages gain without residents feeling used.
plos-pone-0353654:
Raeon Jang and seven colleagues ran a small randomised trial of laser acupuncture delivered inside the knee joint's acupuncture points, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Forty-five people with knee osteoarthritis were split among two laser wavelengths and a sham treatment that mimicked the procedure. Sessions ran twice a week for six weeks, and pain, stiffness, and daily function were tracked afterwards.

Both laser groups improved more than the sham group on pain at rest and in motion, and on standard joint scores, at several follow-up points. No treatment-related side effects appeared. Because the trial was a pilot, the authors call the pain relief a promising signal that larger trials must confirm.
plos-pone-0353754:
Martin Weiß and colleagues track in 2026 how personality and the moment together shape whether people want social contact in daily life. Over two weeks, participants reported many thousands of real interactions through phone prompts, noting their own motives, how they saw their partner's motives, and how much they wanted the interaction. Stable traits for seeking or avoiding contact were measured as well.

A combined view using traits, momentary states, and partner views predicted preferences best. Seeking related traits and states raised the wish to interact, while avoidance states lowered it. Effects faded quickly between interactions. People with poor social functioning wanted less contact overall, with similar underlying patterns.
plos-pone-0353954:
Akihito Nakanishi and eight colleagues test a new way to probe hearing damage. The damage comes from a chemotherapy drug. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The drug, cisplatin, saves lives. But it often costs patients their high-frequency hearing. The team delivered ultrasound through the skull bone. They measured the brain's electrical response. Then they compared shifts in two ranges. One was the bone-conducted ultrasound range. The other was the ordinary hearing range.

Ordinary thresholds worsened clearly after the drug. The ultrasound responses shifted much less. That mismatch carries a warning. The ultrasound route taps a different part of the hearing machinery. It cannot simply stand in for standard tests. Anyone hoping to use it as a quick damage gauge should take note.
plos-pone-0354154:
Ahmed Ali A Shohan and co-authors measure three decades of city growth in five Saudi Arabian cities, from the early nineteen nineties to the early twenty twenties, using satellite images. Fast growth in an arid kingdom strains water, land, and services. The team classified land cover across time with vegetation and water indices and checked their maps carefully, then modeled how land shape steered growth.

One holy city grew most in raw area, the capital grew fastest in proportional terms, and another holy city barely expanded because steep land hemmed it in. Growth patterns differed too: compact and centered in the holy cities, sprawling in the capital and coastal cities. Shohan and colleagues give planners a city-by-city record for steering the next wave of building.
plos-pone-0354254:
Yangming Zhang, Baohui Tian, and Hufeng Guo improve an artificial intelligence detector for cracks in bridge concrete, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Cracks are thin, faint, and easily confused with stains and rough texture, yet they are the earliest visible warning of structural decline. Their modified detector analyses images in the frequency domain as well as the ordinary spatial view, and adds a module dedicated to sharpening edges.

On two public crack datasets the improved detector beat its base model on the standard detection scores, by several percentage points on the stricter measures. Sharper automated eyes could let road agencies survey thousands of bridges from camera footage instead of sending inspectors onto scaffolding.
plos-pone-0354354:
Xuancai Chen led a team of eight authors on this 2026 prostate cancer study that lines up three kinds of molecular evidence. They compared gene activity and protein levels in prostate cancer cells, including drug-resistant ones, with chemical profiles from matched human prostate tissue held in a public database.

Seven genes stood out at both the gene and protein layers, and one enzyme, UPP1, pointed straight at how cells recycle building blocks for DNA. Tissue chemistry backed a broader reshaping of those pathways. Chen stresses the result is a prioritized lead, not proof of cause or a ready diagnostic test.
plos-pone-0354454:
Fatemeh Ahmadnia and co-authors steeped Russian knapweed, itself an aggressive invader, in water and tested the extract on the seeds of three weeds, two crops, and rye. Their 2026 laboratory study measured germination and seedling growth across rising extract strengths, hunting for a dose window where weeds suffer but crops shrug, the basic recipe for a plant-based herbicide.

The window exists. Germination fell in a straight line with dose for everything, but weeds were stopped dead at far lower strengths than wheat or rye needed. Chemical profiling fingered several candidate compounds, including phenolics and a fragrant sesquiterpene. The authors stress these are dish experiments; soil, microbes, and weather may rewrite the story in a real field.
plos-pone-0354754:
Mustafa Çam leads a team of eight studying how storage temperature affects chukar partridge eggs before incubation, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Game bird breeders hold eggs for a week or two before setting them, and standard poultry advice recommends a narrow cool band. The team stored eggs at four temperatures, from near refrigeration to warm room level, for seven or fourteen days, then examined development and hatched the rest.

Most egg and hatching traits barely differed across the whole temperature range. Eggs kept at the middle cool setting produced slightly lighter chicks and took longer to hatch. Warmer storage nudged embryos toward later developmental stages before incubation, without clearly harming outcomes. The authors conclude that partridge eggs tolerate a far wider storage range than industry guidance assumes, a practical finding for small breeders without precise cold rooms, within the storage times tested.
plos-pone-0354954:
Anjelica Martinez and colleagues put a widely used cultural values questionnaire under the microscope for Mexican American college students. The scale was built for teenagers and their caregivers, yet researchers keep using it with college students to study grades and well-being. Using existing data from several hundred undergraduates at Hispanic-serving campuses, the team tested whether the scale's structure, covering family duty, respect, religion, gender roles, and mainstream success values, still fits.

It did not. Formal checks showed clear misfit for Mexican American students, and attempts to stretch the scale to other Latinx students also failed, with the scale behaving differently across groups. Martinez and colleagues warn that results built on this mismatch may mislead, and they call for values measures built or revalidated with college students themselves.
plos-pone-0355054:
Takashi Koyama and co-authors study in 2026 how a receptor on dendritic cells helps those cells swallow tiny vesicles released by other cells and show their cargo to killer T cells. Vesicles are eyed as antigen carriers for cancer vaccines, but how dendritic cells take them in was unclear. Tests used a dendritic cell line and vesicles marked by a surface fat that bridging proteins can link to the receptor family.

Only one receptor in the family strongly boosted vesicle uptake, helped by both bridging proteins. A small inner stretch of that receptor proved vital for showing vesicle antigens onward. Tumour bearing mice had more such dendritic cells, hinting at a vaccine target.
plos-pone-0355354:
Sângia Feucht Freire and colleagues surveyed the heads of intensive care units across Brazil about safe breathing support for sore lungs. Gentler ventilator settings can spare hurt lungs. Their 2026 survey covered units in every region and scored what chiefs knew, felt, and did in daily care.

Most units had a wide range of gear on hand. Most said stocks grew after the COVID-19 pandemic. Clear gaps still split one region from the next. Scores for knowledge ran high on the whole. Units with more gear scored a bit higher, but the link was weak. Freire and colleagues say gear alone does not set good care, and poor regions need a fairer share.
plos-pone-0355554:
Helen Edith Müller and seven colleagues give the first detailed anatomical account of dogs' whisker follicles in this 2026 study, entering a live animal welfare debate. Trimming whiskers for show grooming is common, and some claim dogs' whiskers are reduced and unimportant, especially in poodles. The team examined facial skin from forty-four dogs of varied breeds, ages, and sizes, counting and measuring the follicle-sinus complexes and probing their nerve supply with stains and electron microscopy.

Each dog carried roughly sixty of these complexes, with the muzzle whiskers longest, and size scaled with body weight. The structures held a rich sensory architecture, several kinds of touch receptors and free nerve endings, with nerve tissue making up a substantial share of each complex. No breed, poodles included, showed reduced equipment. The authors say the anatomy refutes the claim that canine whiskers lack function.
plos-pone-0355854:
Emmanuel Kwame Darkwa and co-authors measured how many people with epilepsy in two Ghanaian districts receive no proper treatment. Epilepsy is highly treatable, yet a wide treatment gap persists in poorer countries. Their 2026 population study screened communities inside a long-running health surveillance area across most of a year.

Epilepsy affected just under nine people per thousand. Seven in ten confirmed cases formed the treatment gap; only three in ten used standard seizure medicine. The commonest reason among untreated people was never having been diagnosed at all. Beliefs played a role too: over a third of respondents blamed witchcraft or supernatural causes. Darkwa and colleagues call for diagnosis drives paired with belief-sensitive education.
plos-pone-0356254:
Mazin Mansory interviewed Saudi teachers and school staff about moral injury and burnout during the country's Vision 2030 education reforms. Moral injury means the distress people feel when their work forces them to act against their own values. His 2026 study drew on long interviews with educators across Saudi Arabia, analysed in depth.

Six themes ran through the accounts, including rigid curricula, heavy testing pressure, and a felt lack of care from institutions. Many teachers said set mandates clashed with Islamic teaching values of care and fairness. Newer teachers described shaky professional identity, while veterans described teaching two ways at once. Mansory argues reforms land better when they respect teachers' ethical commitments.
plos-pone-0357054:
Luca Alessandri traced ancient settlement change in Latium vetus, the old region around Rome, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. From the Bronze Age to the Early Iron Age, small settlements grew toward towns. Alessandri applied machine learning methods that can explain their own reasoning to that long shift.

The models highlight which factors best explain where people settled and how sites grew or shrank. Because the methods are explainable, archaeologists can judge the reasoning, not just accept a score. Understanding how early communities clustered helps explain the roots of Rome itself. The study also shows how transparent AI can serve history without turning it into a black box.
plos-pone-0357154:
Zhuozhi Gong and six colleagues check whether hair loss drugs carry a hidden link to male infertility, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Finasteride, dutasteride, and minoxidil are widely used against pattern baldness, and scattered reports have raised fertility worries. The team combined drug safety databases with gene data from testicular tissue to look for both warning signals and a plausible biological route.

Safety reports from American and European systems, covering roughly two decades, showed reporting signals for all three drugs, strongest for finasteride. In tissue from infertile men, one gene, HIF1A, stood out as more active, including in sperm producing and hormone making cells, and its activity tracked with immune and wound healing pathways. The authors present HIF1A as a candidate worth laboratory follow up, not settled proof of harm.
plos-pone-0357754:
Dewi Wulandari led a team of seven authors mapping hepatitis B mutations in Indonesia, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The virus mutates to escape control, notably in two control regions, the precore and the basal core promoter. The team studied patients who lack a certain viral antigen, called HBeAg-negative, yet carry high viral loads.

Wulandari's mutation patterns give doctors information for choosing treatments likely to work. Mutations in these regions affect how the virus copies itself and how disease progresses. Indonesia carries a heavy hepatitis B burden, so local mutation data beat imported assumptions. Knowing which variants circulate helps labs pick the right tests and helps clinics anticipate which patients need closer watching for liver damage.
plos-pone-0358254:
Yonghui Zhang and Fangtao Li modeled how rock breaks under pressure and water, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Wet rock fails differently from dry rock, a fact tunnel and dam builders ignore at their peril. Their statistical damage model includes pore water pressure and the multifractal patterns found in real rock structure.

Zhang and Li's model helps engineers predict rock failure where water and stress combine, such as deep tunnels and reservoir slopes. Better prediction means supports designed for real conditions, not dry-lab ones. Fractal detail matters because rock is not uniform; its cracks follow patterns the model tries to honor. Safer underground works, from mines to metros, rest on models like this being right.
plos-pone-0358354:
Huiyue Pan, Leilei Zhai, Shupeng Zhao, Ziyi Guo, and Ping Yao published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies ulcerative colitis, a chronic inflammation of the colon, made worse by a high-fat diet. The authors focus on fatty acid oxidation, the process cells use to burn fats for energy, and on injury to mitochondria, the cell's power stations.

The mechanism they name runs through the AMPK/PPARα pathway, a signaling route that controls energy use in cells. When that pathway falters, fat burning drops and mitochondria suffer, which the authors present as a key route by which rich diets aggravate colitis. Researchers hunting drug targets for bowel inflammation are the main readers.
plos-pone-0358454:
Zoe Dellaert and Hollie M Putnam studied gene activity across a reef-building coral, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. A coral colony is not uniform: tips, sides, and base live in different light and flow, and do different jobs. The pair used methods that keep location information while reading which genes are active.

Dellaert and Putnam's map shows how the coral Pocillopora acuta divides labor across its own body. That spatial view helps explain how corals grow, feed, and respond to stress as a colony rather than as single polyps. Reefs are in steep decline, and colony-level insight may guide breeding of tougher corals. Basic maps like this underpin every later attempt to help reefs survive warming seas.
plos-pone-0358654:
Konstantinos G Baroutis leads a team of eight exposing a laboratory trap hidden in room light, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Verteporfin, a light activated drug, is widely used in dishes as if it were a plain blocker of a growth protein pair, YAP and TEAD. The team shows that much of its apparent work is photochemistry instead. The compound cross links proteins when samples sit under normal lighting after the cells are broken open.

The effect appeared within an hour in cell free extracts, hitting several proteins at once. Two protective chemicals blunted it, pointing to radical and oxygen based light reactions. YAP itself was highly vulnerable to cross linking, while its partner protein resisted. On a protein blot, that pattern masquerades as selective drug action. The authors warn that part of the record using this compound may need re reading, this time with the lights in mind.
plos-pone-0358754:
Guibo Nie and four co-authors study a Xi'an tourist district that sells history without old buildings, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Datang Everbright City is a themed precinct built to evoke the Tang dynasty through scenery and performance, with no genuine relics on site. The authors asked how such staged surroundings can still stir visitors' cultural identity, and whether that feeling turns into loyalty to the place.

Surveying close to three hundred tourists, they traced how the district's physical and social atmosphere feeds a sense of belonging. Cultural identity carried the effect onward: it fully explained loyalty for several parts of the visitor experience. The findings matter for China's many built from scratch heritage districts, where designers cannot rely on authentic remains and must make symbolism do the work instead.
plos-pone-0359554: Gao and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper that presents OQ-FERNet, a computer system for reading facial expressions. The system is built to keep working when part of a face is blocked from view. It also scores expressions in graded steps rather than simple labels. The authors aim it at live, real-time use between people and machines, where partly hidden faces are common.
plos-pone-0359954:
Nandakumar Ravichandran, Etimbuk Umana, Tomas Breslin, Aoife Cotter, and Walter Cullen wrote this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a study that looks back over records of acute infections that began in the community, in an emergency department in Ireland. These cases crowd emergency rooms daily.

Assessing how such infections present and are handled can expose delays in treatment or admission decisions. A protocol fixes the study's questions and methods before records are pulled. Emergency physicians and infection specialists in Ireland are the readers preparing to learn from their own department's record.
pmc-13226554:
Banjac and colleagues test a practice called meditative relaxation in French hospital doctors. Burnout is common among physicians and has grown worse since the COVID crisis. Standard mindfulness courses can cut stress, the authors note, yet they demand long training, hold people unevenly, and leave emotional and deeper questions untouched.

Meditative relaxation is presented as an original mind and body method. It blends focused attention, the senses, body processes, and guided imagination in one structured sitting. Their randomised exploratory study asks whether such a sitting can help busy hospital doctors at all. A positive signal would justify a larger trial of a tool built for short, real-world use.
pmc-13241054:
Goncalves and Rouco in Lisbon hunted for chaos inside sixteen years of Northern flu records. Weekly shares of positive flu tests ran from January 2009 to March 2025. Shape-based data analysis rebuilt the hidden attractor driving the series. The noise riding on that signal was split out for study.

A low-dimensional chaotic attractor emerged, with a positive Lyapunov exponent that confirmed touchiness. Its noise came in wild bursts rather than steady static. Machine learning on the attractor foretold flu activity over ninety percent right one week ahead. Scores stayed above seventy percent five weeks out, allowing month-ahead risk calls.
pmc-13241454:
Montes Peña's team in Riyadh tuned nerve monitoring settings for children's spinal surgery across 81 patients. Young patients' unripe pathways make motor signals hard to draw out each time. Each child served as their own control across electrode montages and pulse patterns. Motor thresholds scored every setup.

A linked quadripolar montage with double-train stimulation slashed thresholds in every single patient. 3-millisecond pulse spacing proved best; tighter spacing raised thresholds a lot. Younger age and prior motor deficits predicted harder checks on their own. The authors advise the winning setup with threshold-guided tweaks as standard. The team reports gains in every child tested.
pmc-13243054:
Xiangyu Fu and co-authors set out a trial protocol in this 2026 paper on glaucoma, an eye disease that can blind people without warning signs. China has no widely accepted screening model for it, so the team plans to build and test a three-step one for community use.

The model starts with a risk questionnaire, moves to eye checks with image reading helped by artificial intelligence, and ends with firm diagnosis at large hospitals. The trial will enrol 28,275 people across communities, split into no screening, routine screening, and tiered screening groups, with at least six years of follow-up. It will compare detection rates and costs between the groups.
pmc-13243754:
Juan Wang, Shengyu Yang, and Hua Cao report a young woman whose emergency transfusions led to a dangerous lung reaction. Their case study appeared in the Journal of International Medical Research in 2026. The twenty-two-year-old arrived in shock after a corpus luteum cyst ruptured and bled inside her abdomen. Around her surgery she received multiple units of red cells and fresh frozen plasma to keep her alive.

Six hours after the final transfusion she developed transfusion-related acute lung injury, a flooding of the lungs that can turn fatal fast. The authors link its onset to her surgery and the volume of plasma-rich products, layered over an inflammatory backdrop of antiphospholipid syndrome and a leg vein clot. They urge tighter transfusion management and sharper awareness of this reaction. Their warning is aimed especially at hospitals working with scarce blood supplies and limited monitoring resources.
pmc-13244354:
Chadsley Wessinger and co-authors asked whether eating well protects thinking in women at raised risk of Alzheimer's, and whether genes set the limit. Their study appeared in the Journal of Nutritional Science in 2026. They analyzed 102 physically inactive middle-aged women, all with a family history of the disease. Diet quality was scored on a national healthy eating index, thinking was tested across executive domains, and saliva genotyping identified carriers of the APOE-ε4 risk variant.

Better diet quality predicted stronger executive function and working memory overall. The catch sat in the interaction: those benefits appeared clearly only in women who did not carry the risk variant. Carriers showed no comparable diet-thinking link in this snapshot. The authors caution that one cross-section cannot prove cause. Still, prevention advice may one day need a genetic footnote.
pmc-13244954:
Frida Hermansson and colleagues show that defining a heart measurement differently changes the diagnosis. Their study appeared in Echo Research and Practice in 2026. The 2025 American heart-ultrasound guidelines redrew where right-ventricle widths are taken, replacing the 2010 rules. The team remeasured scans from 208 healthy volunteers and 221 lung-artery hypertension patients under the old rules, the new ones, and a new automated method.

The definitions did not agree. Where the calipers land shifted both the numbers and who crossed the threshold for calling the ventricle enlarged. An automated approach following the chamber's curved centerline offered a more consistent reference. The authors warn that switching versions mid-practice can manufacture apparent change in an unchanged patient. Labs, they argue, must adopt the new rules knowingly, flag the switch in reports, and read repeat scans with the ruler in mind.
pmc-13245054:
Piotr Rzymski and colleagues asked whether watching your unvaccinated child hospitalized changes your mind about vaccines, and whether the virus matters. Their multicenter study appeared in Human Vaccines and Immunotherapeutics in 2026. Polish parents of children hospitalized with influenza or with COVID-19 answered surveys on regret, future vaccination plans, and willingness to urge other parents to vaccinate.

Influenza moved parents far more. Nearly two-thirds of flu parents regretted skipping vaccination, against under a quarter of COVID parents. The flu group was also far likelier to plan vaccination next season and to recommend it to others. Statistical adjustment left influenza hospitalization independently tied to regret and future intent. A twist appeared in the COVID group, where more parents wanted reminder messages than planned to vaccinate at all, suggesting openness without conviction. The authors say a hospital scare is a teachable moment, but its teaching depends on which disease did the scaring.
pmc-13246454:
Kei Sato and co-authors present a 2026 case report and literature review about rehab after the loss of both legs at the hip. Their patient was a 46-year-old woman who developed necrotising fasciitis, a fast-moving flesh-destroying infection, and needed both hips removed to save her life.

Full leg prostheses after such surgery demand great strength and long training, and few reports describe what works. The team instead built the plan around a stabiliser brace, aiming at daily activities and taking part in life rather than walking. They frame the approach with a standard health model that weighs body function, activity, and participation together.
pmc-13246754:
Oransa, Zahran, El Sadda, and co-authors tested a nanoscale drug carrier against liver and breast cancer cells, in this 2026 Scientific Reports paper. Curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric, kills cancer cells in the lab but dissolves poorly.
