Walters, Hyde, Berg-Lyons, and their colleagues improved marker gene primers in 2015 for microbial community surveys. Such surveys read a marker gene, often the 16S rRNA gene in bacteria, to census microbes in a sample. A wealth of findings had connected microbes to human and environmental ecology.

The team updated primers for the bacterial 16S gene regions V4 and V4-5 and for fungal marker regions. As knowledge and technique improve, primer tools can be modified to raise accuracy. Better primers capture more of the true community and bias results less. Shared, improved primers let microbiome studies across labs be compared fairly.
pmc-5687754:
Florian Rohart, Benoit Gautier, Amrit Singh, and colleagues introduced the mixOmics software package in 2017. Modern labs produce huge data sets from genes, proteins, and small molecules in the same samples. Making sense of several such data sets at once is hard without the right tools.

mixOmics runs in the R language and helps users pick the most useful features from each data set. It can also combine data sets so shared patterns stand out. Clear plots guide users through each step. For biologists facing multi-part data, the package offers a tested way to find signals that one data set alone would miss.
pmc-5762154:
Aviv Regev, Sarah Teichmann, Eric Lander, and a large international team laid out the Human Cell Atlas plan in 2017. New single-cell methods can profile thousands of cells one by one. The authors argue the time is right to name every cell type in the human body.

The plan calls for shared standards, open data, and maps that combine gene activity with cell position in tissues. Early pilot work would cover key organs before scaling to the whole body. A finished atlas would give medicine a reference much like the human genome. Doctors could compare sick tissue against a healthy standard cell by cell.
pmc-5802054:
Alexander Wolf, Philipp Angerer, and Fabian Theis introduced Scanpy in 2018. Scanpy is a Python toolkit for single-cell gene expression data, which can cover millions of cells. Analysts need cleaning, grouping, and plotting steps that still run fast at that size.

The toolkit covers preprocessing, clustering, trajectory building, and tests for genes that differ between groups. It can also simulate gene networks for method testing. Its design borrows the data handling style of larger machine learning tools. Scanpy became one of the main ways single-cell data are explored, and many later tools build on it.
pmc-6291454:
The GBD 2016 Dementia Collaborators published this global dementia analysis in 2019. More people are living with dementia each year, which strains families, communities, and health systems. A sound response starts with an accurate count of the burden.

The study reports cases, deaths, and disability from Alzheimer disease and other dementias across most countries. Numbers rose mainly because populations grew older and larger. Rates at a given age changed little in many regions. The authors argue that prevention of risk factors like smoking and high blood pressure is the main lever available while cures remain out of reach.
pmc-6591954:
Ryan Wick, Louise Judd, and Kathryn Holt compared nanopore basecalling tools in 2019. Basecalling turns the raw electrical signal from a nanopore sequencer into DNA letters. Every later result depends on getting those letters right.

The team ran several neural network callers on the same bacterial data sets. They measured accuracy, speed, and how errors cluster in hard regions. Newer callers clearly beat older ones, but none was perfect everywhere. Their benchmarks help labs pick a caller and set honest expectations for assembly and variant work. The authors share their test data so future callers can be judged on the same ground.
pratt-voice-of-warning-1854:
Parley P. Pratt wrote A Voice of Warning in 1837, and the eighth edition of 1854 shows how long it kept selling. Pratt, an apostle and tireless missionary of the young Mormon church, aimed his tract at every reader he could reach. Prophecy, the Book of Mormon, and the coming kingdom of God fill its urgent pages.

No Mormon tract of the nineteenth century was reprinted more often or carried farther. Missionaries bore it across America and Britain, and converts often met the faith first in Pratt's clear voice. The book's warnings of judgment and calls to gather shaped how outsiders pictured the new movement for decades.
racine-phedre-french-1854:
Jean Racine wrote Phèdre in 1677, at the height of his career as France's leading playwright. The text here is the French original, in the Didot edition of 1854. Phèdre, wife of King Theseus, burns with a forbidden love for her stepson Hippolytus and cannot master it.

Phèdre's confession sets off a chain of lies, rage, and deaths. Theseus curses his son, Hippolytus dies, and Phèdre takes poison after clearing his name. Racine tells the tragedy in strict, shining verse, with few characters and great pressure. French readers rank Phèdre as the summit of their classical theater, a study of passion and shame.
rondelet-de-piscibus-marinis-1554:
Guillaume Rondelet, a French doctor and teacher at Montpellier, published his Books on Marine Fishes in 1554. The Latin work is a founding text of ichthyology, the science of fishes. Rondelet drew and described Mediterranean species from his own dissections and harbor-side study.

Real fishes fill most of his pages, carefully distinguished kind by kind. Yet the sea-monk and other marine monsters stand among them, reported in good faith. Science and marvel share his learned page without quarrel. Rondelet taught a generation of naturalists, Gesner among them. His fish book marks the moment when close looking began to sort the sea's true tenants from its legends.
smith-dictionary-greek-roman-geography-v:
William Smith edited his Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography in the 1850s, with Volume One, from Abacaenum to Hytanis, in 1854. It is the great Victorian gazetteer of the ancient world. Smith's scholars worked from the classical authors and from travelers' reports.

Each place gets its history, its coins, its ruins, and the ancient authorities that name it. Cities, rivers, mountains, and islands of Greece and Rome fill the pages. Woodcuts of sites and plans help the reader picture lost towns. Classical students used it to map every campaign and voyage in their texts. A companion set on ancient life and customs shares the same editor and plan.

Volume Two of Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography, also 1854, completes the gazetteer, from Iabadius to Zytus. A general index closes the set. William Smith's team matched the biography dictionary in scale and care.

The entries trace the rest of the ancient map: Italy's towns, the provinces, and the edges of the known world. Histories of sieges, colonies, and trade routes gather under each name. Coins and remains ground the literary record in things a reader could still see. The two volumes together gave Victorian readers the fullest ancient atlas in words that English has produced.
the-alchemical-testament-of-john-gybbys-: The Alchemical Testament of John Gybbys of Exeter, 1854. The Exeter testament. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
the-marrow-of-alchemy-1654-1654: The Marrow of Alchemy, 1654. The alchemical marrow. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume four of Casanova's memoirs: further adventures of the Venetian. Duels, loves, and escapes across Europe. The 18th century's most famous life. Casanova's fourth volume: love and duels, the adventurer's star rises, love and duels in volume four.
theologia-germanica-1854:
Theologia Germanica is a small book of soul lore from 1300s Germany. No name sits on the work; a priest of Frankfurt may have wrote it. Susanna Winkworth gave it English dress in 1854. Martin Luther had praised the book three hundred years past.

The text bids the soul let go of self will and rest in God. It sets the life of Christ as the path each soul must walk. Calm, plain words hide a deep and hard call to yield all. The wee book swayed Luther, the first church rebels, and mystics since.
thoreau-walden-1854:
Henry David Thoreau published Walden in 1854, his experiment in deliberate living at Walden Pond. The book is the founding text of environmental thought and simple-living philosophy in the American tradition today. Thoreau lived two years in a cabin he built on Emerson's land by the pond.

He tills beans, watches ants war, and sounds the pond's depth through winter ice in Concord. Economy preaches cutting wants, while Brute Neighbors and Winter Animals crowd the pages with keen natural seeing in detail. The seasons turn one full round, spring's thaw standing for the soul's rebirth in his famous close here. Simplify, simplify is the book's household motto, and its challenge still nettles comfortable readers in every age. Few American books have been reread so often for so many different reasons.
tob-10554:
James Legge rendered Lao Tzu's eighty-one chapters again here under the fuller title The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and Its Characteristics. Legge, the Scottish missionary who became Oxford's first professor of Chinese, translated with a scholar's precision and copious notes. His version first made Chinese philosophy legible to many English readers.

The paradoxes remain intact, starting with the warning that the Tao that can be named is not the eternal Tao. Chapters on ruling without interference, the strength of weakness, and the uses of emptiness follow. Readers meet a Victorian landmark of translation, where careful notes surround verses that resist every attempt to pin them down.
tob-13554:
Extracts from al-Ghazali's Ihya, his Revival of the Religious Sciences, present some religious and moral teachings in digestible portions. Intention, gratitude, patience, and the diseases of the heart are among the subjects drawn from that vast manual. Al-Ghazali wrote the Ihya after his spiritual crisis, to rebuild religious life from the inside.

Shorter and more directly useful than his autobiography, these selections show the theologian as moral physician, diagnosing pride, envy, and heedlessness and prescribing remedies. The Ihya became Islam's classic manual of the inner life. Readers pressed for time can meet its central teaching here, then turn to the Confessions for the author's own story.
tob-4054:
Volume one of a four-volume edition of H. P. Blavatsky's Secret Doctrine carries the subtitle Cosmogenesis, Theosophy's creation story in full. Blavatsky presents stanzas from a claimed archaic book, the Book of Dzyan, surrounded by her vast commentary. The universe unfolds through cycles, rounds, and planes across unimaginable spans of time.

Hindu time-cycles blend with Victorian geology and evolutionary language as spirit descends toward matter. The commentary argues with contemporary science while borrowing its scale. Readers beginning the four-volume set should expect density and digression; the opening volume lays the cosmology on which the later volumes build their accounts of humanity, symbolism, and hidden history.
tob-4254:
A French study of Haitian Vodou spirits appeared in 1918 under the title Les Daimons du Culte Voudo, credited to the pen name Her-Ra-Ma-el. European readers of its day knew Vodou mostly through rumor and fright. The study instead catalogs the lwa, the spirits of the cult, one by one.

Rites, offerings, songs, and the families of spirits receive orderly treatment. Rada and Petro nations, healing and work spirits, the dead and the waters: the pantheon takes shape for a French audience. Verified from the 1919 edition, the book stands as an early European attempt to describe Haitian religion as its worshippers practice it.
treaty-of-kanagawa-1854:
Commodore Matthew Perry of the United States Navy signed the Treaty of Kanagawa with Japan in March 1854. Perry had arrived with warships the year before, pressing Japan to end more than two centuries of near-total seclusion from the West. The talks took place under the shadow of those guns, and Japan's rulers knew refusal could mean war.

The treaty opened two ports, Shimoda and Hakodate, to American ships needing supplies, and promised safety for shipwrecked sailors. An American consul would also live at Shimoda. Trade itself had to wait for a later treaty, but the door was open, and the shock pushed Japan toward rapid change.
un-ga-res-a-69-54:
Many voices, not one, must shape arms deals, argues Resolution A/69/54, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its theme is the push for joint, many-sided work in disarmament and against the spread of arms. The text recalls a 2001 vote that tied such work to the fight against terror, and a chain of votes since 2002 on the same theme.

The UN's core aim frames the call: to guard peace by joint steps that head off threats and halt attacks on the peace. Arms questions, in this view, are too big for any one state or bloc to settle alone. Deals struck by all, the Assembly holds, are the deals that last.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly resolution 69/54 (2014) backs multilateralism in disarmament and non-proliferation. The Assembly is troubled by the erosion of multilateral approaches. It is troubled by states turning to unilateral action on security concerns. It reaffirms multilateralism as the core principle for working out arms rules and for settling compliance concerns. It urges all interested states to take part in multilateral talks openly, with no one shut out. It asks parties to weapons-of-mass-destruction treaties to settle compliance disputes through those treaties' own procedures, rather than through unverified accusations.
un-sc-res-1154: This library holds Resolution 1154 as an official Council record, dated 1998 in its catalog. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1354:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed in June 2001 with a familiar complaint attached. On 15 June 2001 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 December 2001. The Secretary-General's report had again raised the missing persons issue. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay. The Council restated its Cyprus resolutions, led by 1251 of 1999. Aid work on disease control among peacekeepers also drew a welcome.

Turkish Cypriot leaders and Turkish forces had to lift limits placed on UNFICYP in June 2000. They also had to restore the military position at Strovilia. That small village post had become a symbol of the force's blocked movement. The Secretary-General owed a report by 1 December.
un-sc-res-1454: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 1454 is catalogued here under 1990. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1554: Resolution 1554 survives as part of the Council's official record, transcribed for this collection by English Wikisource. The Security Council acts for the whole UN membership on peace and security, and its resolutions are the proof of that work. Inside this text, recitals establish the grounds and numbered clauses carry the decision itself.
un-sc-res-1654:
The Congo arms embargo's expert watchers were re-established on 31 January 2006. The Security Council restated its resolve to track compliance with the embargo set by resolution 1493 (2003) and widened by resolution 1596 (2005). It meant to enforce travel and money measures against those who broke the embargo. The Congo's situation still threatened international peace and security, the Council held.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council asked the Secretary-General to re-establish the Group of Experts within thirty days. The new group's term would run to 31 July 2006. It would carry on the mandate set by resolutions 1533, 1596, and 1649 (2005). The group owed the sanctions committee an update by 10 April 2006 and a written report before 10 July. All parties and states had to cooperate fully with the group. Its members were to get safety, free access to people, documents, and sites, and no delays.
un-sc-res-1754: In 2007 the Security Council adopted Resolution 1754, preserved here through a transcription of the official record. Such texts are negotiated until fifteen governments can live with every clause, which gives the final wording its careful tone. The entry keeps the final wording, so readers meet the compromise exactly as it was struck.
un-sc-res-1854:
Liberia brought the Council to Resolution 1854, adopted on 19 December 2008. Liberia had made steady progress since 2006 in rebuilding the state. Its timber rules were in force, and it had joined the Kimberley Process for diamonds. Yet the Council found too little progress toward the terms for lifting sanctions.

Acting under Chapter VII, the text renews the arms and travel measures for twelve more months. The asset freeze from 2004 stays in force, with yearly review promised. The Panel of Experts gains a new term until 20 December 2009. The panel must check the timber and diamond sectors, judge how the freeze works, and report by June and December 2009.
un-sc-res-2254:
Resolution 2254 set out the Security Council's roadmap for ending Syria's civil war. Years of fighting had killed huge numbers of people and driven millions from the country. For once, the United States and Russia backed the same text.

The plan calls for talks between Syria's government and opposition, a ceasefire, a new constitution, and free elections under UN supervision within eighteen months. It also demands aid access to besieged towns. Readers get the full diplomatic blueprint that later peace talks kept returning to, even as the war went on. The vote itself was unanimous.
un-sc-res-254:
Conditions in Cyprus looked more hopeful in 1968, and the Council wanted the parties to use the moment well. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 11 June, said the peacekeeping force was still needed to maintain peace. Cyprus's government had agreed the force must stay. Resolution 254 was adopted unanimously on 18 June 1968.

The Council reaffirmed its string of Cyprus resolutions, back to Resolution 186 of 1964. The parties were urged to make the most of the favorable climate on the island. They had to keep working together toward the Council's goals, with determination. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 December 1968. The Council hoped that progress by then would allow a withdrawal, or at least a large cut in the force.
un-sc-res-354: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 354, which the catalog dates to 1974. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-454:
South African attacks on Angola were condemned by the Security Council on 2 November 1979. Angola's representative had brought the complaint, with a party communiqué sent on 31 October. Resolutions 387 (1976) and 447 (1979) had already condemned Pretoria's aggression and demanded respect for Angola's borders. The Council called the latest violations planned, persistent, and sustained.

The Council strongly condemned South Africa's aggression against Angola. South Africa had to stop all acts of aggression and provocation at once. It had to respect Angola's independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity in full. It also had to stop using Namibia, a territory it held illegally, as a base for attacks on Angola and other front-line states. Member states were asked to give Angola and its neighbors urgent help to strengthen their defense. The Council said the raids aimed to wreck talks on settlements in Namibia and Zimbabwe.
un-sc-res-54:
Palestine crossed a legal line in Security Council Resolution 54, passed on 15 July 1948. The stopgap state of Israel had agreed in the main to stretch the truce in the land. The states of the Arab League had turned down plea after plea, from the UN mediator and from the Council, to do the same. Fighting had flared up anew in the land as a result.

The Council rules that the state of Palestine is a threat to the peace, in the terms of Article 39 of the Charter. It orders all states and chiefs in the fight to halt all armed acts. Cease-fire orders must go out to their troops, at a time the mediator will fix. It was the first such ruling of the young Council's life.
un-sc-res-754:
Security Council Resolution 754, adopted on May 18, 1992, recommended Slovenia for membership in the United Nations. Some catalog notes give this vote to Croatia; in fact Croatia's bid was handled in the companion text adopted the same day, and this one names Slovenia. The Alpine republic had broken from Yugoslavia in June 1991 and held its freedom through a short war.

The Assembly seated Slovenia on May 22. Admission mattered beyond form: Yugoslavia's seat was in dispute, and each successor republic needed its own place in the world body. The short resolution is one step in the legal unmaking of a federation, taken while wars in Croatia and Bosnia were still raging.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1154, adopted in 1998 under Chapter VII, deals with Iraq's compliance with the disarmament obligations set by resolution 687 (1991) after the 1991 Gulf War cease-fire. The Council says its earlier resolutions form the governing standard of Iraqi compliance and that it is determined to secure immediate and full compliance, without conditions or restrictions.

The Council endorses the memorandum of understanding signed on 23 February 1998. It was signed between Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister and the Secretary-General. The deal was meant to reopen inspections. The Council asks for procedures for presidential sites to be finished quickly, with the heads of UNSCOM and the IAEA. It stresses that Iraq must give both bodies immediate, unconditional and unrestricted access. It warns that any violation would have the severest consequences for Iraq.

Cataloguers sometimes shelve Resolution 1354 under Western Sahara. The text itself is about Cyprus. It was adopted unanimously on 15 June 2001. The Secretary-General's report of 30 May 2001 had reviewed the UN operation there. It pressed both sides to deal seriously with missing persons. Cyprus's government agreed the peacekeepers should stay.

Members extended UNFICYP's mandate until 15 December 2001. A report was due by 1 December. The recurring Strovilia dispute appears again. Turkish Cypriot limits on the force, imposed in June 2000, had to be rescinded. The earlier military position there must be restored. These six-month renewals, repeated for decades, quietly froze the island's green line in place.

Changes to the Goods Review List used in Iraq's oil-for-food programme are adopted on 30 December 2002. The programme had just been extended for 180 days from 5 December. The list decides which imports Iraq may buy freely and which need review because they could serve military ends.

Changes to the list and to the procedures for applying it are adopted. A full review of both is ordered after 90 days and again before the 180-day period ends, with regular reviews after that. The sanctions committee is told to study the list as part of its regular work and suggest additions or deletions.

The Central African Republic became independent from France on 13 August 1960. Ten days later its UN application was already before the Council. Resolution 154 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960. The vote happened at the busy 891st meeting. That same session handled applications from Congo and Upper Volta as well.

Members recommended admitting the Central African Republic. The General Assembly followed within weeks. The landlocked state joined during the famous Year of Africa. Seventeen African nations gained independence in 1960. A UN seat offered the new republic recognition and contacts. It also tied the country to the decolonization debates then reshaping the Assembly's agenda and voting balance.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 29 July 2004, and the Abkhazia deadlock is taken up once more. Geneva meetings of the Group of Friends had kept some momentum in the talks. But the lack of progress toward a settlement is again called unacceptable, and the 2001 helicopter attackers remain unidentified.

Both sides are urged to negotiate in earnest, with a warning that a lasting deal will require concessions from each. They are pressed to work through the Geneva task forces on economic cooperation, refugee return, and political and security questions, and through the Sochi working groups. Law enforcement and safety in the Gali district are to improve so displaced people can return.

Resolution 1654, adopted on 31 January 2006, restarts the expert team policing Congo's arms embargo. The Council said it was determined to watch compliance closely and enforce penalties against violators. Eastern Congo remained crowded with militias despite the formal end of the war, and the embargo was leaking.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council asked the Secretary-General to re-establish the Group of Experts within thirty days, this time running until 31 July 2006. The group had to keep applying the mandate set in earlier resolutions, brief the sanctions committee by 10 April, and file a written report before 10 July. All parties and states were again told to grant its members safety and immediate, unhindered access.

Direct talks between Morocco and the POLISARIO Front on Western Sahara are called for on 30 April 2007. Both sides had just sent the Secretary-General rival proposals, Morocco's in April backed as serious and credible efforts. The long impasse over the territory's future was, for the first time in years, met with a negotiating push.

The parties are called on to enter negotiations without preconditions and in good faith. The goal stays a just, lasting, and mutually acceptable political solution providing for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara. The Secretary-General is asked to host the talks under his auspices, with member states lending help, and to report on their progress by 30 June 2007. MINURSO's mandate is renewed alongside the call.

Liberia's last sanctions are renewed again by Resolution 1854, adopted on 19 December 2008. Timber and diamond measures had already ended, and Liberia was applying Kimberley Process controls and taking part in revenue-transparency initiatives. The Panel of Experts still found too little progress toward the conditions for lifting the arms and travel measures, and none on the asset freeze.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and travel ban for 12 months, with the standing exemptions for vetted Liberian security forces. Notice to the Sanctions Committee is required on delivery. The asset freeze under Resolution 1532 (2004) remains, and the Committee must update the public reasons for each listing. The Panel of Experts is extended to 20 December 2009. It must report midway by 1 June 2009. Its work is to check compliance, judge the forestry law and Kimberley controls, and help keep the listing reasons current.

Resolution 1954, adopted on 14 December 2010, lets Yugoslavia tribunal judges stay past their terms to finish their trials. The tribunal's own completion reports admitted it could not finish all work in 2010, the target set years before. Its president also warned that experienced staff were leaving, threatening the remaining cases.

The Council extended the terms of the judges concerned, so trials and appeals already under way would not collapse for want of a bench. It urged the tribunal to complete its work as fast as possible. The extensions were practical housekeeping with real stakes: war crimes trials for the Balkan wars of the 1990s depended on continuity among the judges hearing them.

The Rwanda tribunal's final stretch is managed by Resolution 2054, adopted on 29 June 2012. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda had to finish work by 31 December 2014 and hand over to the Residual Mechanism, whose Rwanda branch would open on 1 July 2012. One judge was moving to the Appeals Chamber and five ad litem judges were leaving. Staff losses and homes for acquitted persons remained problems.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets three trial judges whose terms expire on 30 June 2012 stay until 31 December 2012 to finish the trial they had begun. It extends the tribunal President's term to 31 December 2014 so the court's work can be completed, with a review in June 2013. The tribunal must report its plan for shifting functions to the Mechanism. States are urged to help arrest and surrender all remaining fugitives and to accept relocated acquitted persons.

Syria's civil war had brought years of suffering by the end of 2015, with no end in sight. On 18 December 2015 the Council adopted Resolution 2254. It set out a road map for ending the war through politics rather than fighting. The plan built on the Geneva Communiqué of 2012. It also built on talks held in Vienna by an international support group.

The Council backed formal talks between Syria's government and the opposition. The talks were to start in early January 2016, under United Nations guidance. Within six months, the process had to set up a credible and inclusive form of government. A timetable for writing a new constitution was part of that step. Free elections under United Nations supervision were to follow within eighteen months. A nationwide cease-fire was to move forward alongside the talks.

By mid-1968, Cyprus renewals had become a New York routine. On 18 June, the Council adopted Resolution 254 without dissent. The Secretary-General reported that the peace force was still needed. Cyprus agreed it should stay past March of that year.

The text restates the long chain of earlier Cyprus decisions. It urges the parties to seize what it calls a hopeful climate for a deal. It then extends the posting to 15 December 1968. One hope is spelled out at the end. Enough progress by then might let the force shrink or go home. That hope came back, unmet, for years.

Cyprus broke into war in July 1974, after a coup and a Turkish military intervention on the island. Resolution 354 was adopted unanimously on 23 July 1974, three days after an earlier cease-fire call. The short text reaffirms Resolution 353 of 20 July in full. It demands that all parties to the fighting obey that call at once. All firing in the area had to stop immediately. All states were asked to show the utmost restraint and to take no action that might make the situation worse.

South Africa's raids into Angola are condemned in Resolution 454. It passed on 2 November 1979. Twelve members backed it, and three did not vote either way. Angola had sent a formal plea and a note from its ruling party, the MPLA. Two past texts had condemned South Africa's attacks on Angola. They had told it to respect Angola's freedom and its borders.

The new strikes are called planned and steady. They hit Angola's air space and its soil. Their timing, the Council said, aimed to block peace deals in the south of Africa, above all the 1978 Namibia plan. The text mourns the lives lost and the homes and goods wrecked by the raids.

The truce in Palestine broke down in July 1948, and the Council hardened its line. Israel had accepted a longer truce in principle. The states of the Arab League had rejected repeated appeals from the United Nations mediator and from the Council itself. Resolution 54 was adopted on 15 July 1948.

The Council determined that the situation in Palestine was a threat to the peace, under Article 39 of the Charter. The governments and authorities involved were ordered to stop military action. They had to issue cease-fire orders by a time set by the mediator. Refusal would count as a breach of the peace. For Jerusalem, an immediate and unconditional cease-fire was ordered within twenty-four hours. The mediator had to supervise the truce, examine alleged breaches, and keep working toward the demilitarization of the city.

Slovenia's smooth exit from Yugoslavia contrasts with the war around it in 1992. On 18 May, the Council adopted Resolution 754 without a vote. The Republic of Slovenia had claimed freedom the June before. It had survived a ten-day war at that time. Wide recognition came in January 1992. It was the first Yugoslav republic to firm up its statehood.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Slovenia. It was seated days later, with Croatia and Bosnia beside it. The calm of its entry stood out sharply. Bosnia was sliding into chaos at that same moment. Slovenia's path marked Yugoslavia's least violent break.
versuch-physicalisch-chymischer-lehrbegr: Versuch physicalisch-chymischer Lehrbegriffe, 1754. The German chemical essay. This book preserves that alchemy. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
zoist-vol-12-1854:
April 1854 to January 1855 fills the twelfth volume of The Zoist. Elliotson's long campaign for mesmerism nears its end in print. Reports still come in: cures under trance, operations without pain, and clairvoyant cases. Cerebral physiology holds its place beside the mesmeric record.

Britain is at war in the Crimea as these pages appear. The journal's world of provincial practice goes on regardless. Thirteen volumes, from 1843 to 1856, would complete the set. Volume twelve is the last full year but one. Its value lies in the unbroken chain of cases. Together the volumes let readers judge the movement from inside.
